en: Now begins the Uṇādi-kosha.
[Then the commencement of the first pāda:
The suffix *uṇ* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *vā*, *pā*, *ji*, *mi*, *svad*, *sādh*, and *śū*. (Uṇādi-sūtra 1)
The artisan; the wind; the protector; the one who conquers; the one who measures; the sweet; the virtuous; the swift; the swift. ||1||

1. He who acts is a *kāru*: a maker or an artisan. He who blows, moves, or knows is *vāyu*: the wind, the purifier, or the Supreme Lord. He who protects is *pāyu*: a protector or the anal organ. He who conquers, overcomes, or subdues enemies is *jāyu*: a fever; or he who conquers swellings, i.e., diseases, is *jāyu*: a medicine or a physician. He who measures or casts forth is *māyu*: [a measure]; or he who measures and casts forth heat is *māyu*: bile (*pitta*).

A jackal is called *gomāyu* because it makes a distorted sound like a cow (*gām vikṛtāṃ vācaṃ minoti*). That which is tasted—that is, desired to be eaten—is *svādu*, meaning palatable food or sustenance. A virtuous person is called *sādhu* because they accomplish righteous action (*sādhnoti dharmyaṃ karma*). It is *tṛprāśu* because it spreads or pervades (*tṛpraśnute vyāpnoti*), meaning "quickly"; or alternatively, it is *tṛprāśu* because it traverses a path immediately (*tṛpraśnute sadyo'dhvānam*), referring to a swift horse. Or, it is *āśu* because it is consumed quickly (*āśyate bhujyate āśu*), referring to fast-ripening grain such as rice (*vrīhi*).

From the use of the suffix *bahulac*: "he bathes" (or "cleanses his limbs"), thus *snāyu* means either a sinew or a channel (*nāḍī*). That by which one becomes *kakka*, i.e., greedy or fickle, is *kāku*; it refers to fear and the like, or a modification of sound (*dhvani*). That by which food is *halyate*, i.e., cut or chewed, is *hālu*, meaning a tooth. He in whom the world dwells, or who dwells in all things, is *vāsu*, namely the Lord (*īśvara*), and so forth.
In the Vedic language (chandas), [the suffix] iṇaḥ [is applied]. ||2||
Life-span. ||2||

2. According to the Veda, from the root *iṇ* (to go), the suffix *uṇ* is applied; thus, "one who goes to" or "attains all" is *trpāyuḥ*, meaning the duration of life. However, the form ending in *-sānt-* will be explained in the second chapter.
The suffix *ñuṇ* is added after the verbal roots *dṛś*, *nij*, *car*, *caṭ*, and *rahi*.
dāru, sānu, jānu, cāru, cāṭu, rāhu. ||3||

3. That which is split or broken is *dāru*, meaning wood or timber. One who gathers (*sanati*), divides (*sambhajati*), acquires (*sanoti*), or gives (*dadāti*) is *sānu*; or *sānu* refers to a portion of a mountain, a peak, a summit, a path, a whirlwind, a leaf, or a forest. From this [root *jan*] it is born, hence *jānu*, the upper part of the shank. Although the rule *janivadhyośca* [Pāṇini 7.3.35] prohibits *vṛddhi*, the *vṛddhi* occurs here by virtue of the two indicatory letters (*anubandha*). That which moves among the eyes and other senses is *cāru*, meaning beautiful. That which splits or breaks is *cāṭu*, meaning a pleasing word. One who leaves behind or abandons faults is *rāhu*, or a particular planet.
4. After the roots *ki*, *jari*, and *śri*, [the suffix *na* is applied]. 4.
The awn of grain; the afterbirth. 4.

4. That by which something is shattered is *kiṃśāru*, or it refers to a specific type of grain. That which reaches the state of being worn out (*jarā*) is *jarāyu*, meaning either the fetal membrane or the birth canal.
The letter *la* is also [substituted] for *ra* and *tra*. ||5||

5. From the verbal root *tṛ*, with the suffix *ñuṇ*, there is the substitution of *l* for the *r*. That part of the mouth from which the phonemes emerge and pass out is the palate (*tālu*). [The word *tālu* is thus derived. 5.

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*): that which is honored or attained is *trprālu*, meaning edible food or a bulbous root; that which nourishes or cuts objects by its own heat is *bhālu*, meaning the sun; that which pierces or harms the mind is *śālu*, meaning an astringent substance, and so forth.
6. And who is it that speaks the word "kṛka"? 6.
The cock. ||6||
The suffix *ñuṇ* is applied after the verbal root *vac* when preceded by the word *kṛka*. Thus, one who speaks with a *kṛka* (throat) is a *kṛkavāku*, which refers to a partridge or a peacock.
The suffix *u* is applied after the verbal roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *śīṅ*, *tṝ*, *car*, *tṛ*, *tan*, *dhani*, *mi*, and *masji*.
bharuḥ, maruḥ, śayuḥ, taruḥ, caruḥ, tsaruḥ, tanuḥ, dhanuḥ, mayuḥ, madguḥ. ||7||

*Bharu* means a master (*svāmī*), as he supports (*bibharti*) or nourishes (*bharati*). *Maru* refers to a waterless region, as living beings die (*mriyante*) therein. *Śāyu* is one who lies down (*śete*), meaning one whose nature is to recline; or it is that by which one crosses over (*tarati*), namely a tree (*taru*). *Caru* is that which moves (*carati*) or is moved by fire, being consumed; it is the sacrificial oblation (*yajñapāka*). *Tsaru* is that which moves crookedly (*tsarati*), namely the hilt of a sword (*khaḍgamuṣṭi*). *Tanu* is that by which actions are stretched out (*tanyante*); it is the body (*śarīra*) or something minute (*svalpa*).

*Dhanuḥ* is that by which wealth (*dhana*) is obtained; it refers to either a treatise or a weapon. *Mayuḥ* is so called because it emits (*minoti*) a beautiful sound; it refers to a monkey. *Madguḥ* is so called because it becomes purified (*majati*) or exists [therein]; it refers to a water-fowl. The substitution of *k* for *g* occurs according to Pāṇini 7.3.53 (*nyaṅkv-ādibhyaḥ kuḥ*).
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), *gaṇḍuḥ* is derived from *gaṇḍati*; it refers to a part of the face, or to a pillow—commonly known as a *takiyā*—or to oil.
8.a. And [the substitution of] *aṇ* [occurs]. ||8||
The atom. ||8||

8. It is called *aṇu* because it sounds (*aṇati śabdayati*) or because it is extremely subtle (*atisūkṣma*). 9. [The suffix *u*] occurs after the root *dhā* when followed by the word *dhānya*. 9. [Sūtra 9.]

Here, by virtue of including the letter *ca*, [the suffix *u*] forms *kaṭuḥ*, meaning "that which causes transformation" (*kaṭati* / *vikārayati*), i.e., a pungent taste; or *vaṭuḥ*, meaning "one who distributes qualities and actions" (*vaṭati* / *vibhajati*), i.e., a young brahmin.
The atoms [are eternal]. ||9||

9. *Trp* means those by which atoms or specific kinds of food are made to resound or produce sound; the addition of the suffix *ni* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
10. And [the suffix *kvasu* is applied] after the roots *śru*, *sṛ*, *snih*, *trap*, *yas*, *vas*, *sih*, *niklid*, *bandh*, and *man*.
aruḥ, svaruḥ, snehuḥ, trapu, asuḥ, vasu, hanuḥ, kleduḥ, bandhuḥ, manuḥ. ||10||

10. Here, the suffix *u* is connected with the augment *niṭ*; it is for this very purpose that it is listed separately. That by which one pierces or strikes is *śaru*: a weapon or anger. That by which living beings suffer or are tormented is *svaru*: the thunderbolt (*vajra*). That in which one becomes moist is *snehu*: a disease or the like. That which, having reached fire, shrinks as if ashamed is *trapu*: tin, lead, or mercury. That which casts forth or emits the vital air (*vāyu*) is *trprasu*: the life-breath (*prāṇa*).

*Asura*: A cloud, so called because it gives (*rāti*) or bestows (*dadāti*) life-force (*prāṇa*) three times (*tri*). *Vasu*: That by which one is clothed (*vas-te*) or covered; that which is a source of happiness (*vasu*); or a forest (*vana*). The eight Vasus, such as Agni and others, are those in whom living beings reside (*vasanti*). *Hanu*: That by which one strikes (*hanyate*); a part of the jaw, a weapon, or death. *Kledu*: That which moistens or makes the heart wet; the moon. *Bandhu*: One who binds through affection; a kinsman. *Īśvara*: The Lord, so called because he contemplates (*manyate*) and knows the world of moving and unmoving things.
*Manu*: A wise royal sage, so called because he reflects upon and understands the scriptures (*manute*).

From the use of the word "bahula" (variously): it is called *bindu* because it is found (*vindati*) or because it becomes a part (*avayavībhavati*); it refers to a measure or a drop of water and so forth.
[Uṇādi Sūtra 1.11: From the root *syand*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the substitution of *dha*.
The Sindhu. ||11||
11. *Sindhu* is that in which waters flow and stream forth. 12. [The suffix *u* is applied after a root beginning with a vowel, and the initial vowel is replaced by *i*. ||12||
The Moon. ||12||
12. From the verbal root *und*, the suffix *u* is applied, and the initial letter is replaced by *i*. Since it moistens (*unatti*) or makes things wet, it is called *indu*, meaning the moon.
13. The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *īṣ*, and it is also *kit*.

13. Here, the words "ca" (and) and "it" (the suffix *it*) are understood from the previous rule; therefore, a short vowel replaces a long one. [The root] *iṣ* means "he desires," "he goes," or "he destroys enemies"; thus, *iṣuḥ* refers to an arrow or a hero. Due to the *kit* designation [of the suffix], there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution.
The arrow. 13.
14. And there is the elision of the *s* in *skanda*.
Itching. ||14||
14. That by which one leaps, goes, or dries up is *kandu*; it is well known as a ball for the play of youths.
15. After the root *sṛj*, the suffix *asuN* is also applied.
Itching. ||15||

15. Here, from the previous sūtra, the phrase "there is elision of *s*" (*salopa*) is understood as a carry-over. An augment *asun* is added to the verbal root, and there is elision of the *s* of *trap-* and so forth. Furthermore, there is the substitution of a semivowel (*yaṇ*) for the *ṛ* sound, and the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaś*) for the *s* of the *trap-* augment. [The word *rajju*] means that by which water is drawn out; or, it means the act of lifting water.
16. And there is a reversal of the beginning and end of the creation.
The spindle. ||16||

16. There is a reversal of the initial and final [letters] according to the meaning: the letter *ta* is at the beginning and the letter *ka* is at the end, with *u* as the suffix. That by which one cuts or tears cloth and so forth is *tarku*, or it is *kartanī*.
17. Nor [is there a fault] if one does not wish [to do so]. ||17||
The antelope. ||17||
17. Those who cross over completely, go across, are the *nyaṅkavas*, a particular species of deer or antelopes.
18. And the phonemes of the *phalipāṭi* and *nimimani* are placed within the *gukpaṭi*. ||18||
kalguḥ, paṭuḥ, nākuḥ, madhuḥ, jatuḥ. ||18||

18. Before the suffix *upratyaya*, there is the augment *guṇa* for the root *phal*. That which bears fruit (*phalati*) or comes into being (*niṣpadyate*) is *phalgu*; or it is that which spreads (*trprasāra*). In the neuter, *phalgu* means "fruit. For the root *pāṭ*, there is the substitute *paṭi*. One who causes to split (*pāṭayati*) or makes known (*jñāpayati*) existent and non-existent categories is *paṭu*—that is, eloquent or wise. For the root *nam*, there is the substitute *nāki*. That which bends (*namati*) is *nāku*, meaning an anthill. For the root *man*, there is the substitute *dha*.

That in which they especially think—that is, know—is "Madhu," namely the month of Caitra; or "Madhūka," meaning liquor, honey, or the nectar of flowers. The substitution of the letter *t* occurs for the verbal root *jan* (to be born); thus, that by which one is born or manifested is "Jatu," meaning lac.
And [the rule] regarding the *balergu* [is also applied]. ||19||
Balguḥ || 19 ||
It is called *balgu* because it moves (*balate*) or breathes (*prāṇayati*); as a neuter noun, *balgu* means "beautiful."
20. [The suffix] śas is also kit and sanvat.
The child. ||20||

20. Due to the application of the *sanvadbhāva* rule, there is reduplication (*dvitva*) and so forth. [The word] *śiśuḥ* means a child or a young boy, one who "wears away" (*śyati*) or makes thin (*tanūkaroti*) the bodies of his parents.
21. And whoever [commits] two [offenses]. ||21||
They went. ||21||

21. Although the term *sanvat* is understood here by way of anuvṛtti (carrying over from a previous rule), the explicit mention of *dve* (the two) is for the purpose of preventing [the substitution of] *itva* (the shortening of the vowel) in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Thus, *yayuḥ* means "that by which they go" or "they reach another place," namely, a horse.
22. And [the word] *kurbhra* [is also used]. ||22||
22. Babhru. 22.

22. Here, the two [terms] "tr" and "pra" are understood to carry over. From the root *bhṛ*, the suffix *ku* is applied, along with reduplication (*dvitva*). Because he supports (*bibharti*) everything, he is called *babhru*—a mongoose, or one who is reddish-brown (*piṅgala*).

Due to the inclusion of the letter *ca* in the rule, the suffix *ku* is also applied after other roots, and their reduplication likewise occurs. For example: from *kṛ* (to do), *cakraḥ* (the doer); from *han* (to kill), *jaghnuḥ* (the killer); from *pā* (to protect), *papuḥ* (the protector), and so forth.
The suffix *kvanip* is applied after the roots *pṝ*, *bhid*, *vid*, *lī*, *dhyai*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *hṛṣ*.
puruḥ, bhiduḥ, vidhuḥ, gṛdhuḥ, dhṛṣuḥ, hṛṣuḥ. ||23||

23. From these [roots], the suffix *ku* is applied. He who carries across (*piparti*), protects (*pālayati*), or fills (*pūrayati*) is *puruḥ*, meaning "many" or "the senses. He who splits (*bhinatti*) is *bhiduḥ*, meaning "the thunderbolt" (*vajra*). He who pierces (*vidhyati*) foul odor or the day is *vidhuḥ*, meaning "camphor" or "the moon"; the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs according to Pāṇini 6.1.16, which applies to the root *vyadh*. That by which one is greedy (*gṛdhnoti*) or desires is *gṛdhuḥ*, meaning "desire. He who is bold (*dhṛṣṇoti*) or becomes confident is *dhṛṣuḥ*, meaning "skillful" (*dakṣa*). He who rejoices (*hṛṣyati*) is *hṛṣuḥ*, meaning "one who causes joy. In an alternative reading where the root is given as *dṛś*, it is *dṛśuḥ*, meaning "one who shows."
24. After the roots √kṛ (to do) and √gṛ (to seize), the augment u is inserted before the suffix NiC.
Kuru; Guru. 24.

He who acts or by whom [one is acted upon] is a *kuru*; the *kurus* are kings. He who recites, teaches, or imparts the knowledge of the Vedas and scriptures as well as proper conduct is a *guru*. Because he is the teacher of all, he is the Lord (*īśvara*), the preceptor (*ācārya*), or the father.
25. After *apa*, *duḥ*, and *su*, [the suffix] *stha* [is used]. 25.
apaṣṭhu, duṣṭhu, suṣṭhu. ||25||

When the words *trp*, *pra*, *duḥ*, and *su* are used as prefixes (*upapada*), the suffix *ku* is applied to the root *sthā*. *Trp pratiṣṭhati* (he stands improperly) becomes *trppraṣṭhu*, meaning the left side or an adverse thing. *Duṣṭhu* (he stands badly) means one who is censured or ill-behaved. *Sustiṣṭhati* (he stands well) becomes *suṣṭhu*, meaning beautiful or excellent. In all these cases, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by virtue of the rule *suṣāmādiṣu ca* (Pāṇini 8.3.98).
26. [The substitution of *u* occurs] for the final vowel of a word ending in *rap*, *ar*, or *ric*.
The enemy. ||26||

26. One who speaks ill—that is, speaks maliciously—is called a *ripu*, meaning an enemy (*śatru*). By the inclusion of the letter *ca* [in the rule], it is understood that when the suffix *kru* follows, only the substitution of *i* for the vowel is added.
27. Also *arji*, *dṛśi*, *kamya*, *miṃsa*, *bādha*, *mṛji*, *paśi*, *tuk*, *dhuk*, and those with a long *h* [are included]. 27.
Ṛjuḥ, paśuḥ, kantuḥ, andhuḥ, pāṃsuḥ, vāhuḥ. ||27||

27. When the suffix *kupratyaya* occurs, the bases *ṛji*, etc., undergo changes such as becoming *ṛju*, etc. One who acquires or accumulates virtues is *ṛju*; or it means "gentle. That by which one sees everything is *paśu*; or that which sees is *paśu*, namely the sacrificial fire (*trpragni*). One who sees or knows its own purpose is *paśu*, namely cattle and so forth. From the root *kam*, there is the suffix *tuk*: that which they desire is *kantu* or *kāma*. From the root *am*, there is the suffix *dhuk*: that which moves, causes pain, or goes is *andhu*, namely a well (*kūpa*).

In this sūtra, because of the inclusion of the letter *ca* or by virtue of the term *bahulam*, the augment *vuñ* also occurs after the root *am*. That by which living beings move (*pramanti*), go, and exert themselves is *trapu*, meaning water. That which makes things appear as if destroyed is *pāṃsu*, meaning dust; [this is derived from] the root *paṃs* with a long vowel. The word *pāṃśu*—ending in a palatal (*tālavya*)—is also seen in the sense of cow-dung collected over a long period for the purpose of a field, and so forth.
Those two by which objects are struck or stirred are the *bāhū*, the arms; this word generally ends in the dual number.
28. There is vocalization (samprasāraṇa) of the vowels in the roots prathi, mṛdi, and bhrasj, as well as the elision of the suffixal *s*.
Pṛthu, Mṛdu, Bhṛgu. ||28||

The suffix *ku* is applied after the roots *prath* and others; when this suffix is present, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the vowels in *prath* and *mrad*, as well as the elision of the letter *s*. One who spreads out is *pṛthu*: a particular king, one who is extensive, or a vast object. One who softens or is capable of being softened is *mṛdu*: intoxicating or tender. One who scorches the body through asceticism is *bhṛgu*: a seer (*ṛṣi*) or one possessed of splendor. The substitution of *k* for *g* occurs because these words belong to the *nyaṅkvādi* group (Pāṇini 7.3.53).

The suffix *saṃ* is applied after the roots *kṛt* (to praise) and *khyā* (to proclaim), and it causes the elision of the nasal (*n*) of the root *pṛthu*. Thus, *pṛthusam* refers to a specific king renowned as Pṛthu, or a well-known object.
29. *laṅdhibaṃhyornalopaśca* || 29 || [The suffix *saṃ* is applied after the roots *laṅgh* (to leap) and *baṃh* (to increase), and there is also the elision of the nasal. 29.
Small; large. ||29||

29. After the roots *laṅgh* and *bahi*, the suffix *ku* is added, and there is the elision of the letter *n*. [Thus,] one who is able to leap or go is called *laghu*. 30. After the root *ūrṇu*, the suffix *ku* is added, and there is the elision of the letter *n*. (30)
The Wide One. ||30||
30. That which covers or conceals is *ūru*, meaning the thigh or shank; the suffix *ku* causes the elision of the initial portion [of the root].
31. And the long [vowel] becomes short. 31.
Wide ||31||

31. From the root *ūrṇu*, the suffix *ku* is applied; in that formation, there is the elision of the *nu* portion and the shortening of the vowel *ū*. Because it covers (*ūrṇoti*) or conceals small things, it is called *uru*, meaning "great."
32. And [the suffix] *ka* is substituted for [the root] *śliṣ*.
Ślikuḥ. ||32||
32. That which clings to and is connected with objects is *śliṣku*; it is dependent on others, or it is luminous.
33. After the prefixes āṅ and pari, the roots khan and śṛ take the suffix ḍi, and [the augment] ṭi is also applied.
An axe; an adze. ||33||

33. That which digs the earth on all sides is a *trprākhu*—namely, a mouse or a boar. That by which one shatters (*śrṇāti*) or destroys enemies (*parān śatrūn*) is a *paraśu*, a type of weapon, such as an axe (*kuṭhāra*). Due to the rule [Pāṇini 6.3.109] beginning with *pṛṣodarādi*, when the syllable *tra* is elided, the word *parśu* is also seen with the same original meaning.
The *druva* [verse] belongs to Hari and Mitra. ||34||
Haridru; Mitadru. ||34||

*Haridra* is so called because it moves with a deer or a horse; alternatively, it refers to *dāruharidrā*. *Mitadru* is so called because it flows in measured or limited amounts, or because its movement is beautiful.
And in the [thirty-fifth] hundred [year], 35.35.
Śatadruḥ || 35 ||
35. It flows in a hundred ways, in many forms; thus it is the Śatadru, a particular river or the Gaṅgā.

In this context, by virtue of the rule of general application (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *ku* is seen to be added even to the root *dru* alone. That which living beings run toward for the sake of their purpose—that is, that which they reach—is *dru*, meaning a tree or a branch. A tree is called *druma* because branches (*dravaḥ*) exist in it; the suffix *ma*, expressing possession (*matvarthīya*), is applied according to the rule [Pāṇini 5.2.108]: "The suffix *ma* is added after *dyu* and *dru*."
36. *Kharu*, *śaṅku*, *pīyu*, *nīla*, and *aṅguli*. 36.

36. Words such as *kharu* and others are derived as irregular forms (*nipātita*) ending in the suffix *ku*. From the root *khan*, the suffix *ku* is applied, and the *na* is replaced by *ra*. Because one digs (*khanati*) the body [with it], *kharu* means desire, a tooth, a destroyer, pride, or a horse. In the sense of "white," however, it functions like an adjective: for example, "this Brāhmaṇī woman is *kharu* (fair)," "the family is *kharu* (pure)," or "the man is *kharu* (handsome). That which, when seen, causes one to hesitate or become doubtful is *śaṅku*; it may mean poison, a wedge, a weapon, a number, a species of tree, a type of water, sin, or a post.

One who drinks or protects is *pīyuḥ*, meaning either time (*kāla*) or a crow (*kāka*). When the suffix *ku* is applied, the root vowel undergoes the substitution of *ī* and the augment *yuk* is added. That which moves or goes excessively is *nīlaṅguḥ*, referring to a species of worm, a bee, or a flower. When the suffix *ku* is applied, the preceding prefix (*upasarga*) is lengthened. That to which everything clings or adheres is *ligu*, meaning either the mind (*citta*) or the act of clinging; in this case, the penultimate vowel of the root *lage* becomes *i*.

By virtue of the rule of diversity (bāhulaka): "He is lame" (khañjati), meaning he becomes crippled in his gait; thus, *paṅgu* means one who is devoid of movement. With the suffix *kupratyaya*, there is the substitution of *paṅg* for the root *khañ*. That which destroys other odors by its own odor is *hiṅgu*, a commodity for merchants.
37. And [the groups] beginning with hunters. 37.
mṛgayuḥ, devayuḥ, mitrayuḥ. ||37||

37. Words such as *mṛgayu* and others are derived by the application of the suffix *ku*. When these words—*mṛga*, *deva*, *mitra*, *kumāra*, and *adhvara*—are used as upapadas (prepositions), the suffix *ku* is applied to the root *yā* (meaning "to go" or "to reach"). One who goes to or reaches the deer (*mṛga*) is a *mṛgayu*, namely a hunter. One who goes to the gods (*deva*), that is, to the learned, is a *devayu*, namely a righteous person. One who goes to friends (*mitra*) is a *mitrayu*, namely one who understands worldly affairs. One who goes to the state of childhood (*kumāra*) is a *kumārayu*, namely a prince. One who goes to the sacrifice (*adhvara*) is an *adhvaryu*, namely a priest. [In this last case], there is also the elision of the final syllable of *adhvara*.

From the rule regarding the suffix *ku*: it causes wonder (*kohayati*) or astonishes (*vismāpayati*), thus it is *kuhu*; that day on which the moon is not seen is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) or *kuhū*. It moves (*paṇḍati*) or goes, thus it is *pāṇḍu*, a particular color or a particular king. It swells (*pīlati*), supports, or obstructs living beings, thus it is *pīlu*, an elephant, a tree, or an atom (*kāṇu*). *Kāṇu* refers to atoms or flowers. *Mañji* is a root from the *Sautra* collection; from it comes *ku*. It gladdens (*mañjati*) the mind and purifies it, thus it is *mañju*, meaning beautiful.
In this same way, words such as *nighaṇṭu*, *palāṇḍu*, *karkareṭu*, *kareṭu*, *ḍamaru*, and so forth should also be understood here, because this [list] is an open-ended class (*prākṛtigaṇa*).
The suffix *urac* is applied after the verbal roots √mandi, √vāśi, √mathi, √cati, √caṅku, and √aṅki.
Mandurā, vāśurā, mathurā, caturaḥ, aṅkuraḥ. ||38||

38. That in which one praises or becomes intoxicated is *mandurā*, meaning a stable for horses or a stall. That which cries out or makes a sound is *vāśurā*, meaning the night. That which churns or agitates is *mathurā*, meaning a city. He who asks or entreats is *caturaḥ*, meaning clever or skillful. *Caṅk* is a Vedic root; that by which one moves about or wanders everywhere is *caṅkuraḥ*, meaning a chariot. That which is marked, characterized, or seen as having emerged is *traṅkuraḥ*, meaning the production of seeds.
In this context, by adding the suffix *ūra* to the group of words beginning with *kharjūra* that will be mentioned later, one also obtains *trapuṅkūra*; the meaning remains the same.
39. There is vocalization (samprasāraṇa) of the root *vyath*, and the suffix *dha* is also applied as *k*.
Vidhura || 39 ||

That from which one trembles and fears is *vidhura*, meaning either extreme separation (*atyantaviyoga*) or the abandonment of the body. In the case of *saṃprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution), the suffix *kit* is used to prohibit *guṇa*. Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the letter *tha* does not become *dha*; thus, the form *vithura* is also established. Furthermore, *vithura* means a thief or a wicked person.
40. Makura and Dardura. ||40||

[The words *makura* and *dardura* || 40 ||] 40. The words *makura* and *dardura* are irregularly formed (nipātita) by means of the suffix *urac*. That by which one adorns (*maṅkate*) or embellishes is *makura*, namely a mirror (*darpaṇa*). Through the elision of the nasal of the root *maṅk*, and by the substitution of *u* for the vowel *a* of the root due to the diversity of the rule (*bāhulaka*), the form *mukura*—also meaning a mirror—is likewise established. It pierces (*dṛṇāti*) or splits apart the heat; thus it is *dardura*: a cloud, a frog, a type of musical instrument, or a type of mountain. By means of the suffix *urac*, the reduplication of the root *dṛ*, the augment *ruk* after the reduplicated syllable, and the elision of the final *ṛ* of the root are irregularly prescribed.
And the madgura fish and others [are also included]. 41.
madguraḥ, karburaḥ, bandhuraḥ, [cikurāḥ], kukkuraḥ; kukuraḥ. ||41||

41. Words such as *madgura* and others ending in the suffix *-urac* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). That which intoxicates or rejoices is a *madgura*, a specific kind of fish; there is the addition of the *guṇa* vowel to the root. That which becomes variegated in color is *karbura*; it is white and spotted.

Or [it is derived from] the root *dhā* with the augment *umā*. That which binds by means of softness is *bandhura*, meaning "pliant" or "beautiful. From the roots *khajūra* and others, with the suffix *rūpa*, *bandhūra* has the same meaning as stated. Those which one gathers (*cinvanti*) or unifies are *cikurāḥ*; here, the augment *ku* is added to the root. Because it takes the object of another word (*parapadārtha*) after the root *kuk*, it is *kukkuraḥ*; *kukkuraḥ* and *śvā* (dog) have the same meaning. In the alternative view, the augment *ku* is applied as a nipātana.

*Trp*: Because it moves (*atati*) without interruption, it goes; thus *trprātura* means one who is unpeaceful. There is a lengthening of the vowel at the beginning of the root. *Vāgurā*: that by which deer are driven (*vānti*) or reached; it is a snare for binding deer, a net for the purpose of capturing deer. In this case, the guṇa-vowel substitution for the root is prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). *Śakula*: that which is able to cross over (*taritum*); it is a fish. *Vakula*: that which bends (*vaṅkate*), becomes crooked; it is a particular kind of tree. In both these cases, the letter *l* replaces the *r* of the suffix, and there is the elision of the *n* of the root *vaṅk*.
42. They were not born from eggs. 42.
The three [are] the Asuras. ||42||

The prefix *pra-* (in *prāsuraḥ*) means "he casts away" or "he scatters," referring to the Dharma and virtuous qualities; it refers either to a cloud or to a wicked person and the like. The prefix is used here for the purpose of the acute accent (*ādyudātta*) on the initial syllable.
And [the rule applies] to the word *māsa* as well. ||43||
Masūra lentils. ||43||

They swell and transform well; these are the specific varieties of *masura* (lentils). Furthermore, in this very fifth quarter [of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*], the form *masūra* is also established by adding the suffix *ūran* to the root *mas*. These two words have the same meaning. Among split pulses (*dvidalānna*), the term *masūra* is well known.
44. [The suffix] śas occurs in the sense of attainment. 44.
Father-in-law. ||44||

44. When the word *śu*, signifying "quickly," is used as a prefix (*upapada*), and the sense of "attaining" (*trp*) is implied, the suffix *uran* is added to the root *aśūṅ*. Thus, *śvaśuraḥ* is derived: he who quickly attains (*aśnute*) the daughter-in-law (*trp*) is the father-in-law (*śvaśuraḥ*), the father of the husband and wife.
The suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied after the words *avimat* and *mahat*.
The poisonless one; the buffalo. 45.

The ocean into which the rivers of Avanti flow is the *trpaviṣa* (the one that satisfies). One who honors greatly through his own human effort is a *mahiṣa*, meaning either a great king or a buffalo; by association with him, a *mahiṣī* is either a queen or a specific type of animal. A river is a *trpaviṣī* because it satisfies (*trp*) living beings.
46. And [the vowel] *am* is long.
Material wealth. ||46||
46. *Tiṣat*: that by which they go toward or consume is *tiṣprāmiṣa*, meaning meat; or, that which, when eaten, causes those who eat it to become sick is *āmiṣa*—these are synonymous.
And there is growth for one who has taken root. ||47||
Rohiṣa. ||47||
47. *Ṭiṣac*: Those grasses which grow or arise are called *rauhiṣa* grasses; or alternatively, *rauhiṣa* refers to a species of deer.
48. Tava-ṇidvā ||48||
The powers; the powers. 48.

The verbal root *tavi* is a Vedic (sautra) root; from it, the suffix *tiṣac* is applied optionally with the *ṇit* augment. Thus, *tavatī* becomes *tāviṣī*; *taviṣī* refers to a river, strength, an army, or the earth.
49. [The suffix *nañ* is applied] after the root *vyath* in the sense of "not. ||49||
The unshakable ones. ||49||
"He does not tremble" refers to the ocean or the sun; "she trembles" refers to the earth or the night.
And [the word] *kila* is also [a particle]. (50)
Sinful one. 50.
That by which one plays and sports through the dullness of discursive thought (*vicāra*) and engages in worldly activities—that is *kilbiṣa*, meaning evil or sin.
The suffix *kirac* is added after the verbal roots √iṣ, √mad, √di, √khid, √chid, √bhid, √madi, √candi, √tim, √mi, √hi, √muhi, √muci, √ruc, √ruj, √bandh, and √śuṣ.
iṣiraḥ, madiraḥ, mudiraḥ, khidiraḥ, chidiraḥ, bhidiram, mandiram, candiram, timiram, mihiraḥ, muhiraḥ, muciraḥ, ruciram, rudhiram, badhiraḥ, śuṣiram. ||51||

51. From the roots *iṣ* and others, the suffix *kirac* is applied after sixteen roots. That by which one desires or accomplishes what is desired (*iṣṭa*) is *iṣiraḥ*, meaning "the fire" (*trpagniḥ*). That by which one becomes intoxicated (*mādyati*) or exhilarated is *madirā*, meaning wine, liquor, or intoxicant. He who rejoices is *mudiraḥ*, meaning a lover; or that by which they rejoice is *mudiraḥ*, meaning a cloud. That by which one suffers (*khidyati*) is *khidiraḥ*, meaning the moon. That by which one cuts is *chidiraḥ*, meaning a sword or an axe. That by which one splits is *bhidiram*, meaning a thunderbolt.

That in which people rejoice, praise, or sleep is a *mandira*, a house, or a city. That by which one shines or is delighted is *candira*, meaning the moon or an elephant. That in which one becomes moistened is *timira*, meaning darkness or an eye disease. He who sprinkles or waters the earth with the water of clouds is *mihira*, meaning the sun. That for whom one is deluded, or he who is deluded, is *muhira*, meaning a desirable object or an uncivilized person.

He who releases his own wealth and gives it to others is *muciraḥ*, meaning one whose nature is giving (*dānaśīla*). That which is pleasing and causes delight is *ruciram*, meaning beautiful; for example, a beautiful garment (*ruciraṃ vastram*), a beautiful son (*ruciraḥ putraḥ*), or a beautiful daughter (*rucirā kanyā*). That which is obstructed by skin is *rudhiram*, meaning blood (*śoṇitam*). He who is bound—that is, rendered incapable of hearing sounds—is *badhiraḥ*, meaning one deficient in hearing. Due to the suffix *kit* in the root *kṛt* (from which *badhira* is derived), there is the elision of the nasal according to Pāṇini 6.4.24 (*nṛtpraniditām*). That by which objects dry up is *śuṣiram*, meaning a hole or space (*chidram ākāśo vā*).
52. He has sat down. 52.
Without a head. ||52||
He who eats things with a sharp tongue is "Trpśiras" (Sharp-headed) or "Trpagni" (Sharp-fire); or rather, the wicked man is "Aśiras" (Headless), for he eats by means of his clamorous speech.
53. *ajira*, *śiśira*, *śithila*, *sthira*, *sphira*, *sthavira*, and *khadira*.

53. *Ajira* and seven others ending in the suffix *kirac* are irregularly formed (*nipātita*). That in which people move about or go is *trp-kiraja*, namely *trp-ajiram*; it refers to a courtyard (*trp-aṅgana*), specifically the front part of a house. This is well known as *trpāṅgana*. That which moves quickly because the days are short is *śiśira*; it refers to the season, snow, or any cool thing. That which slackens or abandons human effort is *śithila*; thus, a *śithila* man, a *śithila* girl, or *śithila* grasses mean things that are soft.

The substitution of *i* for the vowel of the root, the elision of the *r*, and the substitution of *l* for the *r* situated in the suffix are prescribed as irregularities (*nipātana*). That which stands by means of the cessation of coming and going is "firm" (*sthira*), meaning motionless. There is the elision of the letter *ā* from the root. That which expands or increases is "vast" (*sphira*), or it refers to majesty. The elision of the portion beginning with *ā* is an irregularity. Because one is unable to move, one "stands"—thus "aged" (*sthavira*), meaning an old man or a mendicant. The suffix *vuk* is added to the root and there is shortening of the vowel. That which strikes or injures is "khadira," a species of tree.

By virtue of the rule of general applicability (*bāhulaka*): that which lies down is *śivira*, or that place in which they lie down is *śivira*; [this is derived] from the root *śīṅ* with the suffix *vuK* and the shortening of the vowel.
The suffix *ilac* is applied after the verbal roots *sal*, *kali*, *nī*, *mahi*, *bhaḍi*, *bhaṇḍi*, *śaṇḍi*, *piṇḍi*, *tuṇḍi*, *kuki*, and *bhū*.
salila, kalila, anila, mahila, bhaḍila, bhaṇḍila, śaṇḍila, piṇḍila, tuṇḍila, kokila, bhavila. ||54||

54. *Ilac* is added after *salya* and others. That which moves or goes is *salila*, meaning water. That which counts or enumerates is *kalila*, meaning mixed, difficult to accomplish, or dense. That which breathes, lives, or causes to live is *trpranila*, meaning wind. That which is great, that which people honor, or that by which one is honored and worshipped, is *mahila*: a man, a place, or a woman. By adding *ilac* with the suffix *bāhuka*, and changing the vowel *i* to *e*, the form *mahelā* (woman) is also established.

*bhaḍ* is a verbal root found in the *sūtra*. One who *bhaḍati*, meaning "he injures," is *bhaḍilaḥ*, or else a hero. One who *bhaḍati*, meaning "he attends upon" his master, is *bhaḍilaḥ*; one who becomes possessed by disease is *śaṇḍilaḥ*, or a particular *ṛṣi* whose lineage-descendant is well known as *śāṇḍilya*. One who *piṇḍati*, meaning "he forms a mass," is *piṇḍilaḥ*, or an astrologer (*gaṇaka*). One who *tuṇḍati*, meaning "he pierces" or "he causes pain," is *tuṇḍilaḥ*, or a person with a protruding navel. He who *kokate*, meaning "he takes [food] greedily," is *kokilaḥ*, or a specific bird (*kokila*). He who *bhavati* is *bhavilaḥ*, or one fit to become.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (bāhulaka): he who performs crookedness (kauṭilya) is *kuṭila*, or he whose actions are cruel (*krūra*).
55. After the root *kam*, [the suffix *iṣ* is applied]. 55.
Kapila. ||55||
55. *Kamer ilac maḥ paḥ*. From the root *kam*, the suffix *ilac* is applied with the augment *maḥ paḥ*. He who desires is *kapila*; he is either a particular color or a specific sage.
56. The suffix *k* is added after the roots beginning with *gup*.
Gupilaḥ, Tijilaḥ, Guhilam. ||56||

56. The *kit* designation for the suffix *ilac* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*. One who protects (*gopāyati*) or guards (*rakṣati*) the subjects is a *gupila* king; or, one who sharpens (*teja-te*) or makes keen (*tīkṣṇī-karoti*), or who is sharpened (*tijyate*) and endured by all, is a *tijila* moon; or, that which hides (*gūhate*)—being concealed by trees—is a *guhila* forest.

Others also [derive from the suffix -ilac]: *pūjila* means one who is worthy of being honored or revered, i.e., a learned man (*vidvān*); *śuṣila* means that which dries up everything, i.e., the wind (*vāyu*); and *devila* means one who illuminates the Dharma, i.e., a righteous person (*dhārmika*).
57. And [the cities of] Mithilā and so forth. 57.
Mithilā||57||

57. Words such as *mithilā* and others are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) by taking the suffix *ilac*. That which is churned (*mathyate*) is *mithilā*; or, that place where enemies are crushed (*mathyante*) is *mithilā*, the city of the Videha kings. The substitution of *i* for the root vowel of the three types [of roots] is irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*). That which they go to or reach (*gacchanti/prāpnuvanti*) is *gatilā*, or it is a cane-stick (*vetralatā*). For the root *gam*, there is the substitution of the letter *t* at the end. That which lives with difficulty (*taṅkati*) is *tikalā*, or it is a medicinal herb (*trpoṣadhi*). There is the elision of the nasal (*nalopaḥ*). That which devours or eats (*camati*) is *caṇḍilā*, or it is a certain river.
The augment *ḍu* is added to the verbal root. One who recites or travels continuously is called *pathilaḥ* or *pathikaḥ*, and so forth.
The suffix *erak* is applied after the verbal roots *pati*, *kaṭhi*, *kuṭhi*, *gaḍi*, *guḍi*, and *daṃśi*.
pateraḥ, kaṭheraḥ, kuṭheraḥ, gaḍeraḥ, guḍeraḥ, daśeraḥ. ||58||

*Patera*: that which falls or goes; a traveler or a bird. *Kaṭhera*: one who lives with difficulty; a prison guard. *Kuṭhera*: likewise one who lives in hardship, or a leaf-eater (a type of ascetic); known as *kaṭahara*. *Gaḍera*: that which sprinkles or pours; a cloud. *Guḍera*: he who protects; a guardian. *Daśera*: that which bites with its fangs; a predator or a living being; [here] there is the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika*).
59. And there is also the elision of *kum* and *bha*. 59.
Kubera. ||59||

59. He is called Kubera because he "holds" (kumbati) others and "shelters" (ātacchādayati) them; he is the lord of wealth or the wise one. Since the root is marked with *idit*, the elision of the *n* (nalopa) does not occur [by Pāṇini 6.4.24], and it is prescribed that the suffix *erak* is applied.
And [the suffix] śatṛ is used after a root denoting desire. 60.śadestaśca||60||
Śateraḥ || 60 ||

60. It is called *śatera* or *śatru* because it causes one to fall (*śīyate*), cuts down (*śātayati*), or produces suffering (*duḥkhākaroti*); [in this derivation], there is a substitution of the letter *t* for the letter *d* of the verbal root.
61. *Mūla* and the others [are the names of constellations]. 61.
mūleraḥ, gudheraḥ, guheraḥ, muheraḥ. ||61||

61. Words such as *mūlera* and others are derived irregularly (*nipātyante*) by adding the suffix *erak*. One who acts as a root (*mūlati*), standing at the very top, is a *mūlera*, namely a sovereign or a king. One who encircles or surrounds on all sides (*gudhati*) is a *guvera*, namely a protector. That by which one hides (*gūhate*) is a *guhera*, namely an iron-smelter. One who becomes bewildered or distracted (*muhyati*) is a *muhera*, namely a fool. Alternatively, that by which a bull or similar animal is made to become bewildered (is bound) is a *muhera*, namely the head-harness for a bull used in threshing grain and other tasks; this very term *muhera* is well-known in the colloquial language (*bhāṣā*).
62. And after the *kaberoṭa* [there is another]. 62.
The pigeon. ||62||
The suffix *otac* changes the letter *va* to *pa*. Because it is called "variegated-colored" (*vicitravarṇa*), it is *kapota*, which refers to a species of bird.
The suffix *ḍavatup* is applied after the root *bhā*.
"O Venerable One, you shine, you are radiant, or you cause others to shine; this word is both a denoter of all nouns and is designated as a pronoun."
64. The suffix *a* is applied after the verbal roots *kaṭhi* and *caki*.
Hard; the cakora bird. ||64||
64. He who lives with difficulty is "kaṭhora" or "kaṭhina," meaning harsh or full; he who is satisfied by [even a little] is "cakora," a specific kind of bird.
65. And [the words] *kiśora* and so forth [are also included]. 65.
Kiśoraḥ; sahoraḥ. ||65||

65. Words such as *kiśora* and others are irregularly formed (*nipātana*) by adding the suffix *oran*. *Kiśora*: That which hears or destroys is a *kiśora*; it refers to a young animal or a calf. This is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) consisting of the elision of the *ma* of *kimaḥ* and the elision of the *ṛ* of the root *śṛ*. *Sahora*: One who has the habit of enduring, or one who is virtuous. *Gaura*: That which sings or makes sound is *gaura*. The term *tpraruṇaḥ* [is used] for white, pure, or stainless; it is a word whose gender varies according to its referent (*vācyaliṅga*). Examples include: *gauraḥ kumāraḥ* (a fair boy), *gaurī kanyā* (a fair girl), *gauraṃ kulam* (a fair family), *gauraṃ kamalam* (a white lotus), *gauraḥ sarṣapaḥ* (a white mustard seed), and so forth.

When the substitution of *ā* for the vowel of the root *gai* is applied, there is a single substitute (*ekādeśa*) by *vṛddhi* [of the preceding and following vowels] together with the suffix *trp*. However, the substitution of *trp* occurs only when the substitution of *āt* is not applicable.
The suffix *olac* is applied after the verbal roots *kapi*, *gaḍi*, *gaṇḍi*, *kaṭi*, and *paṭi*.
kapolaḥ, gaḍolaḥ, gaṇḍolaḥ, kaṭolaḥ, paṭolaḥ. ||66||

66. That which trembles or moves is *kapola*; the elision of the *n* occurs by virtue of the very rule (*sūtra*) itself. That which swells or pours is *gaḍola*. That which swells (*gaṇḍati*) is *gaṇḍola*, or it refers to a part of the face. *Gaḍola* and *gaṇḍola* are synonyms for *guḍa* (molasses). That which is harsh, rains, or covers is *kaṭola*, or it is *kaṭu* (pungent) and *ala* (moving). That which moves or goes is *paṭola*, whether a specific fruit or a specific garment.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), that which scratches or intoxicates is *kaṇḍola*, or it is *cāṇḍāla* (an outcaste).
67. After the root √mī, ūr is substituted [for the suffix na]. 67.
The peacock. ||67||

It is called *mayūra* because it "measures" (*mīnāti*) or "destroys" (*hanti*). It is a specific kind of bird. [The form is derived] from the verbal root with a substitution according to its class; by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*), there is a prohibition of the long vowel *ā* for the root *mī*.
68. And there is vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa) of the root syand.
Sindūra. ||68||
68. It flows or trickles; that *sindūra* is red powder or a type of tree, and so forth. With the suffix *-ura*, there is the attainment of the root [meaning].
The suffix *tuN* is applied after the verbal roots *si*, *tan*, *gam*, *mi*, *mā*, *sic*, *vyadh*, *añj*, and *kruś*.
Setu, tantu, gantu, mastu, saktu, otu, ghātu, kroṣṭu. ||69||

69. *Setu*: that which binds or ties; it refers to a bridge or the ocean. By the rule *titutratathasasisusara-ka-seṭi ca* [Pāṇini 7.2.9], the augment *iṭ* is prohibited. *Tantu*: that which extends or spreads; it refers to a thread or a cord. He who extends (*tanoti*) the most excellent knowledge (*varām uttamām vidyām*) is the *varatantu*, namely the sage Muni. The treatise taught by the *varatantu* is called the *vāratantavīya*. *Gantu*: one who goes; it refers to a traveler or a wayfarer. *Prāganta*: one who comes from all sides or wanders about; it refers to a guest. *Mastu*: that which matures or transforms; it refers to the water that has separated out from curd.

They are called *samavetāḥ* (assembled). They are made; they are *saktavaḥ*, or the powder of cooked barley and so forth. He who protects and performs such acts is a *trpotaḥ*; or it is a cat. By the rule *jvaratvara-* [Pāṇini 6.4.20], the augment *ūṭh* is applied to the penultimate vowel and the letter *v* of the root *ava*. That which holds, supports, or nourishes is a *dhātuḥ*; it is a modification (*vikāraḥ*) such as gold and the like, or the wind and other elements within the body. He who cries out, calls, or weeps is a *sakroṣṭuḥ*; he is a *kroṣṭā*, or a jackal.
70. [One should dwell] constantly in a dwelling place. ||70||
The site. ||70||
That place where they dwell is a site or a house; elsewhere than *trapu* and *gāra*, there is an absence of the *ṇit* designation. That substance or property by which they dwell is their possession.
71. [The suffix] *pa* is applied after a verbal root ending in a consonant. 71.
Of the father. ||71||

That which drinks water and the like, or protects—that is, guards—living beings is *pītuḥ*, such as fire or the sun; due to the *kittva* [designation of the suffix], there is the substitution of *ī* for *u*.
And [the suffix] *tu* is added after verbal roots ending in *ṛ*. (Pāṇini 3.1.72)
The season. ||72||
The suffix *tu* is *kit*. That which comes again and again, goes, or returns is called *ṛtu*; it refers to the seasons beginning with spring, or the time of the onset of menses in women.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the verbal roots √kam, √mi, √nij, √gam, √āy, and √hi.
*kantuḥ*, *mantuḥ*, *jantuḥ*, *gātuḥ*, *bhātuḥ*, *yātuḥ*, *hetuḥ* ||73||

That by which one desires is *kaṃtuḥ*, or it is *kāmaḥ* (desire), or it is the mind (*cittam*). That by which one thinks or knows is *mantuḥ*, or it is an offense (*trp- aparādhaḥ*). That which is born—that is, manifested through the maintenance of the body and so forth—is *jantuḥ*, or the living soul (*jīvaḥ*). That which sings or utters sounds such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth is *gātuḥ*, or a singer (*gāthakaḥ*). One who goes or moves is *gātuḥ*; this refers to a traveler, or a bee, or a gandharva. That which shines or illuminates is *bhātuḥ*; this refers to the sun (*sūryaḥ*). That which goes or causes to reach is *yātuḥ*; this refers to a traveler on a long road, or time (*kālaḥ*). That by which one impels, or that which increases in the form of an effect, is *hetuḥ*, or the cause (*kāraṇam*).
74. And [the word] cāyaḥ means "iron" (kī). 74.
The banner. ||74||
Whether one honors, worships, observes, or causes others to hear it, that is a banner, a planet, or a flag; it is a comet, a portentous omen.
75. And there is the shortening of the vowel in the root *āp*.
[The state] of one who has attained [it]. ||75||

The term *trprāptuḥ* refers to one who reaches (*prāpnoti*) or pervades (*vyāpnoti*) all objects; it denotes either the body or [the agent]. In the formation of this word, the suffix *tup* is applied to the root *trpṛ* (in the form *trpṛ-āplṛ*), resulting in the shortening of the vowel.
The suffix *kṛtṛ* is applied after the root *kṛ* (to do).
Sacrificial rite. ||76||

76. The suffix *kratu* is applied after the root *kṛ*. That which is performed or that by which one performs is called *kratu*, meaning either wisdom or sacrifice. Because it is marked with *k* (kit), there is *yaṇ*-substitution and the absence of *guṇa*.
And for the roots √edh and √vah, the substitution of *tu* occurs [in place of the suffix *liṭ*].
The roots *edh* and *vah* take the suffix *tu*. (77)

77. *edhatuḥ* means "he prospers" (*edhate*) or "he grows" (*vardhate*); it refers to a man or [the verb] *edhaduḥ*. *Vahatuḥ* means "one who carries a burden" (*vahati bhāram*), that is, a bull (*trp-anaḍvān*). The inclusion of the letter *c* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta (accented).
78. Life is the life-force. 78.
The life-sustainer. ||78||
That by which one lives, or that which lives, is *jīvātu*; it refers either to the means of living or to medicinal herbs.
79. Also, there is the suffix *ātṛc* and *vṛddhi*.
The physician. ||79||

79. From the verbal root *jīv*, the suffix *ātṛkan* is applied; when this suffix is present, a vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) also occurs. He who lives until the full span of life is called *jaivātṛka*, meaning long-lived, or the moon.

The suffix *ū* is applied after the verbal roots *kṛṣ* (to plough), *cit* (to collect), *mā* (to measure), *nidhā* (to deposit), *nisṛj* (to emit), and *kharj* (to scratch), when forming feminine nouns.
karpūḥ, camūḥ, tanūḥ, dhanūḥ, sarjūḥ, kharjūḥ. ||80||

80. The suffix *ū* is added after [roots such as] *kṛṣ* and others. One who draws or pulls objects is a *karṣū*: dried cow-dung, fire, or a river. One who drinks or consumes is a *camū*: an army that devours its enemies. That by which one extends actions is a *tanū*: the body. One who holds or acquires wealth is a *dhanū*: a weapon. One who emits or accomplishes tasks is a *sarjū*: a Vaiśya. One who scratches or causes irritation is a *kharjū*: an itch.
81. And there is *guṇa* substitution for the root *mṛj*.
The pure one. ||81||

The word *marjūḥ* means that which cleanses (*mārṣṭi*) or purifies (*śodhayati*). Although the suffix *-ū* is prescribed by rule (*nyākin*), and thus the *vṛddhi* substitution would have been obligatory, it is superseded by the *guṇa* substitution.
Or [the word] *khaḍerḍuḍ* [is used]. 82.
khaḍḍūḥ; khaḍuḥ || 82 ||
It is called *khaḍḍū* because it cuts or pierces; *khaḍḍū* refers either to an ornament for the arms and thighs or to a bed for the deceased.
And half of a *vaha*. 83.
The bride. ||83||
She is called *vadhū* because she carries [one] or brings about happiness; it refers either to a newly married woman or a wife.
84. Also after *kaṣ* and *cha*.
Scabies. ||84||
84. It is called *kacchū* because it scrapes (*kaṣati*), injures (*hinasti*), or causes pain (*duḥkhayati*). It is commonly known as *khāja*. The letter *ṣa* has been changed to *cha*.
85. The suffix *ṇit* is applied after the root *ṛt* when followed by the word *kaśipu*. 85.
*kāśūḥ*, *pādūḥ*, *trprārūḥ* ||85||

85. After the roots *kaṣ* and others, the suffix *ū* becomes *ṇit*. That which goes to or governs what is difficult (*kaṣṭa*) is *kāśūḥ*, meaning a person with defective limbs or strength. That by which people go or walk is *pādūḥ*, meaning sandals. He who reaches or attains is *trprārūḥ*, meaning tawny (*piṅgala*).
86. After the word *aṇ*, there is also the suffix *ḍa*.
Āḍūḥ || 86 ||
The word *trprāḍ* means "that which causes to sound" (*śabdayati*) from the root *trp*; or it refers to a substance that moves upon water. The substitution of *ḍ* for *ṇ* occurs here.
87. There is also the elision of the nasal.
The gourd. ||87||
87. When the suffix *ū* is applied, there is no elision of the *l* in the root *lamb*. That which does not hang down, does not flow, but moves, is called *trapulābū* or *tumbī*.
88. And [the suffix] *śra* is applied after *eraṅ*.
Kaśerū (the medicinal plant Kaśeruka). ||88||

The suffix *ū* is added to the root *śās* preceded by the prefix *kakāra*; in this formation, the root undergoes the substitution of *eṅ*. That which rules over what is difficult (*kaṣṭe śāsti*) is *kaśerūḥ*, a grass-root or a tuber. Due to the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*), when the suffix *ū* is shortened, the form *kaśeruḥ* ending in a short vowel is also observed.
89. And [the suffix] *tra* is also applied after a word ending in *du*. 89.
Tardūḥ || 89 ||
That by which or that with which one crosses is a *tardū*—either a man holding a wooden pole or a staff itself. The suffix *dū* is added to the root *tṛ* with the augment *duk*.
90. And there is the elision of *yā* after the root *dṛ* (to tear). 90.
Ringworm. ||90||

90. When the suffix *ū* is added to the root *daridra*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the phonemes *ri* and *tra*. Since one who suffers from poverty (*daridrāti*) undergoes a miserable state (*durgatiṃ karoti*), the term *dardrūḥ* refers to a type of leprosy (*kuṣṭhabheda*). Alternatively, by the rule of the *mṛgayvādi* group, through the elision of *ri* and *tra*, the form *dadrūḥ* is also established. Furthermore, in this very sūtra, when *ri* and *tra* are elided, the form *dadar* also occurs.
91. After the verbal roots *nṛt* (to dance) and *śudh* (to purify), the suffix *kū* is applied.
nṛtūḥ | śrṛdhūḥ ||91||

One who dances is *nṛtūḥ*, namely a dancer (*nartaka*). One who utters contemptible sounds is *śr̥dhūḥ*, or it refers to the wind that drinks moisture; because the suffix is marked with *k* (kit), there is a prohibition of *guṇa*.
92. And [the suffix] *am* follows the word *ṛte*.
The seasons. ||92||

92. *Ṛta* is a verbal root belonging to the *sautra* class. From the sense "he feels aversion" (*ṛtīyate*) or "he feels loathing" (*ghṛṇāṃ karoti*), the word *ratūḥ* is derived, meaning either truth or the celestial river; the augment *am* is added to the root.
93. Andūdṛmphujambūkaphelūkarkandhūdidhiṣūḥ || 93 ||

93. Words such as *trpandū* and others are derived by adding the suffix *ū*, and are treated as irregular forms (*nipātana*). That by which one binds or ties is *trpandū*; it is a chain for binding elephants, commonly known as *jaṃjīra*. It is called *dṛmphū* because it causes intense suffering; it is a species of serpent. That which they eat or consume is *jambu*; it is a specific species of tree. The augment *vuk* is added to the root, and by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *ū* is shortened, resulting in *jambu*.

It is also seen thus: *kāmayate* means "he desires" or "he is one who seizes the property of others. The suffix *vuk* is added to the root. *Kaphelūḥ* means "one who takes or receives phlegm (*kaphaṃ śleṣmāṇaṃ lāty ādadāti*)," or it is a specific medicinal herb. The form of the word *kapha* ending in *e* is due to a grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). *Karkandhūḥ* means "one who holds or bears thorns (*karkaṃ kaṇṭakaṃ dadhāti dharati*)," or it is the fruit of the jujube tree (*vadarīphala*). Due to the *kit* designation, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*; the addition of the augment *nuk* to the prefix is also due to irregularity. *Didhiṣūḥ* means "one who abandons steadfastness (*didhiṃ dhairyam*) because of weakness of the senses," or it is a remarried woman (*punarbhūḥ*). The change to the sibilant *ṣ* is due to irregularity.
The suffix *u* is applied after the roots *mṛ* and *gṛ*. (Pāṇini 3.2.161)
Marut-garut 94.
He dies or causes [others] to die; he is a mortal, belonging to the human race or to the state of existence (*bhavana*). He swallows or devours, thus he is *garut*, or a winged bird.
95. And [the suffix] *muṭ* [is applied]. 95.
Garmut || 95 ||
That by which one swallows is *garmut*, or it is a specific variety of golden grass.
96. After the root *hṛṣ*, the suffix *ulac* is applied [to form a noun denoting the instrument].
Harṣulaḥ ||96||
96. He who rejoices and becomes satisfied is *harṣulaḥ*; this refers either to a deer or to desire (*kāma*).
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), that which moves, rains, or covers is *caṭulaḥ*, or it means beautiful.
The suffix *iti* is applied after the verbal roots *hṛ*, *sṛ*, *ruh*, *yā*, and *vā*.
The green river, the ruddy woman. ||97||

*Trpṛ*: that which seizes or takes hold of a substance is *harit*, meaning a direction, a color, grass, or a particular kind of horse; that which flows or moves is *sarit*, meaning a river; that which grows or appears is *rohit*, meaning a specific type of creeper or a female deer (*hariṇī*). *Yuṣ* is a verbal root belonging to the Vedic (Sautra) tradition; alternatively, there is a reading with a phonetic modification from *juṣ*. That which is enjoyed, served, or gratified is *yoṣit*, meaning a woman.
98. And there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi* after the root *taḍ*.
Lightning. ||98||

It is called *taḍit* because it strikes (*tāḍayati*) or afflicts (*pīḍayati*), namely lightning (*vidyut*). Although the suffix *ṇi* would be elided by the rule for the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) would still occur; therefore, the elision (*luk*) is specifically prescribed.
99. From the root *śam*, the suffix *ḍha* is applied. 99.
A eunuch. ||99||
99. *Śaṇḍha* means one who is pacified or becomes tranquil; it is commonly known as *vṛṣabha* (bull) when independent, or it refers to a eunuch (*napuṃsaka*).
100. Kameraṭhaḥ || 100 ||
Kamaṭha ||100||

He desires; thus he is *kāmaṭha*, or a tortoise (*kacchapa*), or a type of vessel (*bhāṇḍabheda*). This is due to the rule of multiplicity (*bāhulaka*). He decays, meaning he becomes devoid of his state [of youth] or has pale limbs; thus he is *jaraṭha*. Or he is *śamaṭha*, meaning one who is tranquil (*śānta*).
There is also the substitution of *vṛddhi* for *ram*. (Pāṇini 6.4.101)
Asafoetida. ||101||
*Rāmaṭha* is that in which one delights (*ramate 'smin*); it refers to asafoetida (*hiṅgu*). By the suffix *traṭha*, there is the vṛddhi strengthening of the root *ram*.
102. The suffix *kha* is applied after the root *śam*.
Śaṅkha ||102||

102. *Śaṅkha* means "it becomes calm"; it refers to a specific kind of treasure (*nidhibheda*), or to something born in water, or to the bone of the forehead. Due to the use of the plural form (*bahulavacanāt*), the designation *itsaṃjñā* does not apply to the word *khāra*.
103. Kaṇeṣṭhaḥ. ||103||
The throat. ||103||
103. That by which one utters sound is the *kaṇṭha* (throat), which refers either to the neck or the resonance.
104. And [the element] time is also [a cause]. 104.
Tṛpalā ||104||

104. The suffix *kal* is applied to the root *tṛp*. That by which one is satisfied is *tṛpalā*, meaning a creeper (*latā*). Because the letter *ca* is included in the rule for the root *tṛp* (in the *Dhātupāṭha*), the suffix *kal* is also applied to the root *tṛph*; thus, *tṛphalā* is also established. *Tṛphalā* and *triphalā* are synonyms for a specific medicinal plant.

Due to the rule of *bāhulaka* (generalization): that which is desired is *kamala*; or *kamala* is a lotus (*padma*) or water, copper, and a medicinal herb; *kamala* is also a species of deer; *kamalā* is the beloved of the Lord of Śrī (Lakṣmī). That which adorns, beautifies, or establishes is *maṇḍala*; *maṇḍala* is circular, a specific region, a reflection, a *kadamba* tree, a type of sacrifice, and a dog. That which burns or consumes is *kuṇḍala*; it is a bracelet, a snare, or an ear-ornament. That which moves or goes is *paṭala*; it is an eye disease or a sectarian mark (*tilaka*), and so forth. That which cuts or shatters the intentions of others is *chala*.
105. And [the augment *iṭ* is applied] after the root *śam*.
Śabala. ||105||
105. He who curses or reviles is called *śabala*; or it refers to a distinction of color.
106. Also after *vṛṣan* and those ending in *adhi*.
The outcaste. ||106||

The suffix *kala* is also applied after verbal roots such as *vṛṣ* and others. From *vṛṣ* (to rain/to sprinkle): one who rains or sprinkles is a *vṛṣala*, meaning a Śūdra; his wife is a *vṛṣalī*. From *kuś*: one who cries out, embraces, or knows how to conduct legal affairs is *kuśala*, meaning skillful, or *kuśala* meaning welfare (*kṣema*). By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), with the *guṇa* strengthening, *kośala* refers to a particular region. From *pal* (to go): that by which one goes is *palala*, meaning sesame powder, mud, or meat. From *div* (to play/to shine): one who plays or desires to conquer the unrighteous is *devala*, meaning a righteous person.

It is *sarala* because it moves everywhere (*sarati*) or goes; it means straight or noble. It is *dhavala* because it runs (*dhāvati*), goes, or becomes pure (*śuddha*); it means white or pure. The shortening of the vowel in *dhāva-* occurs by virtue of the rule of diversity (*vāhulaka*). Because the group beginning with *vṛṣa* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*, words such as *kevala*, *kabala*, *tarala*, *anala*, *jambhala*, *peśala*, and *mardala* should also be understood [as falling under this category]. It is *musala* or *muśala* because it crushes (*musyati*), breaks, plunders, or steals.
*Muśalam* and *musalam* refer to the iron-tipped implement used for pounding, while *muṣala* also refers to a thief.
107. Kamberuka || 107 ||
Kambala. ||107||
That which is desired or sought after is *kaṃbala*, meaning either woolen cloth or water. It is derived from the root *kam* with the suffix *kalap* and the augment *vuk*.
108. And there is an increase in the *laṅgi*. 108.
The plough. ||108||
That by which food and other things are reached (laṅganti) is a plough (lāṅgala) or a harrow (hala);

this is due to the rule allowing for various forms (bahulavacanāt). Or, that which calls out (kaṇdati) is the plantain tree (kadalī), a species of tree well-known as "kelā"; here, the elision of the nasal (na-lopa) occurs from the verbal root due to its frequent occurrence (bāhulakāt).
109. The suffix *muṭ* is added after the roots *kuṭ*, *kaś*, and *kauti*.
A bud; dejection; tender. ||109||

The augment *muṭ* is added to the suffix *kala*, which is prescribed after roots such as *kuṭ*. From *kuṭ* (to bend), we have *kuṭmalaḥ*. By way of *bāhulaka* (irregularity/extension)—from *kuṇḍ* (to burn)—we have *kuḍmalaḥ* [or *kuṇmalaḥ*], which is the name for a flower that has slightly blossomed. That which moves with difficulty or governs it is *kaśmalaḥ*; *kaśmalaṃ* means impurity, sin, or evil. From *ku* (to sound), we have *komalaḥ*; *komalaṃ* means soft or water.
By virtue of the rule of general prevalence (*bāhulaka*): he describes or paints (*piṅkte varṇayati*) is *piṅgala*; or it refers to a particular color.
110. There is elision of the suffix *iṣṭhan*, and [the substitution of] *mṛj*.
Impurity. ||110||
110. That which is wiped away or cleansed is "mala" (impurity), namely feces, sin, or a wretched person; [the form "mala"] results from the elision of the suffix *ṭi* after the root *mṛj*.
111. [The substitution of *u* for *a* occurs] in place of the penultimate vowel of a root ending in *c*, *ū*, or *ṛ*.
Fickle. ||111||

*Copati* means he moves slowly and slowly; *sacapalaḥ* means momentarily or quickly. *Capalā* refers to long pepper or lightning. There is a substitution of the vowel *a* for the letter *u* of the verbal root.
112. The affix *niC* is applied after the roots *śak* and *śam*.
śakalam | śamalam ||112||
112. That which is capable (*śaknoti*) is *śakala*, meaning a fragment or a type of fish. That which is pacified (*śāmyati*) is *śamala*, meaning impurity or that which is not purified.
113. And [the vowel] *u* is short when followed by *g*, *gh*, or *r*. 113.
The goat. ||113||
113. It is called *chagala*, *chāga*, or *varkara* because it "leaps" (*chyati*) or "cuts" (*chinatti*); there is the addition of the suffix *guṇa* and the shortening of the vowel.
114. After the verbal root √yam, the suffix ḍa is applied.
daṇḍaḥ, raṇḍā, khaṇḍāḥ, maṇḍaḥ, baṇḍaḥ, aṇḍaḥ, ṣaṇḍaḥ, gaṇḍaḥ, caṇḍaḥ, paṇḍaḥ, paṇḍā. ||114||

114. *Ñam* is a technical abbreviation (*pratyāhāra*) for the inclusion [of certain letters]. Since these letters—*ña*, *ma*, *ṅa*, *ṇa*, and *na*—end in *m*, the suffix *ḍa* is applied after them. Due to the rule of "diversity" (*bahulavacana*), the designation of *it* (indicatory letter) is prohibited. One by which they are tamed or pacified is *daṇḍa*: either a staff or a type of punishment. One who takes pleasure is *raṇḍā*: a widow or a woman. That which is broken or split is *khaṇḍa*: a division or a piece of sugar-candy; the well-known term *khāṇḍa* refers to something broken or a distinct object. Alternatively, it may mean a category (*padārtha*).

*Maṇḍa*: that which thinks or knows is *maṇḍa*. It is explained as "the nurse (*dhātrī*)" or "the water of boiled rice. *Vaṇḍa*: that which seeks, sounds, or enjoys is *vaṇḍa*; or it refers to one whose hand is severed. *Trpaṇḍa*: that by which they satisfy or obtain sexual union is *trpaṇḍa*, or it is a part of a living being's limb. *Ṣaṇḍa*: that which gathers or gives is *ṣaṇḍa*; it refers to a eunuch, a forest, a cowherd, or a multitude. *Gaṇḍa*: that which goes is *gaṇḍa*; or it is a specific disease of the cheek. *Caṇḍa*: that which bestows or gives is *caṇḍa*; it means a violent person or something intense.

A woman who is prone to anger is *caṇḍī*. From the root *caḍi* meaning "to be angry," the word *caṇḍaḥ*—derived with the suffix *ghañ*—means "one who is wrathful. One who *paṇayati* (negotiates, deals, or praises) is *paṇḍaḥ*; [in this sense] it refers to a eunuch, or else *paṇḍā* means "intellect. That in which one *phaṇati* (moves or goes) is *phaṇḍaḥ*, meaning a path; or *phaṇḍam* means "the belly. 115.
*kvādibhyaḥ kit* (The suffix *ka* is added after roots beginning with *kva*, and it is marked with the *k*-indicator).
kuṇḍam, kāṇḍam, guḍaḥ, ghuṇḍaḥ ||115||

From roots beginning with the *ka*-group, the suffix *ḍa* is applied as *kit*. *Kuṇati* means "he makes a sound," "he assists," or "he acts"; thus, *kuṇḍaḥ* refers to a son born from another man while the husband is still living, or a particular type of water reservoir; *kuṇḍā* or *kuṇḍikā* [are its feminine forms]. *Kāmyate* means "it is desired by people"; thus, *kāṇḍam* refers to a section of a book, a specific measure, an arrow, or an occasion. *Gavate* means "he makes an indistinct sound"; thus, *guḍaḥ* refers to a ball or the boiling of sugarcane. *Ghoṇate* means "he wanders" or "he buzzes"; thus, *ghuṇḍaḥ* refers to a bee.
116. After the verbal roots √sthā, √ci, and √mṛj, the affixes ālac, vālan, and ālīyac [are respectively applied].
The *sthāla*, the *cātvāla*, and the *mārjālīya*. ||116||

That in which things stand is a *sthāla*, a specific type of vessel commonly known as a *thāla*; a *sthālī* is a cooking pot for soup and the like (formed with the suffix *ṅīp* after the word *sthālī* belonging to the *gaura-ādi* group). From the root *cat*, the suffix *vālan* is applied: that which begs or asks is a *cātvāla*, meaning either a sacrificial pit (*yajñakuṇḍa*) or *darbha* grass. From the root *mṛj*, the suffix *ālīyac* is applied: that which cleanses is a *mārjālīya*, meaning either a cat or a place for cleansing.
117. The suffix *ālaṅ* is added after the two roots *paṭi* and *caṇḍi*.
The netherworld; a Caṇḍāla. ||117||

117. That region where they fall and go is *pātāla*; or, it is *pātāla* because it exists at the bottom (*tala*) of the foot (*pāda*). It is established by virtue of belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. One who rages or is angry is a *caṇḍāla*, or a *mātaṅga*. Even in the compound "one whose ornament (*ala*) is sufficient (*alam*) for the enraged (*caṇḍa*) [person]," *cāṇḍāla* is established.
The suffix *kālan* is applied after the verbal roots *tam*, *viś*, *viḍ*, *mṛṇi*, *kuli*, *kapi*, *pali*, and *pañci*.
tamālaḥ, viśālaḥ, viḍālaḥ, mṛṇālam, kulālaḥ, kapālam, palālam, pañcālaḥ. ||118||

118. That which people long for and desire is the *tamāla*, a species of tree. That which enters everywhere is *viśāla*; *viśālā* is a proud wife, *viśāla* is a handsome man, *viśālā* is said to be Ujjayinī, and *viśāla* is a large house. That by which one leaps about or moves is *viḍāla*, a cat; the female is *viḍālī*. That which crushes or destroys is *mṛṇāla*, a potter (or a lotus stalk). That by which one trembles is *kapāla*, a human skull or a fragment of a jar.

*Palāla* is that which is obtained or reached; it refers to fruitless rice-straw, as is well known from the expression *vāpyāra*. *Pañcāla* is so called because he makes (*pañcati*) things manifest, or it is a particular deity.

Due to the rule of *bahulagrahaṇa* (the principle of diversity), the suffix *kālan* is applied even after the root *śo* (to sharpen); thus, *śālā* is a house, for in it they perform (*śyanti*) subtle activities.
The suffix *pateraṅ* is applied after the word *aṅga* when it means "bird. (119)
The sun-bird (the sun). ||119||

The suffix *aṅgac* is applied to the verbal root *pat* when a bird is to be denoted. One who flies or moves is a *pataṅga*, a bird. Although it is stated that [the suffix applies] when a bird is to be expressed, by virtue of the rule's diversity (*bāhulaka*), it also serves as a name for the sun, fire, a horse, a locust, a variety of rice, and so forth.
120. And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the roots *tṛ* and others.
Waves; cloves. 120.

120. That by which one crosses or floats is *taraṅga*—meaning a wave of water, a garment, or a fold; that by which one cuts is *lavaṅga*—meaning a medicinal herb. This is an *ādy-ākṛti-gaṇa* (a class of words beginning with these).
The suffix *ka* is added after *viṭ* and the following words, and it is marked with the *k*-diacritic (*kit*).
Viḍaṅga, mṛdaṅga, kuraṅga. ||121||

121. It is called *viḍaṅga* because it "scatters" (*viḍati*) or "reviles" (*ākrośati*); it is either a specific medicinal herb or a type of musical instrument. That which is "crushed" (*mṛdnāti*) is *mṛdaṅga*; it is either a specific musical instrument or a drum. It is called *kuraṅga* because it "scatters" (*kirati*) or "disperses" (*vikṣipati*); it is a deer (*hariṇa*). The feminine form is *kuraṅgī*, meaning a female deer; the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *gaura*. By virtue of the general rule (*bāhulaka*), there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel *ṛ*, and *ra* is substituted for the following consonant.
122. There is also vṛddhi for the roots sṛ and vṛñ.
Sāraṅgaḥ | Vāraṅgaḥ ||122||

122. From the roots *sṛ* and *vṛñ*, the suffix *aṅgac* is applied, and there is *vṛddhi* of the root vowel. That which moves (*sarati*) everywhere, goes, is a *sāraṅga*: a bird, a deer, or a bee. That which chooses (*vṛṇoti*) or seizes (*gṛhṇāti*) is a *vāraṅga*: the hilt of a sword or the like.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—that which leads (*nṛṇāti*) or carries (*nayati*) is a *nāraṅga*: a juice, long pepper, or a particular tree and fruit.
123. [The suffix *yat* is applied after verbal roots] denoting motion (*gamya*) and eating (*ada*). 123.
maṅgaḥ | adgaḥ ||123||

123. *Gaṅgā* is a specific river because it "goes" (*gacchati*). Or, *trapradgaḥ* refers to a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), for it is "satisfied" (*trpyati*) or "consumed" (*adyate*, *bhakṣyate*). By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *gan* is also applied here from the root *trapram* in the sense of "going" and so forth. [Regarding *trapraṅgam*:]* That by which one goes to or attains actions or sense-objects is *trapraṅgam*; it means a limb (*gātra*), a means (*upāya*), a secondary part (*pratīkam-apradhānam*), or a particular place (*deśaviśeṣaḥ*).
124. After the roots *chāpū* and *khaḍi*, [the suffix *ktvā*] is marked with the *k* it-marker.
Goat, betel-nut tree, rhinoceros. ||124||

The suffix *gan* with the augment *kit* is applied after the roots *dhā* and others. That which cuts is a *chāga*, a young goat (*varkara*). That by which the mouth is purified is a *pūga*, a species of areca nut (*kramuka*) commonly known as *supārī*, or a collection. That by which one strikes or cleaves is a *khaḍga*, a weapon, specifically the rhinoceros (*gaṇḍaka*) commonly known as *geḍā*.

By virtue of the rule of "abundance" (bāhulaka)—the suffix *seṭ* is disregarded, and thus it is *ṣiḍga*; or it refers to a gem situated in the middle of a necklace whose brilliance is flickering. Precisely because of the statement regarding abundance, there is a prohibition of the *satva* change.
125. After the root *bhṛ* ("to carry"), the suffix *ki* is applied, and it carries the augment *nuṭ*.
The bhr̥ṅga [is the syllable]. ||125||

The suffix *gan* is added to the root *bhṛñ* (to carry, to support, or to nourish), and it is *kit*; furthermore, the augment *nuṭ* is applied to it. That which carries, supports, or nourishes is a *bhṛṅga*, namely a bee.
126. And there is shortening of the vowel in the root *śṛ* [to form *śīrṣan*].
Śṛṅgaḥ || 126 ||
126. The suffix *nuṭ* follows from the previous rule. That by which one pierces or strikes is *śṛṅga*: a horn, a mountain peak, a type of fish, a type of medicinal herb, or a type of gold.
127. The word *gaṇ* [is used] in the sense of "bird. 127.
Śārṅga. ||127||
127. Because the suffix *gaṇ* has the marker *ṇ*, there is *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) of the root as before, and the augment *nuṭ*. That which pierces (*śṛṇāti*) is a *śārṅga* bird.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the addition of the vowel *a* at the beginning of the suffix also results in the form *śāraṅga*.
128. *mudi* and *grau* are *gagga*. 128.
Mudga; Garga. 128.

128. From the root *mud*, the suffix *ga* is applied. He rejoices (*modate*), thus he is *mudga*; or it is a type of bean (*trapuṣabhedah*). One who takes (*lāti*) or seizes (*gṛhṇāti*) beans is *mudgala*, the sage; it is well known that his lineage descendant (*gotrāpatyam*) is *maudgalya*. One who speaks (*gṛṇāti*) or teaches is *gaga*, or a particular seer (*ṛṣiviśeṣaḥ*). The suffix *ga* is applied to the root *gṛ*.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *sṛ*, *bhṛ*, *vṛ*, and *ñi* (to choose).
Karaṇḍa, saraṇḍa, bharaṇḍa, varaṇḍa. ||129||

129. The suffix *aṇḍan* is applied after roots such as *kṛ*. That which is made (*kriyate*) is a *karaṇḍa*, a specific type of flower-basket; a *karaṇḍa* is also a vessel made of bamboo, commonly known as a *piṭārī*. That which moves or goes is a *saraṇḍa*, or a bird. That which supports or nourishes is a *bharaṇḍa*, a master. That which covers or accepts is a *varaṇḍa*, a disease of the mouth or a collection.

Due to the rule of *bāhulaka* (generalization): that which crosses over is *taraṇḍa*, or a means for crossing water; he who desires (*vanati*) or resorts to (*saṃbhajati*) dharma is *vataṇḍa*, or a particular sage; the substitution of the letter *t* at the end of the root occurs [in these cases]. He who devours or consumes is *chamaṇḍa*, or one devoid of mother and father; he who lies down is *śayaṇḍa*, or a sensual object (*viṣaya*). Words such as these are established solely by virtue of the *bāhulaka* rule.
130. The suffix *adi* is applied after the verbal roots √śṝ, √dṛ, and √bhṛs.
śarat, darat, bhasat ||130||

130. The suffix *adi* is applied after the roots *śṝ*, *dṝ*, and *bhas*. That in which one hears or destroys is *śarat*, a particular season or a time-period (*ṛtu*). That which is torn asunder is *darat*, such as the heart or a riverbank. He who fears or threatens, or who shines forth, is *bhasat*; or it refers to the private parts (*jaghana*).

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—that in which one sprinkles, or feels affection, or by which the mind becomes pleasant and serene, that is *parṣat*, meaning an assembly (*sabhā*), a gathering (*samāja*), or the like.
131. After the root *dṛmā*, there is the substitution of *ṣuk* and the shortening [of the vowel].
A stone. ||131||
This stone or rock is split; when the suffix *trap* is applied, the augment *ṣuk* and the substitution of a short vowel occur for the root.
132. [The suffix *kta* is applied] after the roots *tyaj*, *ji*, and *ni*. 132.
tyad, tad, yad || 132 ||

132. That which abandons [defilements] and becomes free from afflictions and the like is *tyad*; that which extends and becomes expanded is *tad*; that which sacrifices and becomes associated with all categories of objects through its rays is *yad*. These are the three names of Brahman. Since *tyad* and the others are designated as pronouns (*sarvanāman*), they are general designators.
133. And [the suffix] tuṭ is also [added]. 133.
This [is so]. ||133||

133. The suffix *adi* is added to the root *i*, and it takes the augment *tuṭ*. [The word] "eti" means "he goes" or "he attains. Furthermore, the pronoun *etad* also receives the designation of a sarvanāman (pronoun).
134. The Path of the Stream-enterer (Srotāpanna). 134.
The lizard. ||134||
It moves and goes, thus it is *saraṭ*, meaning wind or cloud; the suffix *aṭ* is applied to the root *sṛ*.
135. After the root *laṅgh*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel.
The small jar. ||135||
It leaps and dries up, thus it is *laghaṭ*, or it is the wind (*vāyu*); there is the elision of the root vowel (*dhātu-nalopa*).
The suffix *aj* is added to the root *pārayati*.
Pāraka 136.

It is called *pāraka* because it carries across (*pārayati*) or completes the task; alternatively, it refers to gold. The suffix *ac* is applied to the root *pāri*, as in the case of "thief" (*caura*) and similar words.
137. After the root *prath*, there is the suffix *kit* and the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the semivowel.
Separately. ||137||

It is called *pṛthak* because it extends (*prathayati*) from a collection (*saṅghāta*) and thus becomes expanded (*vistṛta*), or because it signifies diversity (*nānātva*). Its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) results from its inclusion in the list beginning with *svar*.
After the word *bhiyas*, [the suffix] *ṣuk* is applied, and the vowel is shortened. ||138||
The physician. ||138||

This person fears [it]; he is a physician (bhiṣaj) or a healer (vaidya). Because of the irregular formation (nipātana) [of the word] *sumaṅgalabheṣaja*, the guṇa substitution is applied, resulting in *bheṣaja*. That which is a remedy (*bheṣaja*) is itself the medicine (*bhaiṣajya*).
The suffix *madik* is applied after the roots *yu* and *asu*.
The [substitution of] *yuṣmad* and *asmad* [occurs]. 139.

He who serves you (*yuṣpati*)—the root *yuṣ* is a Vedic (sautra) root. He who casts away (*trprasyati*), that is, throws another away, is *trprasmad*. These two are words expressing pronouns (*sarvanāman*).
The suffix *man* is applied after the verbal roots *ṛ*, *tu*, *su*, *sṛ*, *dhṛ*, *kṣi*, *kṣu*, *bhā*, *yā*, *vā*, *pad*, and *yakṣiṇī*.
armmaḥ, stomaḥ, somaḥ, homaḥ, sarmaḥ, dharmaḥ, kṣemam, kṣomam, bhāmaḥ, yāmaḥ, vāmaḥ, padmam, yakṣmaḥ, nemaḥ. ||140||

140. That which one reaches or attains is *trpma*, or it is an eye disease. That by which one praises is *stoma*, or it is a collection. That which flows forth as a cause of sovereignty is *soma*, or it is camphor, or the moon. That which is offered or given is *homa*, or it is a sacrifice. That which is traversed or gone to is *sarma*, or it is movement. That which is maintained for the attainment of happiness and is practiced is *dharma*, or it is impartial justice, or righteous conduct. That which destroys ignorance and annihilates it is *kṣema*, or it is well-being.

*kṣoma* is that which sneezes or makes a sound; it refers to a type of cloth or the *atasī* flower. *Bhāma* shines or is radiant; it denotes anger, the sun, or light. *Yāma* is that which is traversed or reached; it refers to a watch of the night. *Vāma* blows or moves, or grasps a book; it means beautiful, wicked, or the left side. *Padma* goes or reaches; it is a lotus, a treasure, or a conch shell. *Yakṣma* worships or honors; it is a chronic disease (consumption). *Nema* leads; it refers to the base of a rampart. However, the word *tṛpra*, denoting "half," is designated as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
141. After the root *hā*, there is the substitution of *san*-class suffixes and the elision of the vowel *ā*.
Crooked. ||141||
