The word *manin* follows [as a suffix]. That which abandons (*jahāti*) or casts off (*tyajati*) is *jihma*, meaning crooked or dull-witted.
142. After the root *av*, there is the elision of the suffix *ti*.
The third chapter. 142.

In the word *praṇava*, there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of the suffix *man* [from the root *nam*], and *ūṭh* is substituted for the penultimate *u* and the *ka* of the root. It means "that which protects" (*avati*) or "performs protection" (*rakṣādikaṃ karoti*). *Praṇava* signifies the beginning or the consent. Its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is due to its inclusion in the *cādi* group.
And [the word] graserā [is also used]. 143.
The village. ||143||

143. *Grāma* means that which swallows (*grasate*) or that which is swallowed (*gramyate*); it is a collection of houses or a dwelling for living beings, or a battle (*saṅgrāma*). A *grāma* of rice plants is a multitude, as in *śāligrāma*. Likewise, there is a *grāma* of sounds (*śabdagrāma*), and in the science of music, a *grāma* refers to a classification of musical notes (*svarabheda*).
144. The suffix *i* is added after the roots *avi*, *śvi*, and *śuṣ*, and it is *kit*.
ūmam, syūmaḥ, simaḥ, śuṣmam ||144||

144. *Umā*: That which possesses protection (*rakṣaṇa*) and so forth is *ūma*; with the feminine suffix *ṭāp* applied and shortening by way of irregularity (*bāhulaka*), it means a woman distinguished as *Umā*. *Syūma*: that which sews (*sīvyati*) threads or extends them; it means a ray (*raśmi*). *Sima*: that which binds (*sinoti*) or fastens; it is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and a synonym for "all" (*sarva*). *Śuṣma*: that which dries up (*śuṣyati*) or makes sapless; it means fire (*agni*) or wind (*vāyu*).
The suffix *mak* follows the verbal roots *iṣ*, *yudh*, *indh*, *das*, *śās*, *dhū*, and *sū*.
iṣmaḥ, yudhmaḥ, idhmaḥ, dasmaḥ, śyāmaḥ, dhūmaḥ, sūmaḥ. ||145||

145. That which desires or is desired is *iṣma*, meaning desire (*kāma*) or the spring season (*vasanta-ṛtu*). He who fights or that by which one fights is *yudhma*, meaning a warrior or an arrow. That which kindles or shines, or that by which one kindles, is *idhma*, meaning fuel (*samiddha*). He who destroys, consumes, or causes suffering is *dasma*, meaning a destroyer or a sacrificer (*yajamāna*). He who moves, goes, or reaches is *śyāma*, meaning green, dark, or black; likewise, a woman who has recently given birth is called *śyāmā*, as are a creeper or a medicinal herb, and so forth.

It is called *dhūma* because it shakes or causes trembling; or alternatively, it is so named because it arises from fire (*dhū*). It is called *sūma* because it brings forth, generates, or releases the embryo of living beings; or alternatively, it is so named because it is the intermediate space (*sū*).

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*): that which swells, moves, or trembles is *īrma*, meaning a wound or a sore; that which makes a sound by sneezing is *kṣumā*, meaning linseed or flax; that which is born or produced is *janman*, meaning birth or origin.
146. For the roots *yuj*, *ruc*, and *tij*, the substitute *ku* is applied [in place of the suffix *na*].
A pair; gold; sharp. ||146||

146. *Mak* is joined with that [suffix] to form a pair (*yugma*). The connection of two [words] in a single action [is expressed]. That which shines, having a radiant color, is *rukma*; it is either a specific color or gold due to its association with that color. Because it possesses the color of *rukma*, it is *rukmaṃ suvarṇaṃ* (gold). A woman who has *rukma* as her color is called *rukmiṇī*. That which heats or cuts is *tigma*, meaning sharp. This word follows the gender of the noun it qualifies: *tigmā dhīḥ* (sharp intellect), or *tigmaḥ tīvraḥ* (sharp/intense).
And indeed, one should abandon it. ||147||

147. That which is hot or foul-smelling becomes "cold" (*hima*) in the winter season (*hemanta-ṛtu*), as does frost or sandalwood; [in this sense] *mahat* [preceded by *hima*] forms *himānī*, with the suffix *ṅīṣ* added after *trapu* and *anuka*.
148. Or [the vowel *i*] after *bhī* becomes *uṣ*. 148.
Bhīma; Bhīṣma. ||148||

That from which or that of which one fears—whether it is *bibheti* or *bibhyati*—is *bhīmaḥ* or *bhīmā*. [Likewise,] *bhīṣmaḥ* or *bhīṣmā*. *Bhīmaḥ* may mean "terrifying" or the son of Pāṇḍu. One whose army (*senā*) is *bhīmā* (terrifying) is *Bhīmasenaḥ*; similarly, there is also *Bhīṣyasenaḥ*.
149. *Gharma* and *grīṣma* [are synonyms for summer]. 149.

149. Two words ending in the suffix *mak* are irregularly formed (*nipātyete*). That by which living beings or the world are heated (*jigharti*), flows away (*kṣarati*), perishes (*naśyati*), or is illuminated (*dīpyate*) is *gharma*: [it means] sacrifice (*yajña*), heat (*tṛpra*), the summer season (*grīṣma-ṛtu*), or sweat (*sveda*). That which swallows (*grasate*) the cold or the juices and so forth is *grīṣma*: [it means] the time of intense heat (*tṛpratyuṣmākāla*). From the root *gras*, the form *grī* occurs and the augment *ṣuk* is added by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
After the root *prath*, the suffixes *ṣivan*, *ṣvan*, and *ṣvana* are applied, and there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the vowel.
pṛthivī, pṛthavī, pṛthvī ||150||

It is called *pṛthivī* because it spreads out (*prathate*) and becomes extensive (*vistīrṇā*); thus *pṛthavī*, *pṛthivī*, and *pṛthvī* are three words with the same meaning. It refers either to the earth or to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
The suffix *kvan* is added after the verbal roots *aśū*, *pruṣi*, *laṭi*, *kaṇi*, *khaṭi*, and *viśi*.
*trpraśvaḥ*, *pruṣvaḥ*, *laṭvā*, *kaṇvam*, *khaṭvā*, *viśvaḥ*. ||151||

*Trpraśvaḥ*: that which spreads or pervades; it refers to a horse or fire. Due to its inclusion in the *trpra-ja* group, it is feminine as *aśvā*, meaning a mare. *Pruṣvaḥ*: that which sprinkles, becomes moist, pours, or fills; it refers to water or the sun. *Laṭvā*: that which moves like a child; this is a word restricted to the feminine gender, denoting a type of *karañja* tree, its fruit, a musical instrument, or a species of bird. *Kaṇvaḥ*: that which sounds, closes [the eyes], or exerts itself; it refers to sin (*kaṇvam*), or the sage Kaṇva.

That by which [the Veda] was first taught is known as the *kāṇvī śākhā*. That which is desired or sought after is a *khaṭvā*, or a type of bed. That which enters everywhere is *viśva*; it refers to the entire world (*viśvaṃ jagat*) or all objects of experience (*viśvā ativiṣayā*). Furthermore, because it is listed among the words beginning with *sarva*, it bears the technical designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*).
The suffix *van* is applied after the roots *iṇ* and *śī*.
Thus: "The auspicious one. ||152||

The word *eva* means "he goes" or "he attains. By virtue of its frequentative usage (*bāhulaka*), the indeclinable *eva* is used in the sense of restriction; thus, *śevaḥ* refers to that which lies down—namely, either the mouth or the penis.
The suffixes *sarvanighṛṣ*, *ariṣva*, *laṣva*, *śiva*, *paṭva*, *prahva*, and *eṣa* occur when the suffix *at* follows. (Pāṇini 6.4.153)

153. Words beginning with *sarva* and ending in the suffix *van* are treated as irregular forms (*nipātana*). That which moves everywhere is *sarva*; it denotes "complete" and is designated as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), serving as an adjective. That which grinds or crushes intensely is *nighṛṣvaḥ*; there is an absence of the *guṇa* strengthening here. Or [it means] a hoof. That which injures or harms is *riṣvaḥ*, meaning a destroyer. He who desires or longs for is *laṣvaḥ*, or a dancer. He who lies down is *śivaḥ*; there is shortening of the verbal root. *Śiva* refers to the Lord (*īśvara*), or *śiva* means auspiciousness, happiness, water, or a myrobalan fruit (*harītakī*). *Sarvādayo vanpratyayāntā nipātyante*. Words beginning with *sarva* and ending in the suffix *van* are prescribed as irregular forms. *saratīti sarvaḥ sapūrṇavācī sarvanāmasaṃjñī viśeṣaṇam*. That which moves is *sarvaḥ*; it expresses "full" and is designated as a pronoun, acting as an adjective. *nitarāṃ gharṣati pinaṣṭīti nighṛṣvaḥ*. That which grinds or crushes excessively is *nighṛṣvaḥ*. There is an absence of *guṇa*. *khuraṃ vā*. Or [it means] a hoof. *reṣati hinastīti riṣvaḥ hiṃsakaḥ*. That which injures or harms is *riṣvaḥ*, meaning a destroyer. *laṣati kāmayate'sau laṣvaḥ narttako vā*. He who desires or longs for is *laṣvaḥ*, or a dancer. *śete'sau śivaḥ*. He who lies down is *śivaḥ*. *dhātorhrasvatvam*. There is shortening of the verbal root. *śiva īśvaraḥ śivaṃ bhadraṃ sukham udakaṃ ca*. *Śiva* is the Lord; *śiva* [also means] auspiciousness, happiness, water, and so on. *saśivā harītakī*. *Saśivā* (accompanied by Śiva) is the myrobalan fruit.

*Paṭvaḥ* refers to the world of earth (*bhūloka*), so called because people walk (*paṭyante*) or go (*gacchanti*) upon it; or it means one who abandons (*prajahāti*) or relinquishes (*tyajati*), thus *prahvaḥ*. The elision of the vowel *a* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). *Īṣvaḥ* refers to one who does not harm (*na hinasti*) ignorance (*ajñāna*); or it refers to the teacher *Trp*. Why [is the suffix] *trp* mentioned in the rule? So that the words *sarva* and others, which are listed in the rules beginning with "sarttā" and "sāraka," do not become merely derivative (*yaugika*) in meaning. By virtue of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*): *hrasvaḥ* means one who makes a sound short (*hrasati*), namely a dwarf (*vāmana*), or a phoneme consisting of a single measure (*ekamātra*).
154. śevāya, vajra, jihvā, grīvā, āp, and āmīvā [are words ending in long vowels]. 154.

154. Words such as *śeva* and others ending in *van* are treated as irregular forms (*nipātana*). That which lies down is *śeva*, meaning either a mark or a shape. That which sacrifices is *yahva*, meaning a sacrificer; here, the letter *ja* becomes *ha*. That by which one conquers is *jihvā*, meaning either a sense organ (the tongue) or the faculty of speech; here, *hu* is substituted for the verbal root. That by which one binds is *grīvā*, meaning either the neck or a limb of the body; here, the change to *grī* occurs for the verbal root. That by which one reaches is *trprapvā*, meaning the region of the throat. That which measures or injures is *mīva*, meaning either a worm in the belly or the like.
The suffix *va* is applied after the verbal roots √kṛ, √gṝ, √śṝ, and √dṝ.
karvaḥ, garvaḥ, śarvaḥ, darvaḥ. ||155||

*Karva* is that which scatters or disperses the mind; it refers either to desire (*kāma*) or pride (*māna*). *Garva* is that which swallows; it refers either to egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) or to happiness (*sukha*). *Śarva* is that which destroys suffering; it refers either to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) or to bliss. *Darva* is that which pierces or tears apart living beings; it refers either to a harmful person or to a weapon.
156. Kanin, yu, vṛṣi, takṣi, rāj, dhanvi, dyut, and pratidiv. ||156||
yuvā, vuṣā, takṣā, rājā, dhanvā, dyuvā, pratidivā ||156||

156. *Yuvā* is one who unites, mixes, or does not mix; it refers to a person in the middle stage of life or a youth. *Vṛṣā* is one who rains [semen]; it refers to the sun. *Takṣā* is one who carves or makes thin; it refers to a carpenter or woodworker. *Rājā* is one who shines or has attained sovereignty; it refers to a lord of the earth or the moon. *Dhanvā* is one who runs or goes; it refers to a bow or the act of shooting an arrow. *Dyuvā* is one who approaches or moves toward; it refers to the sun. *Pratidivā* is that in which they play against one another; it refers to the day.

Due to the rule of multiplicity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *kanin* is applied even to the root *div-* alone; by this, forms such as *divā* and *divānau* are also established. Alternatively, *daśan* means "he counts," referring to a specific number, or *navan* means "he leads," referring to the number nine. In these cases, the *guṇa* strengthening occurs due to the rule of multiplicity.
157. After the roots *sap* and *śubh*, the augment *tuṭ* is also inserted [before the suffix *ktvā*].
Seven or eight. 157.

It is called *sapta* because it "binds together" (*sapati*) or "unites" (*samavaiti*); or it is a specific number. It is called *triṣṭubh* because it "measures across" (*tṛpraśnute*) or "pervades" (*vyāpnoti*); or it is a number.
By virtue of the rule of abundance (*bāhulaka*), it is called *pañcan* because it "makes manifest" (*pañcati*); or it is a word denoting a number.
158. [The substitution of *na* occurs] for the root *hā* when followed by the suffix *ni*.
A day (*dinam*) is so called because it abandons (*jahāti*), casts off (*tyajati*), and separates itself from (*pṛthakkaroti*) darkness (*andhakāram*). Thus it is derived from three verbal roots.
159. *śvan*, *ukṣan*, *pūṣan*, *palīhan*, *kledan*, *snehan*, *mūrdhan*, *majjan*, *aryaman*, *viśvapsan*, *parijvan*, *mātariśvan*, and *maghavan* [are words ending in -an]. 159.
Śvan, ukṣan, pūṣan, plīhan, kledas, snehas, mūrdhan, majjan, aryaman, viśvapsas, parijman, mātariśvan, maghavan. 159.
Thus ends the first quarter in the Uṇādi [section]. ||1||

159. Thirteen words beginning with *śvan* are derived as *kanin*-suffix formations by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). That which barks, moves, or grows is *śvan*, meaning a dog; in the feminine, with the suffix *ṅīṣ*, it is *śunī*. That which sprinkles or moistens is *ukṣan*, meaning a bull; [the penultimate vowel] undergoes lengthening. That which thrives or increases is *pūṣan*, meaning the sun or the wind. That which is reached or attained within is *plīhan*, meaning a disease of the abdomen; [here too] there is lengthening of the penultimate vowel of the root. *Kilān* refers to the moon; [here] there is *guṇa* substitution for the root vowel. That which causes affection or thirst is *snehāḥ*, meaning a disease; [here] the suffix is applied directly.

The root *mūrv* undergoes *guṇa*. That which binds or ties is *mūrdhā*, meaning "head. There is a lengthening of the vowel *u* and the change of *v* to *dh*. *Majjā* is that which sinks or purifies; it means marrow or the essence of the bone. *Viśvapsā* is one who measures out the lord of the world; it refers either to *trpā* (the earth) or to fire. *Parijvā* is that which moves around or becomes swift; this refers to the moon. The root *ju* is a Vedic (Sautra) root, and here it undergoes the *yaṇ* substitution. *Maghavā* is he who swells, goes, increases, or is honored in the atmosphere (*trpā*); he is the sun.

In the word *maha*, the letter *h* undergoes the change to *gh*, and the augment *vuk* is added. This word *maghavan* is also seen ending in *t*; in that case, it means "one who possesses wealth (*magha*)," thus forming *maghavān*, *maghavantau*, and *maghavantaḥ*—these ending in the suffix *matup*. However, those ending in the suffix *kanin* are: *maghavā*, *maghavānau*, *maghavānaḥ*, *maghavan*, *maghavānam*, *maghavānau*, and *maghonaḥ*.

In this rule, the word *iti* is used in the sense of "of such a kind. Other words ending in *kanin* should be formed accordingly according to usage. Alternatively, the word *iti* serves to mark the end of the section (pāda).
Thus ends the first quarter in the commentary on the Uṇādi-sūtras, within the Vaidikalaukika-koṣa. ||1||
Now begins the second quarter:
1. After the roots *kṛ* and *hṛ*, the suffix *eṇu* [is applied].
Kareṇuḥ | Hareṇuḥ ||1||

1. That which acts (*karoti*) is a *kareṇu*, meaning either an elephant (*hastin*) or a female elephant (*hastinī*). That which carries away (*harati*) is a *hareṇu*, a fragrant substance or a bundle (*kalāpa*), commonly known as *maṭara*.
The suffix *kthan* is applied after the verbal roots *han*, *kuṣi*, *nī*, *rañj*, and *aś*.
Hathaḥ | Kuṣṭhaḥ | Nīthaḥ | Rathaḥ | Kāṣṭham ||2||

2. That which is killed or that by which one is killed is *hatha*; it is either the suffering [itself] or a particular kind of weapon. That which tears or pulls incessantly is *kuṣṭha*, a type of disease, or the medicinal herb known as *kūṭa*. That which is led or the act of leading is *nītha*; one who possesses a beautiful (*su*) *nītha* is *sunītha*, meaning one whose character is righteous (*dharmaśīla*). That in which one delights or that by which one delights is *ratha*; it is a vehicle, the body, a foot, or the reed (*vetasa*). That which shines or glows is *kāṣṭha*; it is fuel, a place, a measure of time, or the cardinal direction (*kāṣṭhā*); it is also wood or turmeric.
3. After the root *bhṛ* (to carry), [the suffix] *ave* [is added].
The final purificatory bath. ||3||
3. *Kthan*: *Travapravṛtti* means either a specific type of bird (*pakṣibheda*) or the ritual bath at the conclusion of a sacrifice (*yajñāntasnāna*).
The suffix *than* is added after the roots *uṣ*, *kuṣ*, and *gārti*.
oṣṭhaḥ | koṣṭhaḥ | gāthā | arthaḥ ||4||

4. That which burns when dry (*tṛpra*) or by means of which one burns is *tṛproṣṭha*, or it refers to a part of the face. That which scrapes (*kuṣṇāti*) or draws out continuously is *koṣṭha*; *koṣṭha* may mean the belly (*kukṣi*), a granary (*kuśūla*), or an inner room. That which is sung is *gāthā*, a type of speech or a verse (*śloka*). That which is sought after or attained is *trprartha*; for words, it means the expressed meaning (*vācya*), wealth, cause, substance, purpose, cessation, or object. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—it thins (*śyati*) or makes lean—is *śotha*, a particular disease; this is an exception to the prohibition of *ātvam* (the substitution of *ā*) for the root *śo* "to thin."
5. [The suffix] ṇit follows the root sṛ. ||5||
This is the summary. ||5||
That which moves or goes is a caravan (sārtha), meaning a group; the vowel *vṛddhi* strengthening occurs because the suffix *than* is marked with the *ṇi* indicator.
The suffix *ūthan* is applied after the roots *jṝ* and *vṛñ*.
Jarūtha; Varūtha. 6.

6. That which decays and becomes devoid of vitality is *jarūthaḥ*, meaning either flesh or [something that has become worn]. That by which one chooses or accepts is *varūyaḥ*, meaning either iron or the protective covering of a chariot.
The suffix *thak* is added after the verbal roots *pā*, *tṛ*, *tu*, *div*, *ci*, *ric*, and *sic*.
pīthaḥ, tīrtham, tutthaḥ, uktham, riktham, siktham. ||7||

7. That which drinks or that which is drunk is *pītha*; it is the sun or clarified butter (*ghṛta*). That by which or where one crosses over is a *tīrtha*; it is the teacher, sacrifice, human purpose, a minister, or a reservoir of water. That which pierces or by which one suffers pain is *tuttha*; it is copper, collyrium, the *tutthā* plant, indigo, the *trp* herb, a cow, a mare, or small cardamom—commonly known as *choṭī ilāyacī*. That which is spoken or recited all around is *uktha*; it is the Sāmaveda.

One who studies or knows the *uktha* is called an *aukthika*. That which separates or divides is *rikya*, meaning inheritance or wealth, or gold. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *thak* is also applied to the root *ṛc* (in the sense of "to praise"); thus, that for the sake of which one praises is *ṛktha*, meaning wealth. That which sprinkles or pleases is *siktha*, known as beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*)—or else, it refers to the scum (*maṇḍa*) extracted from boiled rice.
8. Artterniri || 8 ||
The slaughter-ground. ||8||
That in which they reach or go without interruption is the *nirṛtha*, namely the Sāmaveda.
9. Verses on the concealment of the night. 9.

9. *Niśītha*: That in which one sleeps profoundly; it refers to the third watch of the night, midnight, or the entire night. *Gopītha*: One who protects (*pāti*) speech (*gāṃ*, i.e., *vāṇīm*) or the earth (*pṛthivīm*); it refers to a wise man or a king. *Avagātha*: That in which cows drink water; it refers to a reservoir of water. *Trpravagātha*: One who plunges into, enters, or knows; it refers to one who has attained [knowledge] or has performed an immersion (*snāna*).
10. And the impelling [is the tenth]. ||10||
The Udgītha. ||10||

10. The suffix *thak* is applied after the root *gādh* when preceded by the prefix *ud*. That which is sung aloud, that which sounds loudly, is the *udgītha*; it is the sound of the *sāman* or the *praṇava*.
11. Samīṇaḥ ||11||
The one who has been kindled. ||11||
11. *Samithaḥ* means "one who attains" (*sameti*) objects correctly (*samyak*); it refers either to fire or to the sun.
12. *titha*, *pṛṣṭha*, *gūtha*, *yūtha*, and *protha* [are derived from the root √sthā with the prefix vi-]. 12.

12. Words such as *titha* and others ending in the suffix *-tha* are *nipātas* (irregularly formed words). That which heats (*tijate*) or endures (*sahyate*) is *titha*: the sacrificial fire (*trp-agni*) or desire (*kāma*). That which sprinkles (*parṣati*) or by which one sprinkles is *pṛṣṭham*: the hind part of the body or a hymn (*stotra*). That which bellows (*garvate*) or by which one bellows—that is, makes an indistinct sound—is *gūtham*: the path of drinking (*trpa-pāna-mārga*) or excrement (*purīṣa*). That which joins (*yauti*), mixes, or does not mix is *yūtha*: a collection or a herd. That which moves forward (*pravate*) or goes by means of it is *protha*: the horse's nostril.
A departing man, a particular tree, dear water, food, and the fetus of a woman are called *protha*.

The suffix *rak* is applied after the verbal roots *sphāyi*, *tañci*, *vañci*, *śaki*, *kṣipi*, *kṣudi*, *sṛpi*, *tṛpi*, *tṛpi*, *dṛpi*, *vandi*, *undi*, *śvit*, *vṛti*, *aji*, *nīpa*, *di*, *madi*, *mudi*, *khidi*, *chidi*, *bhidi*, *mandi*, *candi*, *dahi*, *das*, *dambhi*, *vasi*, *vāśi*, *śīṅ*, *has*, *si*, *dhī*, and *śubh*.

Sphāram, takram, vakraḥ, śakraḥ, kṣipram, kṣudraḥ, sṛpraḥ, tṛpraḥ, dṛpraḥ, vandraḥ, udraḥ, śvitram, vṛtraḥ, vīraḥ, nīram, padraḥ, madraḥ, mudrā, khidraḥ, chidram, bhidram, mandraḥ, candraḥ, dahraḥ, dasraḥ, dabhraḥ, usraḥ, vāśraḥ, śīraḥ, hasraḥ, sidhraḥ, śubhram. ||13||

13. That which expands or increases is *sphāra*; it may be a transformation of gold and the like, or a bubble (*budbuda*). [In the word *valirepha*, there is the elision of *ya*. That which contracts or causes to shrink is *takra*, meaning churned curd or buttermilk. That which deceives or deludes is *vakra*, meaning crooked, curved, or cruel. That which is able is *śakra*, meaning capable or a specific type of tree (*kuṭaja*). That which is thrown or impelled is *kṣipra*, meaning swift or quick. That which cuts or grinds is *kṣudra*, meaning base, cruel, or miserable.

The word *sṛpra* has its gender determined by the context (*vācyaliṅga*): it refers to a lowly woman (*veśyā*), the *kaṇṭakārikā* plant (bhaṭakaṭāī), or a honey-bee. It is called *sṛpra* because it "creeps" or "moves," thus referring to the moon. That which is satisfied, or that by which one is satisfied, is *tṛpra*; it refers to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). That which becomes arrogant, rejoices, or is infatuated is *dṛpra*; it refers to one who is powerful. One who salutes, addresses, or praises is *vandru*; it refers to one who shows honor. That which wets or becomes moist is *udra*; it refers to an aquatic creature. That which wets thoroughly is *samudra*. [This is according to Pāṇini 6.1.207].

[4.24] Thus, there is the elision of *n*. That which becomes distinguished by color (*varṇaviśiṣṭa*) is *śvitram*, meaning a type of leprosy (*kuṣṭhabheda*), or [the white mark on a horse]. That which always exists is *vṛtraḥ*, meaning a cloud, an enemy, darkness, a mountain, or a wheel (*cakra*). He who moves swiftly toward enemies or casts them down is *vīraḥ*, meaning a brave warrior, an excellent one, a crossroads (*catuṣpatha*), or [the plant *vīrā*]. *Vīrā* refers to *kṣīrakākolī*, a woman with husband and children, or the medicinal plant *madhuparṇikā*. That which leads the body is *nīram*, meaning water.

*Padra*: that in which one goes or moves; a village, a dwelling, or a place. *Madra*: that by which one intoxicates; joy, or a specific region. *Mudrā*: that by which people rejoice or are delighted; a seal, or something made of gold and other metals. *Khidra*: that which causes distress or by which one becomes wretched; a disease or poverty. *Chidra*: that which is cut; a hole or cavity. *Bhidra*: that by which one pierces; a thunderbolt or diamond. *Mandra*: that which praises or sounds low; a deep tone.

He who gladdens or causes joy is *candra*, such as camphor or the moon; he who burns or reduces to ashes is *dahra*, such as a forest fire; he who destroys or diminishes diseases is *dasra*, such as a physician or a thief; he who deceives or acts with guile is *dabhra*, such as a base person or the ocean; he who dwells is *usra*, such as a ray of light; *usrā* is a cow; he who bellows or makes sound is *vāśra*, such as excrement, a day, a temple, or a crossroads; he who lies down is *śīra*, such as a great serpent.

*Hasraḥ* means one who laughs, or a fool. *Sighraḥ* means one who moves quickly or succeeds; it refers to a virtuous person or a species of tree. *Sidhrakāḥ* are trees that are poorly grown; their forest is called *sidhrakāvaṇam*. According to the rule *vanaṃ puragāmiśrakāsidhrakāḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.4], the *ṇa* substitution occurs. *Śubhram* means that which shines or glitters; it is radiant, white, or pale yellow.

By virtue of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bāhulakāt*): *Miśraḥ* means he "mixes" or "makes sound," or it refers to a conjunction (*saṃyoga*). *Puṇḍraḥ* means he "divides" or "breaks," or it refers to one who is wicked (*duṣṭaḥ*). *Sirā* means she "binds" or "ties up" flesh, blood, and so forth, or it refers to a vessel (*nāḍī*). *Musram* means that which "crushes" or "breaks," or it refers to the water of the eyes (*netrodakam*). *Trprasram* means that which "flows out" (*trprasrati*), or it refers to blood (*rudhiram*). *Trprasrapaḥ* means a "stinging insect" (*daṃśaḥ*) because it "drinks" the flowing [blood].
14. [The substitution of *u* for the final vowel of a verbal root] before the suffixes *cak* and *krami*, as well as when a vowel other than *a* (*uc*) precedes the penultimate letter (*upadhā*).
Cukram. Rumraḥ. 14.

That which causes one to feel pain, to be satiated, or to be repelled is *cukra*; examples include *trpma*, *amlavetasa*, and so forth. That in which they delight is *rumra*; examples include *trpra* and *aruṇa*, or that which is beautiful.
15. [The suffix] *vau* is applied after the root *kas*. 15.
Vikusraḥ ||15||

It is called *vikusra* because it blossoms (*vikasati*) or moves with distinction (*viśeṣatayā gacchati*); [this refers to] the moon. The vowel *u* is substituted for the penultimate vowel of the root *kasa*.
16. And it is immeasurable and long. 16.
The mango; the copper. 16.
That which is tasted, shared, or enjoyed is *trprāmr̥*; or it refers to the mango tree (*cūta*). That which faints or longs is *tāmra*, meaning either a specific mineral or something of red color.
17. And there is the elision of the nasal in *nind* [before a suffix beginning with a consonant].
Sleep. 17.
That which censures, or that which is sleep, or the act of lying down.
18. And [the vowel] *ā* is long. 18.
Moist with heat. ||18||
18. That which decays, moves, or begs is *ārda*; it is a moist substance or the constellation Ārdrā.
19. And [the substitution of] *śu* occurs for *daś* [in the word *śuci*]. 19.
A Śūdra. ||19||

And the long vowel [of the suffix] follows. One who sorrows is a *śūdra*, or a servant. In the sense of a female associated with a male (*puṃyoga*), the feminine forms are *śūdrī* or *śūdrā*, or it denotes that caste.
20. When the suffix *dur* is present, there is elision [of the initial *d*].
Far away. ||20||

20. From the prefix *dur* [the suffix] *upapada* is applied; by the rule "after the root *iṇ* and *dhā*, *ra* is substituted and there is elision of the root," that which is reached with difficulty—that is, attained—is called *dūra*, meaning remote or distant.
After the suffix *kṛt*, there is the substitution of *ch* for *i*, and *krū* is also substituted [for *kṛt*].
He is difficult to overcome; he is cruel. ||21||

21. For the root *kṛt*, the final letter is replaced by *cha* and the whole root is replaced by *krū*; furthermore, the suffix *rak* is added. Thus, from "he cuts" (*kṛntati*) or "he cleaves" (*chinatti*), we derive *kṛcchraḥ*; and *krūraḥ* means hard, painful, or wicked.
22. And there is the elision of the suffix *ṇi*. 22.
Rudra. ||22||
Rudra is so called because he causes the wicked to weep; he is the Lord (Īśvara), the ten Rudras beginning with Prāṇa, or the individual soul (jīva).

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇerluk*) occurs not only in these cases, but also after other roots in technical terminology (*saṃjñā*), Vedic usage (*chandas*), and in general nominal suffixes (*sāmānyapratyaya*). For example: one who holds a noose (*pāśa*) as a bond is *pāśadhara*; likewise *śūladhara*, *cakradhara*, *vajradhara*, or *śaktidhara* [referring to] Kumāra; *udakadhara* for a cloud; *daṇḍadhara* for a king. In all these instances, when an *ac*-ending suffix follows, there is the elision of *ṇi* after the root *dhṛ*. One who withers, releases, or causes to grow leaves (*parṇa*) is *parṇaśuṭ*, *parṇamuṭ*, or *parṇaruṭ*.

Thus, from the root *śuṣ* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *kvip* is applied and the *ṇic* is elided. The grammatical operations such as *jaśtva* and *kutva* then take effect. "Winds blow that wither the leaves; other winds blow that shed the leaves; thereafter winds blow that cause leaves to grow; then the god rains."
And [the section] on the pair, 23.23.
Jīraḥ || 23 ||

23. From the root *ju* with the suffix *rak*, there is the substitution of *ī*. Since he becomes subtle (*sūkṣma*), he is *jīra*; [it refers to] a small sword or merchant's goods. According to the consensus of the author of the Mahābhāṣya, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for *jyā* before the suffix *rak*. [In the rule] *bhāo* 1.1.4, there is vocalization for the root *jyā* meaning "loss of age" when the suffix *rak* follows. Because he conquers or abandons his state, he is *jīra*. Likewise, according to the consensus of the author of the Mahābhāṣya, there is the suffix *anuk* after the root *jīv*. Because he lives—that is, he sustains the vital breaths—he is *jīradānuḥ*.

This is a Vedic form; and here, the *kal* suffix after the root *jīv*, the elision of *val*, and the prohibition of *ūṭh* occur precisely by virtue of *bāhulaka* (diversity/irregularity), and so forth.
The suffix *kran* is applied after the roots *su*, *sūdha*, and *gṛdh*.
Suraḥ | Sūraḥ | Dhīraḥ | Gṛdhraḥ ||24||

*Sūra* means one who impels or causes to arise, or one who possesses sovereignty; it refers to a wise person known as a "god" (*deva*), while in the feminine form *surā*, it means wine. Alternatively, *sūra* or *sūrya* is so called because he generates or impels living beings and sustains them. *Dhīra* is one who holds all things or nourishes them; it means a learned or wise man. *Gṛdhra* is one who covets or desires intensely; it may also refer to a specific type of bird.
25. And [the vowel] is long before the suffixes *śu*, *si*, *ci*, and *mī*. 25.
śūraḥ, soraḥ, cīram, mīraḥ. ||25||

25. *Śu* is a verbal root belonging to the Sautra class. One who moves (*śavati*) or goes is a *śūra* (hero), or a person characterized by valor. That which binds or fastens is *sīra*, or a plough. That which gathers is *cīra*, or bark-cloth. That which measures out or casts forth is *mīra*, or the ocean.
26. Or [the suffix] *vindh* [is applied]. 26.
Pierced through. ||26||
It blazes forth and shines intensely; that is the clear [mind], pure by its very nature.
The suffix *ran* is applied after the roots *vṛdhi* and *vap*.
Vardhra means a rampart. ||27||
That which increases is a *vardhra* or a hide; that which sows seed or cuts [grass] is a *vapra*, meaning a father, a field, a rampart, or a bank.
28. Ṛju, indra, agra, vajra, vipra, kubra, cubra, kṣura, khura, bhadra, ugra, bheha, bhela, śukra, śukla, gaura, vatri, rāma, and lā. ||28||

28. Nineteen words beginning with *ṛjra* are derived through irregular formation (*nipātana*). *Ṛjra*: He who moves, goes, or stands straight is *ṛjra*; or he is a leader. There is an absence of the [guṇa] vowel-strengthening. *Indra*: He who possesses supreme sovereignty is *indra*. He is capable, the inner self, the sun, or yoga. *Prāgra*: That which moves forward or goes is *prāgra*; it refers to the primary element or the upper portion. *Vajra*: That which strikes, reaches, or is reached is *vajra*; it is a diamond or a weapon. *Vipra*: He who sows righteousness is *vipra*; or he is a wise man.

*Kubra* means that which covers (*kumbati*) or a forest (*araṇya*). *Cubra* is that which kisses (*cumbati*) or that by which one kisses; it refers either to the mouth or [the word] *tra*. In both cases here, there is no elision [of the nasal]. That which scrapes (*kṣurati*), marks, or cuts with something is *kṣura*; it refers to a cutting substance such as *kokilākṣa*, *gokṣura*, hair-cutting tools, or a barber’s instrument. That which digs (*khurati*) or cuts, or that by which one does so, is *khura*; it refers to a hoof or [the word] *tra*. In both these instances, by the suffix *rak*, there is elision of the letter *r* and the absence of *guṇa*.

*Bhadra* means auspicious (*kalyāṇa*); it is that which shines (*bhandate*) and performs what is good (*kalyāṇaṃ karoti*). There is an elision of the letter *na*. *Ugra* refers to Maheśvara, meaning he who speaks or rules; or it means fierce (*utkaṭa*), or a warrior (*kṣatra*). *Bhera* is that from which one fears; it refers to a kettle-drum (*bherī*) or a drum (*dundubhi*). By virtue of belonging to the *gaurādi* group, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied. In another view, there is a substitution of *la* for the sound in the word *bhera*—thus *bhela*, meaning a means of crossing water, an old body, or a coward. *Śukra* is that which becomes pure (*śucyate*); it refers to Brahmā, fire, the month of Āṣāḍha, the seed of living beings, or an eye disease.

By the rule of *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (optional application), there is optionally the substitution of *l* for *r* in this very case: one who utters (*gavate*) indistinctly—whether it be white (*śuklaḥ*), or white (*śvetam*), or silver (*rajatam*)—is called *gauraḥ*, meaning white, red-colored, or fair-complexioned. *Gaurī* is a woman; [the suffix] *ṅīṣ* is applied. One who desires (*vanati*) or resorts to is a *vannaḥ*, meaning one who possesses divisions (*vibhāgī*). That by which one goes (*eti*) or moves is *irā*, meaning water or wine. *Irāvān* is the ocean; *Airāvatī* is a river. One who becomes intoxicated (*mādyati*) by *irā*, that is, by wine, is *irammadaḥ*. One who measures (*māti*) or becomes a cause of measurement is a *mālā*, a garland of flowers and the like. *Mālam* is a field. *Mālaḥ* is a person.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*): that by which one endures is *tīvra* or *tīkṣṇa*; and there is the substitution of *va* for *ja* and the lengthening of the vowel of the root.
29. Who is my enemy? 29.
He is one who wanders about. ||29||
29. He who moves or goes in a crooked manner is *saṅkasuka*; he is one who has fallen into doubt, or is fickle, or wicked.
30. After the roots *pac* and *ci*, the suffixes *na*, *u*, *ka*, *kan*, *nu*, and *mau* [are applied].
pākukaḥ | naṃśukaḥ ||30||

30. The suffix *ṇukan* is added to the roots *pac* and *naś*. For the root *pac*, the letter *c* is replaced by *k*; for the root *naś*, the augment *num* is added. Thus, one who cooks is a *pākukaḥ*, meaning a cook (*sūpakāra*). One who perishes is a *naṃśukaḥ*, meaning that which is minute (*aṇu*).
31.bhiyaḥ krukan||31|| The suffix *krukan* is applied after the word *bhī* (fear).
Bhīruka. ||31||
31. One who fears, or from whom one fears, is a timid person or a coward.
32. [The suffix *kvan* is applied] after verbal roots denoting crafts (*śilpa*) and perceptions (*saṃjñā*), even if they have not occurred previously.
A washerman; a sugarcane-crusher; a carpenter; a constant person; mica; a wandering mendicant; a drinking cup; [a breaker; a wooden statue; a doll; a flower-gatherer]; a dog; a barking dog. ||32||

32. When the sense of a craftsman (*śilpin*) or a proper name (*saṃjñā*) is to be understood, the suffix *kvun* is added to a general verbal root, whether it is accompanied by a prefix (*sopapada*) or not (*anupapada*). For example: *rajati* (he colors) becomes *rajakaḥ*, meaning a dyer or a washer of clothes. *Ikṣūn kuṭṭayati* (he crushes sugarcane) becomes *ikṣukuṭṭakaḥ*; this is a name for a producer of molasses (*gauḍika*). *Takṣati* (he fashions or makes thin) becomes *takṣakaḥ*, meaning a carpenter or a craftsman. *Dhrūvakaḥ* refers to a person who causes the release of the fetus, or it is a proper name. *Tṛprabhramati* (by which one moves with difficulty) becomes *tṛprabhramakam*, meaning a medicinal herb that causes such movement; this is a proper name.

*Carakaḥ*: one who moves about (*carati*), thus a physician (*vaidyakaśāstragantṛ*) or a wanderer. *Caṣakam*: that in which one tastes (*caṣati*) or consumes; thus a drinking vessel or a cup. *Bhañjakaḥ*: one who breaks (*bhañjati*); thus a species of fish or a wall. *Śālabhañjikā*: a game in which they break down shrubs (*śālān*). *Puṣpapracāyikā*: a game in which they gather flowers from wood (*kāṣṭham*). *Śunakaḥ*: one who goes or runs (*śunati*); thus a dog. *Bhaṣakaḥ*: one who barks or scolds (*bhaṣati*); thus a dog.

The suffix *kvun* should be understood in the following cases, which are both technical terms for artisans (*śilpin*) and proper names (*saṃjñā*): 1. *Tṛprāmalaka*: That which bears or supports the *tṛpra* (a type of grain) is the *tṛprāmalaka*, a specific tree. By virtue of belonging to the *gaurādi* group, the feminine form is *tṛprāmalakī*. 2. *Kalāpaka*: That which protects or guards a portion (*kalām aṃśam pāti rakṣati*) is the *kalāpaka*, namely the moon. Alternatively, it may mean that which possesses fragrance or gold. 3. *Kaṭaka*: That which covers or encircles a limb (*kaṭati āvṛṇoti aṅgam*) is a bracelet, a type of ornament, or what is commonly known as *kaḍaā*; it may also refer to a mountain peak, a royal capital, or a slope (*nitamba*). 4. *Laṭaka*: That which acts like a child (*laṭati bāla iva bhavati*) is a rogue or wicked person (*durjana*). In such instances, the suffix *kvun* is to be recognized.
And after the letter *r*, [the augment] *a* is optionally *l*.
Ramaka; Lamaka. ||33||
He delights, thus he is *ramaka*, or one whose nature is to delight; *lamaka* is also that very same person.
34. And likewise, two [factors] are abandoned by seeing. 34.
The snake-catcher. ||34||
34. *Jahaka* means one who leaves, abandons, or causes loss; it refers to a renouncer or time (*kāla*).
35. *dhma* and *dham* [are also used]. 35.
The bellower. ||35||
One who blows, making a sound, or one who joins the fire with bellows, is a "blower," namely a smith or a laborer.
36. And there is killing and striking. 36.
The Obstructor. ||36||
One who kills is a slayer; that is, a perpetrator of violence.
37. The suffix *bahu* is used diversely in other cases as well.
Kuhaka, kṛtakam, bhidakaḥ, chidakam, rucakam, laṅgakaḥ, ujbhakaḥ. ||37||

Due to the frequent occurrence of the suffix *kvun*, it is applied elsewhere as well: that which causes wonder or produces astonishment is a *kuhaka*—a hypocrite or mist; that which cuts or severs is a *kṛtaka*—a falsehood; that by which one pierces is a *bhidaka*—a sword; that by which one cuts is a *chidaka*—a thunderbolt; that by which one shines is a *rucaka*—a citron (commonly known as *vijaurā nīṃbū*) or a necklace; that which leaps or moves is a *laṅgaka*—a lover; that which ejects or casts forth is an *ujbhaka*—a yogi or a cloud.
38. According to the Easterners, the vowel *ṛ* is substituted for *kṛṣi* when it takes the suffix *vṛddhi*.
Kārṣakaḥ; kṛṣakaḥ. ||38||
38. One who plows is a *kārṣaka*, or a *kṛṣaka*, or a *kṛṣībala*.
And water. ||39||
It is called *udaka* or *jala* because it moistens (*unatti*) or causes to become wet (*kledayati*).
40. The suffix *ki* is applied after the verbal roots *vṛśca* and *kṛṣ*.
Scorpion; plowman. ||40||

40. It is called *vṛścika* because it "tears" (*vṛścati*) or "cuts" (*chinatti*); it is a venomous creature, a specific type of living being, or a "thorny insect" (*śūkakīṭa*), commonly known as a *keṃcutrprā*. That by which one plows is a *kṛṣika*, or it refers to the plowshare (*phāla*).
41. Before [the word *prāṅ*], [the term] *paṇikaśaḥ* [is used]. 41.
prāpaṇikaḥ; prākaṣikaḥ ||41||

41. He praises [the goods] extensively and all around; thus he is a merchant (*prāpaṇika*) or a seller of merchandise (*paṇyavikrayin*). Or, because he drags away (*prākaṣati*) or destroys, he is a robber (*prākaṣika*), such as one who administers poison (*pāradādika*).
42. And there is lengthening of the vowel in the root *muṣ*.
The mouse. ||42||

It is called *mūṣika* (a mouse) because it steals (*muṣṇāti*) objects; alternatively, it is *trprākhu*. In the feminine, it is *mūṣikā*, with the suffix *ṭāp* applied due to its inclusion in the *trprādi* group.
43. There is also vocalization (samprasāraṇa) of the root *śyami*.
Sīmikaḥ || 43 ||
43. *Syamati* means "he calls out"; thus, *sīmika* refers either to a particular tree or [a person who calls out].
44. This is the action. 44.
A buyer. ||44||
44. One who purchases another object with wealth, or gives or takes it, is a *krayika*, a buyer; one who sells is a *vikrayika*, a seller.
45. After the prefix *āṅ*, [the suffix *kvi* is applied] after the roots *paṇi*, *pani*, *pati*, and *khan*.
āpaṇikaḥ, āpanika, āpatikaḥ, ākhanikaḥ ||45||

One who buys and sells on all sides is a *trpāpaṇika*, a Vaiśya; the statement [of the suffix] is for the sake of the accent (*nitsvara*) when the secondary suffix (*ṭhak*) is applied in the sense of "one who deals by means of a marketplace" (*trpāpaṇena vyavaharati*). Or, one who causes a marketplace to be established is a *trpāpaṇika*, a mleccha tribe. One who flies everywhere is a *trpāpatika*, a hawk. One who digs everywhere is a *trpākhanika*, a mouse or a boar.
46. The suffix *inac* is applied after the roots √śās, √hṛ, and √av.
śyenaḥ, styenaḥ, hariṇaḥ, avinaḥ ||46||

46. *Śyena* means "he glides" or "he moves," thus it is a type of bird; or, he who "coagulates," "makes sound," or "forms a mass" is *styena*, meaning a thief. *Harina* means "he seizes," thus it is a deer or one of pale color; in the feminine, *hariṇī* means a beautiful woman, a specific meter, or green-colored. *Trpavina* means "he performs protection and so forth," thus it is a protector or a priest.
The root √vṛj takes the suffix *k* and is also *kit*.
47. Furthermore, it is called *vṛjina* because it shaves (*vṛkte*) or avoids [virtue]; it refers to hair, evil, or that which is crooked.
48. And [the term] *ajeraja* [is also used]. 48.
The deerskin. ||48||
That which goes quickly or throws [objects] is *trprajina*, or it is leather (*carma*); the mention of *trpra* is for the purpose of excluding [other] types of movement.
49. It occurs abundantly elsewhere as well. ||49||

49. It is *kaṭhina* because it lives with difficulty, or it is hard (*kaṭhora*). He is *kuṇḍina* because he burns or consumes; the son of that sage is *kauṇḍinya*. It is *barhiṇa* because it becomes preeminent, or it is a peacock (*mayūra*). It is *phalina* because it bears fruit or becomes shattered; it is a tree possessing fruit (*phalavān*). It is *nalina* because it becomes fragrant, or it is a lotus (*kamala*). It is *masina* because it matures or transforms, or it is well-grounded (*supiṣṭa*). It is *malina* because it holds or maintains, or it is soiled (*malayukta*).

He who harms or desires to kill is Druhiṇa, namely Brahmā; or, he who pierces (dyati) or shatters darkness (tṛpna) is Dinam, namely the day. Due to the *kit* suffix *inac*, there is the elision of the vowel *ā*.
50. The suffix *inan* is applied after the roots *du* and *dakṣi*.
Wealth; the dexterous one; the sacrificial fee. ||50||

50. That which flows, moves, or is obtained is *draviṇa*; it refers to gold or valor. He who is capable, increases, or acts swiftly is *dakṣiṇa*; it also denotes one who is straightforward, the right side, that which is dependent on another, and compliance. In the feminine, *dakṣiṇā* means a gift or a sacrificial fee (*pratiṣṭhā*).
51. After the root *ṛ*, [the suffix] *i* is added, and it is also marked with the *k* indicatory letter (*kit*).
A barren wasteland. ||51||
51. That which people reach or go to—namely, a desert (iriṇa), meaning a barren or saline wasteland—is so called.
52. And there is shortening of the vowel in the roots *vep* and *tuhy*.
A forest; cold. ||52||

That which trembles or shakes, or where it is dense like a forest, that which moves or goes, or that which begs—these are *tuhina* or *hima* (snow/frost). When the suffix *guṇa* is applied, the vowel becomes short.
53. And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the roots *tali* and *puli*.
The sandy bank is soft. ||53||

It is called *talina* because it spreads out (*tālayati*) or stands firm (*pratitiṣṭhati*), meaning it is sparse, separate, very small, or transparent. It is called *pulina* because it swells (*polayati*) or becomes large, or because it is near the water (*jala-sāmīpya*).
54. They should be honored. 54.
A pregnant woman. ||54||
She who is proud, or who attains [pride], or who causes pride, or who releases it, is called *gurviṇī* or *garbhiṇī*.
55. And [the rule applies] to *ruha* as well. 55.
Rohiṇas. ||55||

It grows from a seed; thus it is born, and is called *rohiṇa*, such as a sandalwood tree (*candanavṛkṣa*). From a word denoting a genus (*jāti*), the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to form *rohiṇī*, such as a cow (*gauḥ*). By virtue of belonging to the *prajñādi* group, the suffix *aṇ* is applied to form *rohīṇa*.
And [the suffix] maherin also [is applied]. 56.
Māhinam; mahinam. ||56||
56. That which is honored or worshipped greatly is "māhinam"; it refers either to greatness or to sovereignty, and it conforms to the usage of the *cādi* group.
57. After the roots vac, pracch, śri, sru, dru, pru, and jū, the suffix kvip is added; there is lengthening of the vowel and no vocalization (saṃprasāraṇa).
vāk, prāṭ, śrīḥ, srūḥ, drūḥ, kaṭaprūḥ, jūḥ. ||57||

*Vāk*: that by which one speaks or utters sounds. *Prāṭ*: one who asks. *Śabdaprāṭ*: one who asks about words; a student (*śiṣya*). *Śabdaprāśaḥ*: [variant of the above]. According to Pāṇini 6.4.19, *chvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca*, the *ch* is replaced by *ś*. *Śrīḥ*: that which flows toward or is resorted to; the arrangement of the Lord or beauty. *Srūḥ*: that which flows or from which it flows; a means for sacrifice (*yajñasādhana*). *Drūḥ*: that by which one is driven or by which suffering is experienced; gold (*hiraṇya*).

One who moves by means of a *kaṭa* (a mat or hip-region) is a *kaṭaprūḥ*, meaning a lustful person or an insect. One who goes swiftly is a *jūḥ*, meaning a hare, a horse, a bull, light, or knowledge. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—that in which clouds rain is the *prāvṛṭ* season; that by which one closes or shuts is a *dvāḥ* (door); [nominative dual] *dvārau*; that which swells or increases with water is *udaśvit*, meaning buttermilk; and that by which they praise or recite is an *ṛk* (verse).
58. And there is the shortening of the vowel in the root *āp*.
The waters. ||58||
58. *Trp* means "waters," because they reach (*āpnuvanti*) the body. This term is always plural and feminine. Examples: *trpāpaḥ*, *trpadbhiḥ*, *adbhyaḥ*, and so forth.
59. After the root *vraj*, when followed by another word (*para*), the substitute *ṣ* is applied at the end of a word (*padānte*).
The wandering mendicant. ||59||
59. *kvip*: He wanders everywhere, on all sides, is a *parivrāj* (wandering mendicant); [the forms are] *parivrājau*, *parivrājaḥ*, or a *saṃnyāsī* (renunciant).
60. *Hu* is treated like *ślu*.
The *juhū* ladle. ||60||
That by which one offers oblations, gives gifts, or eats is the *juhū*; it is either a specific sacrificial ladle or a general term for a type of ladle.
61. What is a *sruva* ladle? 61.
The *sruva* ladle. ||61||
That from which clarified butter flows is a *sruva*, or it is an instrument for accomplishing sacrifice.
And also sixty-two.
Sruk || 62 ||
62. The suffix *cik* also occurs after the root *sru*. That from which the clarified butter (*dhṛta*) flows is a *sruk* (ladle), or it refers to the substance appropriate for sacrifice.
63. And for the root *tan*, [the suffix] *va* is substituted for *ana*. 63.
Skin. 63.

It is called *tvak* because it extends or spreads out; thus there are the forms *tvac*, *tvacau*, and *tvacaḥ*. It refers to the covering of the body, whether it be skin (*carma*) or bark (*valkala*).
The suffix *ḍau* is applied after the roots *glai* and *nud*.
glauḥ | nauḥ ||64||
*Glauḥ* means "the moon" or "one who suffers," as it causes exhaustion and the loss of joy; *nauḥ* means "a boat" or "a means for crossing water," as it pushes forward and impels one across.
65. The indeclinable *cvi* [is used] in the sense of "becoming that which it was not before. 65.

P. 65. A word ending in the suffix *trp*, one ending in a suffix marked with the indicatory letter *e* (*ejant*), and one ending in the suffix *śatṛ* (*śatṛśānac*) alone receive the designation of indeclinable (*avyaya*). By this restrictive rule, in the view that the *uṇādi* derivatives are derived from roots, words ending in such suffixes do not receive the designation of indeclinable by the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* (P. 1.1.39). Examples include: *glaukaroti* ("he makes into the moon"), *glaubhavati* ("it becomes the moon"), *glausyāt* ("may it be the moon"); *naukaroti*, etc. [The forms] *glauḥ* and *nauḥ* [are examples]. Since there is no designation of indeclinable for these alone, the elision of case-endings does not occur.
The suffix *ḍai* is applied after the root *rāti*.
The letter *rāḥ* || 66 ||

66. That which gives (*rāti*), causes to be given (*dadāti*), or is given (*dīyate*) is *rāḥ*; [the forms are] *rāyau*, *rāyaḥ*—meaning wealth or gold. With the suffix *cvi*, one says "he makes into wealth" (*rai karoti*), and so forth.
67. *gamer ḍoḥ* ||67|| [The suffix] *ḍo* [is applied] after the root *gam*.
The cow. ||67||

67. That which goes (*gacchati*) wherever or by whatever means is called *go* (cow). It may refer to a beast, a sense organ, happiness, a ray, a thunderbolt, the moon, the earth, speech, or water. Just as *go* means "going," so too does *gamanam* or *prāptiḥ* (attainment) signify this. *Gavayaḥ* is a specific wild animal resembling a cow; [it is derived from] *go* with the suffix *aya*. The feminine form is *gavayī*, due to its inclusion in the *gaurādi* group, taking the suffix *ṅīṣ*. With the suffix *cvipratyaya*, one says *gokaroti* ("he makes into a cow"), and so forth. By way of irregularity (*bāhulakāt*): that in which or by which the worlds shine (*dyotante*), or that which shines, is *dyauḥ* (the sky or heaven); it refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). The dual is *dyāvau*, the plural is *dyāvaḥ*, and so on.
And from delusion, suffering arises. 68.
*bhrūḥ* (the brow) and *agregūḥ* (one who goes at the head) [are formed with the suffix *ū*]. ||68||

68. The suffix *ḍū* is added to a verbal root after the prefix *cād*. Thus, from the root *bhram* (to wander/to move), one gets *bhrūḥ*, meaning either "the eyebrow" (a line above the eyes) or "one who wanders. From the root *gam* (to go) with the prefixes *tri-pra-agra*, one gets *tripragregūḥ*, meaning "a servant" (one who goes before).
69. *damerḍosiḥ* ||69||
The arm. ||69||
That by which one tames or becomes tranquil, or that which is itself tamed or tranquil, is *doḥ* or *doṣaḥ*, meaning either a fault or an arm.
70. And after the words *paṇa* and *ijyā*, the suffix *vaḥ* [is applied]. 70.
The merchant. ||70||

One who bargains or trades is a *vaṇik* or *vaṇij*; the plural is *vaṇijaḥ*, or it may refer to a *vaiśya*. By adding the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the base itself according to the rule for words beginning with *prajñā*, one forms *vāṇijaḥ*.
71. The suffix *vaś* is optionally treated as having an indicatory *k*.
The seeker. 71.
71. He who desires, or that which is desired, is *uśik* and *kuśika*, or *uśijaḥ*; [this refers to] Agni or clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
72. After the root *bhṛ* (to carry), [the suffix] *uc* is applied.
The Bhurik [meter]. ||72||
72. *Ijiḥ* is *kit*. That which supports (*bharati*) and sustains (*dharati*) everything is *bhurik*, or it is the earth (*bhūmi*). [The forms are: *bhurijau*, *bhurijaḥ*.
The suffix *jasi* (nominative plural) is replaced by *sah*, *ur*, and *in*.
The victorious one; the triumphant one. 73.

That which withers, releases, causes to decay, or destroys is *jasuri*, meaning either the thunderbolt (*vajra*) or the sun. That which endures a burden is *sahuri*, meaning either the sun or the earth.
74. The suffix *yuc* is applied after roots ending in *sū*, *yū*, and *vṛ*.
Savanaḥ, yavanaḥ, ravaṇaḥ, varaṇaḥ. ||74||

74. That which flows, produces, or distills—that is, extracts—flavors is *savana*, such as the moon. That which joins, mixes, or does not mix is *yavana*, such as a type of barbarian (*mleccha*). That which cries out or makes sound is *ravaṇa*, such as the cuckoo bird. That which covers or accepts is *varaṇa*, such as water or a type of tree.
75. [The suffixes] aś and raś [are applied after the verbal root √i]. 75.
The girdle. ||75||

75. From the root *dhā*, there is the substitution of *raś*. Because it "reaches" (*aśnute*) or pervades, it is called *raśanā*; it refers to a woman’s girdle or an ornament. However, the word *rasanā*, which contains a dental *s*, ends in the suffix *lyu* (ana) according to the rule for the *nandī*-group; that by which one tastes or relishes is the *rasanā*, the tongue. According to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* [Pāṇini 3.3.113], the suffix *lyu* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
76. And there is the elision of the penultimate vowel.
Rice porridge. ||76||
76. That which does not become moist when boiled is called *trp-odana*, or *bhakta*.
77. And [the suffix] *ga* is substituted for the root *gam*.
The sky. ||77||
77. *Gagana* is that in which beings (*ga*) go; it is either the sky or the atmosphere.
78. There are many [instances] elsewhere as well. ||78||

The suffix *yuc* frequently occurs after other verbal roots as well: that which shines or illuminates is *dyotanaḥ*, such as a lamp; that which flows, trickles, or moves is *syandanaḥ*, such as a chariot; that by which form is led or attained is *nayanam*, such as the eye; that which gladdens or delights is *candanam*, such as a fragrant tree; that which pleases is *rocanā*, such as the medicinal substance *gorocana*; that which casts forth or projects is *prasanaḥ*, such as a yellow-colored *śāla* tree.

That which surpasses the king is *rājātana*, or it is a flower; that by which one hears is *śravaṇā*, or it is a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). In this same way, other words ending in the suffix *yuc* should also be derived according to their respective usage.
The suffix *kyun* is applied after the root *rañj*.
The dyeing [of the robes]. ||79||

79. That by which clothes are dyed is *rañjana*; *kusumbha* (safflower) is an example. In the feminine gender, with the suffix *ṅīṣ*, it becomes *rajanī*, meaning turmeric (*haridrā*). When the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied, it remains simply *rañjanam*, though there is a difference in accent.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the word *kṛpaṇa* is derived in the sense of "one who is greedy" or "one who is full of desire."
In the Vedic language (chandas), the suffix *kvasu* is applied after the roots *bhū*, *sū*, *dhū*, and *bhrasj*.
The world; the place of birth; the place of sexual union; the place of roasting. ||80||

80. *Bhuvana* means "it exists," thus it refers to the world or the universe; by virtue of the rule allowing for frequent usage (*bahulavacana*), it is also employed in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*). *Suvana* means "he brings forth" or "is brought forth," referring to the Lord (*īśvara*) or the Sun (*sūrya*). *Dhuvana* means "it shakes" or "it causes to tremble," referring to the wind or fire. *Nidhuvana* means amorous play or dalliance. *Bhṛjjanam* is that in which something is roasted or becomes fully cooked; it refers to a pan for roasting grain (*annabharjanakapāla*).
The affix *kyu* is applied after the roots *kṝ*, *pṝ*, *vṛj*, *mand*, and *dhāñ*.
Radiance, fulfillment, the enclosure, the delight, the conclusion. ||81||

81. It is called *kiraṇa* because it scatters (*kirati*) or disperses darkness. It is called *samudra* because it nourishes (*piparti*), protects (*pālayati*), or fills (*pūrayati*); or it is so called because it becomes full with waters (*jalaiḥ pūrṇo bhavati*). It is called *vṛjana* because it excludes (*vṛkte*) or avoids; *vṛj* means the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) or strength (*bala*). That by which one praises (*mandate*), sleeps, or desires is *mandana*, meaning a hymn of praise (*stotra*). That which holds firmly (*nitarāṃ dadhāti*) is *nidhana*, meaning death (*maraṇa*). By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the word *dhana* may also be derived from the root alone.
82. After the root *dhṛṣ*, the substitute *dhiṣ* is applied when a name is being formed.
Dhiṣaṇā. ||82||

He who inspires confidence (*dhuṣṇoti*) or bestows boldness (*prāgalbhya*) is *dhiṣaṇaḥ*; [or] *dhiṣaṇā* means intellect (*buddhi*). Here, by the inclusion of the term "technical name" (*sañjñā*), it is understood that the *uṇādi* suffixes have etymological (*yaugika*) meanings in their general sense, because a technical name is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in that specific sense. If, through the division of base and suffix, an etymological meaning did not emerge from the *uṇādi* suffixes, then all words formed with *uṇādi* suffixes would be exclusively denoters of technical names; in that case, the further mention of "technical name" would be redundant.
83. After *han*, [the suffix] *ghurac* [is applied]. 83.
The roaring one. ||83||
That which arises through striking or by means of a blow is the sound *ghuraṇa*.
84. When expressing the present tense, the suffixes *pṛṣat*, *bṛhat*, *mahat*, and *jagat* are used, and they are treated like words ending in the *śatṛ* suffix.

84. Words such as *pṛṣat* and others, which denote present meaning, are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) by adding the suffix *tra*. And for these words, grammatical operations are performed as if they were [words ending in] the suffix *śatṛ*. That which sprinkles (*parṣati*), pours (*siñcati*), or strikes (*hinasti*) is *pṛṣat*; it refers either to a specific kind of deer or to a drop (*bindu*). In the feminine, it is *pṛṣatī* or *pṛṣanti* (the form *pṛṣatī* is used). It grows (*barhati*, *vardhate*)—it is *bṛhat*. It is used in three genders in the sense of "great. In the feminine, it is *bṛhatī*, referring to a particular type of Vedic meter. That which is great (*mahati*), honors (*pūjayati*), or is honored (*pūjyate*) is *mahat*; [in the masculine] *mahān*. The state of being great is *mahimā*.

The suffix *ṅīp* is applied after *mahat* to form *mahatī*, meaning either Nārada’s seven-stringed lute (*vīṇā*) or the world. That which moves is called *jagat*; here, the verbal root undergoes the substitution *jagad*. *Jagat* is neuter when it signifies the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), or masculine when it signifies wind. When denoting that which is mobile, it possesses all three genders. In the feminine, *jagatī* refers to a specific type of meter or to people.
85. Saṃścat, tṛpad, vehat. 85.

85. These also are irregularly formed (nipātita) with the suffix *at*. That which is piled together is *saṃścat*, meaning either a deceiver (*kuhaka*) or [something else]. There is the augment *suṭ* for the suffix and the elision of the vowel *i* of the root. "It behaves like one who piles together" is *saṃścāyate*; the smoke (*dhūmaḥ*) [is so called], because of the suffix *kyaṅ* due to its inclusion in the *bhṛśādi* group. That which satisfies or pleases is *tṛpat*, meaning a parasol (*chatra*). That which strikes specifically is *vehat*; it strikes the fetus (*garbha*), thus it is a cow that destroys the fetus (*garbhopaghātinī*).

The substitution of the single vowel *e* for the prefix *vi-* and the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) of the verbal root are separated from the preceding rule in order to prevent the application of the *śatṛ*-treatment (*śatṛvad-bhāva*). By this, forms such as *vehatī*, *vehatas*, and *saṃścatas* are established.
In Vedic (chandasi), the suffix *asān* is applied after the roots *śu* and *jṛ*.
Exerting himself; growing old. ||86||

86. *Śavasānaḥ* is that in which beings (*śavanti*) go; it is either a path or one who grows old (*jīryati*) when his youth has declined, thus *jarasānaḥ*, meaning an elderly person. By virtue of the rule of abundance (*bāhulaka*), *darasānaḥ* is that which pierces or rends darkness; it is light. *Tarasānaḥ* is that by which one crosses over; it is a boat. *Varasānaḥ* is that which covers; it is one who has taken a wife.
The suffix *i* is added after the roots *ṛji*, *vṛdhi*, *mandi*, and *sahi*, and it is marked with the *k*-diacritic.
ṛñjasānaḥ, vṛdhasānaḥ, mandasānaḥ, sahasānaḥ. ||87||

87. *Ṛñjasānaḥ* is that which causes plants and the like to grow, namely the cloud; or it is one who increases, namely a man. *Vṛdhasānaḥ* is one who gladdens by means of praise and so forth, namely the individual soul (*jīva*) or fire (*agni*). *Sahasānaḥ* is one who endures, namely a peacock or the sacrifice (*yajña*).
The suffix *guṇa* is also [substituted] for *śuṭ*.
Trprarśasānaḥ || 88 ||

He who goes to or attains all [desires] is *sarvatrirpsānaḥ*, meaning "one who is satisfied with everything" or "one whose fire is satisfied. There is a *guṇa* substitution for the root, the suffix *anaḥ*, and the augment *śuṭ*.
89. *Samyāna* is [the substitute] for *stu*. ||89||
Free from intimacy. ||89||
One who praises correctly is "saṃstavānaḥ," or alternatively, "vāgmī" (eloquent).
90. After the words *yudh*, *budh*, and *dṛś*, [the suffix] *rak* is also applied.
yudhānaḥ, budhānaḥ, dṛśānaḥ ||90||

He fights, thus he is *yudhānaḥ*—meaning either an enemy or a warrior; he awakens, thus he is *budhānaḥ*—meaning either a teacher or one who is conscious; he sees, thus he is *dṛśānaḥ*—meaning either a world-protector (*lokapāla*) or the sun. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), that which becomes capable is *kṛpāṇaḥ*—meaning a sword; that which makes solid or becomes massive is *pāṣāṇaḥ* (a stone), where the vowel lengthening occurs due to the suffix being marked with *ṇ*.
91. After the root *hurcch*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffix *san* and elision (*lopa*) of the letter *ch*.
The one who is crooked. ||91||
It is called *juhurāṇaḥ* because it becomes crooked (*hūrchati*) or because it refers to the moon.
92. And [the substitution of] *śvit* is also [subject to the same rule]. 92.
The one who feels remorse. ||92||

92. There is elision of the suffix *san*, and the letter *t* is replaced by *d*. Because the term *kit* is understood [from the previous rule], there is a prohibition of *guṇa* substitution. Thus, one who performs evil deeds is called *śiśvidānaḥ*, meaning "he who shines white" (or "is purified").
93. After the roots *muci* and *yudhi*, the suffix *san* is optionally applied [to form the desiderative].
Releasing; fighting. ||93||
He who releases is *mumucānaḥ*, a releaser (*mocakaḥ*); he who fights is *yuyudhānaḥ*, a warrior (*yoddhā*).
The suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are applied after the verbal roots *śaṃs*, *kṣad*, and others, when used as proper names (*sañjñā*), and they are without the augment *iṭ*.
śaṃstā, śaṃstarau; kṣattā, kṣattārau. ||94||

94. From the roots beginning with *śaṃs* and those beginning with *kṣad*, the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are applied respectively; both of these are without the augment *iṭ*. Thus, one who praises or lauds is called *śaṃstā* (a praiser) or *stotā* (a singer). Because the word *naptṛ* and others are listed separately in the rule *tṛpraptṛntṛcaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.11], the *tṛn* and *tṛc* suffixes derived from the *uṇādi* list are not included here. Consequently, in forms such as *śaṃstarau* and *śaṃstaraḥ*, the lengthening of the vowel does not occur. One who instructs or trains in dharma and so forth is a *śāstā* (teacher) or a scholar. A *praśāstā* is a king. [Dual: *praśāstārau*. [Plural: *praśāstāraḥ*.

The suffix *ghañ* is applied for enumeration: the root *kṣad* in the sense of "to cover" is a Vedic (sautra) root. One who covers or conceals is a *kṣattṛ*, namely a charioteer or a doorkeeper, or one born of a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother. That by which one cuts or grinds is a *kṣottṛ*, namely a pestle. One who brings forth duties is an *unnetṛ*, namely a priest (*ṛtvij*). One who thinks or knows is a *mantṛ*, namely a wise man. One who kills is a *hantṛ*, namely a thief. A supporter is the Lord (*īśvara*), and an instructor is a teacher (*guru*), and so forth.
95. Neptṛ, neṣṭṛ, tvaṣṭṛ, hotṛ, potṛ, bhrātṛ, jāmātṛ, mātṛ, pitṛ, and duhitṛ [have ṛ in the first syllable].

95. Ten words beginning with *naptr* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) by means of the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc*. *Naptā* (nephew) is derived from the root *naś* ("to perish") with the suffix *tṛ*; it refers to a grandson (*pautra*) or a daughter’s son (*dauhitraka*). The son of a *naptṛ* would be a *pranaptā*. *Naptrī* is the feminine form meaning a granddaughter. Here, the original form of the negative particle *nañ* is preserved. From the root *nī* ("to lead"), with the augment *puk*, we have *neṣṭā*, meaning one who leads or a priest (*ṛtvij*). *Tvaṣṭā* (the carpenter-god or sun) is derived from the root *tviṣ* ("to shine"); here the vowel *i* is replaced by *a*. *Hotā* (the invoker or sacrificer) is derived from the root *hu* ("to offer"). *Potā* (the purifier; Viṣṇu or Īśvara) is one who purifies everything through his pervasiveness. *Bhrātā* (brother) is derived from the root *bhrāj* ("to shine"); it refers to a uterine brother (*sodarya*).

There is the elision of the letter *j*. He who measures (*māti*), fashions (*minoti*), measures out (*mimīte*), or purifies (*mārjayati*) his wife—the maiden—is the son-in-law (*jāmātā*), the husband of the daughter. In the root *mṛj*, when the letter *r* is present, there is the elision of the letter *j*. She who honors (*mānayati*) or shows respect is the mother (*mātā*), or she who gives birth. Because it belongs to the *svasṛ*-class, there is the prohibition of the suffix *ṭāp*. He who protects (*pāti*) is the father (*pitā*), or the progenitor. She who milks (*dogdhi*) [the milk of] her duties—that is, fulfills them—is the daughter (*duhitā*), or the female child. The offspring of the daughter is the "daughter's son" (*dauhitraḥ*).
That is the ninth [chapter], the *Avaserṛn*.
With the teeth. ||96||
One who breathes well is called *svasā*, meaning a sister or a female sibling.
97. And there is vṛddhi for the root *yati*.
She has gone. ||97||
97. The agent of *yat* [becomes the object] of the brothers' wives; they become mutual agents of going.
98. Also after the root *nand*, when preceded by the negative particle *nañ*.
Nanāndā; nanandā. ||98||

She who does not rejoice but is contented is called *nanāndā*; due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is an absence of the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*), and thus *nanandā* refers to the husband's sister.
99. Various [types] || 99 ||
The gods. 99.
They are called *devas* because they play, sport, and so forth; or they are the younger brother of the Lord (*pati*).
The suffix *ṇic* is applied after the root *nī*, and it is also *ḍit*.

100. Because the suffix *ṛt* is marked with the *ḍi*-indicator, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the vowel preceding the final consonant). One who leads (*nayati*) matters to be done is a *nā*; [the forms are] *narau*, *naraḥ*. A *nārī* is a woman whose hair is bound or whose husband has died.
In the Vedic language, [the form] *savye* occurs when it is used as a locative.
The one who stands on the left. ||101||

101. Due to the *ḍit* suffix, there is elision of the vowel *ā*. One who stands on the left (*savye*), that is, on the left side, is a *savyeṣṭhā*, namely a charioteer. There is elision of the *trc* suffix after the locative case ending.
The suffix *ani* is applied after the verbal roots *ṛ*, *sṛ*, *dhṛ*, *dham*, *yam*, *yaś*, *vī*, and *tṝ*.
Araṇi, saraṇi, dharaṇi, dhamani, trpramani, aśani, avani, taraṇi. ||102||

102. That by which one goes or attains is a *tṛpraṇi* (a fire-drill), consisting of two pieces of wood for the production of fire. A *saraṇi* is that in which things flow or move; it is a path. From the root *sṛ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the suffix *ani* is applied to form *sāraṇi*; in the feminine, it is *sāraṇī*. By way of irregularity (*bāhulaka*)—it pierces or destroys, thus *śaraṇi*. It supports everything, thus *dharaṇi*, meaning the earth. *Dhami* is a Vedic (Sautra) root. It blows or causes [fluids like] sap to flow, thus *dhamana*, meaning a vessel or tube.

*Trpramaniḥ*: that by which one eats (*trpram atti*), or that which goes (*gatiḥ*); or he who eats, enjoys, or pervades (*vyāpnoti*)—that is *trpraśaniḥ*, meaning the thunderbolt (*vajram*). Or, *trpravaniḥ*: that which performs protection and so forth (*trpravati rakṣaṇādikam karoti*), meaning the earth (*bhūmiḥ*). *Taraṇiḥ*: that by which or that which crosses over (*tarati*); it refers to the sun (*sūryaḥ*), a maiden (*kumārī*), a boat (*naus*), or a specific medicinal herb (*auṣadhiviśeṣaḥ*). By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulakāt*): *rajaniḥ* means "she who colors" (*rajati*), referring to the night (*rātriḥ*). There is the elision of the nasal (*nalopaḥ*). In the feminine, *rajanī* means the night, or the grape (*drākṣā*), or turmeric (*haridrā*).
In the Veda, the suffix *san* is added to the root *śuṣ* after the prefix *āṅ*.
The one who desires to burn brightly. ||103||

103. The suffix *ani* is added after a root ending in *san* when preceded by the prefix *ā*. That by which objects are completely dried up is *trpāśuśukṣaṇiḥ*, or *trpāgniḥ* (the fire that thoroughly desires to consume).
104. After the root *kṛṣ* and after a prefix beginning with a vowel, [the suffix *ghañ*] is replaced by *dha*.
The subduer. ||104||
One who rubs is a *gharṣaṇi*, meaning either a man or an unchaste woman; with the suffix *ṅīṣ*, it becomes *gharṣaṇī*.
105. And [the suffix] *muṭ* is also applied after the verbal root *ad*.
Without pride. ||105||
105. *Attī* means one who consumes; it refers either to hunger or to fire.
106. And because of concealment. ||106||
The path. ||106||
That upon which one proceeds is the *vartanī*, meaning either a path or a single track.
The suffix *ki* is applied after the root *kṣip*.
The thrower. ||107||
One casts enemies with this; thus it is called *kṣipaṇi*, or it is a weapon.
The suffix *isi* is applied after the verbal roots *arc*, *śuci*, *husṛpi*, *chādi*, and *chardi*.
*arcis*, *śocis*, *havis*, *sarpiḥ*, *chadis*, *chadis* || 108 ||

That by which one is praised is *trprarciḥ*, or it means "flame. That which burns or causes to burn is *śociḥ*, or it means "light. That which is offered is *haviḥ*, or it is a substance fit for oblation (*homa*). That by which one moves or glides is *sarpiḥ*, or it is clarified butter (*ghṛta*). That by which one covers is *chadiḥ*, meaning a covering or a means of covering such as grass; here the short vowel substitution occurs according to Pāṇini 6.4.97. That which one vomits is *chardiḥ*, meaning vomiting or a disease.
By virtue of the rule regarding diversity (*bāhulaka*), that which descends from all sides is *trprāviḥ*, meaning "manifestation"; this is an indeclinable word.
109. After the root *bṛṃh*, there is elision of the nasal (*n*).
Barhis (109): It is called *barhis* because it expands (*bṛṃhati*) or increases (*vardhati*); or else, it refers to the *darbha* grass.
110. After the root *dyuti* and after [a verbal root ending in] a palatal (*j*), there is the substitute *ja*.

That which shines or illuminates is *jyotis*, such as fire, the sun, and so forth. A treatise composed concerning *jyotis* is called *Jyotiṣam*. Because a grammatical rule based on a specific technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), the prohibition of *vṛddhi* [substitution] applies here.
111. After *vasu*, [the suffix *kvip* is applied] in the sense of "name" (*sañjñā*) when it refers to *ruc*. 111.
Vasurocis. ||111||

111. He shines upon the Vasus, Agni, and others; thus he is Vasurocis, or [he is] Sacrifice (Yajña). By virtue of the rule of diversity (bāhulaka), the word *rociḥ* may also denote a flame even when used alone.
112. The suffix *kit* follows the root *bhu*.
The root *bhu* (to be). ||112||
112. That which exists within or that by which one exists is the earth, or it is the ocean.
113. *saha* and *dha* [are also used]. 113.
The root *sadhi*. ||113||
113. One who bears a burden is a *sadhi*; it refers either to a companion or to an ox.
114. *thuk* is substituted for the root *pā-* (to drink) [in the present indicative].
The path. ||114||
That by which one drinks, or that which is drunk, is the path; it is either the eye or the ocean.
115. Janerusiḥ || 115 ||
Januḥ || 115 ||

That which is born is *januḥ*; [the forms] *januṣī* and *jananam* also occur due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). Furthermore, from the root *man*, by virtue of the same rule of diversity, one who thinks or knows is *manuḥ* (masculine) and *manuṣī* (feminine).
116. *manerdhaḥ* in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).
Madhu ||116||
That by which one thinks or perceives, or that which is thought or perceived, is either honey or a purifying substance.
The suffix *ni* is added after the verbal roots *artti*, *pṛ*, *vapi*, *yaji*, *tan*, *dhan*, and *tap*.
aruḥ, paruḥ, vapuḥ, yajuḥ, tanuḥ, dhanuḥ, tapuḥ. ||117||

117. *Paruḥ*: that which one reaches or attains; it refers to a joint or a wound. *Paruḥ*: that by which one fills; it refers to a knot or a joint. *Vapuḥ*: that from which one sows seeds and so forth; it refers to the body. *Yajuḥ*: that by which one sacrifices; it refers to a specific portion of the Veda. *Tanuḥ*: that by which one extends activities; it refers to the body. *Dhanuḥ*: that by which one acquires wealth and so forth; it refers to a bow or the act of discharging an arrow. *Tapuḥ*: that which heats or causes suffering; it refers to the sun, fire, or an enemy.
118. And it is eternal. 118.
The lifespan is three [years]. ||118||
118. That which is gone to or attained is *trpāyuḥ*, meaning life or existence. From the prefix *jaṭā* [with the root *i*], *jaṭāyuḥ* is formed, referring to the king of birds.
The suffix *śi* is also applied after the root *cakṣ*. (119)
The eye. ||119||
One sees form by means of this, or experiences it; thus it is the "eye" (*cakṣus*) or the "organ of sight" (*netra*). That which is grasped by the eye is "visible" (*cākṣuṣa*), namely, form.
120. The suffix *k* is also applied after the root *muh*. 120.
Repeatedly. ||120||
120. *Muhyati* means "he becomes deluded" or "he wanders"; *muhuḥ* is an indeclinable used in the sense of repetition.
The suffix *svarac* is applied after the verbal roots √kṛ, √gṛ, √śṝ, √vṝ, and √caṭi.
*karvaraḥ*, *garvaraḥ*, *śarvarī*, *varvaraḥ*, *catvaram* ||121||

*Karvara* means one who scatters or disperses; it refers to a tiger or a wicked person. *Karvarī* refers to the night or a wicked tigress. *Garvara* means one who swallows or devours; it refers to pride (*abhimāna*). A hero (*nāyaka*) is called *garvara* because of his association with such pride. *Śarvarī* means the night, as it destroys or harms while manifesting [darkness]; or it refers to a barbarian (*varvara*), so called because he covers or obstructs. *Catvara* refers to that which is frequented, requested, or accepted; it is a quadrangle or a courtyard.
122. After the root *sad*, [the suffix *ktvā*] takes the augment *naU*.
Niṣadvara. ||122||
Thus ends the second quarter of the Uṇādi-sūtras.
122. That in which one sits down, or that where one sits, is *niṣadvaraḥ*; it refers to mud (*paṅkaḥ*) or the night (*rātriḥ*). *Niṣadvarī* [is used] for the night.
Thus ends the second quarter of the Vaidikalaukikakośa, a commentary on the Uṇādi-sūtras.
Now begins the third quarter [of the chapter]:
1. *chitvara*, *chatvara*, *dhīvara*, *pīvaramīvara*, *cīvara*, *tīvra*, *nīvara*, *gahvara*, *kaṭvara*, and *saṃyadvara*. ||1||

1. The eleven words beginning with *chitvara* are irregularly formed (*nipātana*) by adding the suffix *svarac*. One who cuts is *chitvara*: a rogue, an enemy, or an instrument for cutting. One who covers or conceals is *chatvara*: a house or a place covered by creepers. In both cases, the dental *d* of the verbal root is changed to *t*; furthermore, in the case of the roots *ḍudhāñ* (to hold), *pā* (to drink), and *mā* (to measure), the final vowel becomes *ī*. One who holds is *dhīvara*: a boatman or fisherman. One who drinks milk and so forth is *pīvara*: fat or stout.

He who measures, destroys, or injures is *mīvaraḥ*, meaning a harmful person; or it refers to *cīvaraḥ*, which means clothing or the dwelling place of a sage (*muni*). It is derived from the root *ci* (to gather), with the vowel lengthened: that which gathers grass and so forth, or by which one is covered, is *cīvaraḥ*. *Tīvaraḥ* refers to one who brings an end to action—that is, one who completes a task—or a specific class of people; here there is elision of the letter *r* and an absence of *guṇa* strengthening. *Nīvaraḥ* refers to one who leads, such as a wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*); here there is a prohibition of *guṇa*. *Gahvaraṃ* or *gahanaṃ* refers to that which plunges into or churns; here there is the substitution of a short vowel.
That which cuts, rains down, or covers is *kaṭvaram*, meaning food or a condiment. One who restrains (*saṃyacchati*) is *saṃyadvaraḥ*, such as a king; here, the letter *da* replaces the letter *ma*.

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), one who offers oblations (*upajuhoti*) is *upahvaraḥ*, such as a chariot. Because the suffix *svarac* is marked with the indicator *ṣ*, in the feminine there is the form *chitvarī* and so forth; in all these cases, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.
The suffix *na* is applied after the verbal roots *iṇ*, *siñji*, *dīṅ*, *uṣ*, and *vī*.
inaḥ (ruler), sinaḥ (sin), jinaḥ (conqueror), dīnaḥ (miserable), uṣṇaḥ (hot), ūnaḥ (deficient). ||2||

*Eti* means "he goes," thus *inaḥ* refers to a lord, a king, a master, or the sun. That which exists together with a master (*ina*) is called *senā* (an army). *Sinoti* means "he binds," thus *sinaḥ* refers to one who is blind or one-eyed. *Jayati* means "he conquers," thus *jinaḥ* refers to one who is very old, one who is victorious, or a type of nihilist (*nāstika*). *Dīyate* means "he becomes diminished," thus *dīnaḥ* refers to one who is miserable or wretched. *Trpnoti* means "it burns," thus *uṣṇam* refers to that which is hot or slightly heated; it is a term whose gender varies according to the object. *Trpnoti* means "it protects" and so forth, thus *ūnaḥ* refers to one who is incomplete or deficient.
3. Phena and Mīna. 3.
