3. That which swells and increases is *phena*, namely *hiṇḍīra*, commonly known as "sea-foam," or a transformation of water; or it refers to one who acts like foam (*phenāyate*). That which measures or destroys is *mīna*, meaning a zodiac sign or a fish.
4. [The suffix *kan* is applied] after the verbal root *kṛṣi* when expressing a quality (*varṇa*). 4.
Kṛṣṇa. ||4||
4. He who ploughs (kṛṣati) is *kṛṣṇa*, meaning either dark-colored or the black pepper (*pippalī*).
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), that by which the mind is smeared (*jigharti*) or flows away is *dhṛṇā*, meaning dejection (*daurmanasya*).
5. And [the substitution of] *bandha*, *bradhna*, and *budhna* [occurs]. ||5||
The sun; the awakening one. ||5||

5. He who makes things burst forth (bradhnoti) is *bradhna*; he who makes things grow from the bottom (budhnāti) is *budhna*. *Bradhna* is the great one, or the sun; *budhna* is the cloud, or the root, or the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
The suffix *na* is applied after the roots *dhā*, *pṛ*, *vas*, *jyā*, and *at*.
dhānāḥ, parṇam, vasnaḥ, venaḥ, atnaḥ. ||6||

6. *Dadhāti* means "he places"; thus *dhānāḥ* refers to barley grains roasted in fire; it is always feminine and plural. *Piparti* or *pālayati* (he nourishes or protects); thus *parṇam* or *patram* means a leaf. That by which one dwells is *vasnaḥ*, meaning price or wages. *Trprajati* (he moves or attains); thus *venaḥ* means the desirable one, Prajāpati, or the Lord. *Atati* (he moves continuously); thus *trpratnaḥ* means the sun. By way of irregularity (*bāhulakāt*): *śrṛṇoti* (he hears); thus *śroṇaḥ* means a cripple.
7. After the word *lakṣa*, the suffixes *aṇ* and *muṭ* [are applied]. 7.
The definition; the characteristic mark. ||7||

7. He who marks or characterizes is *lakṣaṇaḥ*; *lakṣmaṇam* means a mark, a sign, or a name; or *lakṣmaṇaḥ* refers to the brother of Rāma; or *lakṣmaṇā* refers to a female swan or a female crane (*sārasī*).
8. [The substitution of *u* for *v* occurs] when the penultimate (*upadhā*) vowel is *e* or *o*.
Vennā || 8 ||
That which is desired or shared is the river Vennā.
9. After the root *iṣ* (to wish), there is also the suffix *yū*.
The sewn one. 9.
9. He sews (*sīvyati*) and extends the threads, thus he is *syūnaḥ*; or rather, the sun (*ādityaḥ*). The substitution of *yū* for the suffix *ti* occurs by virtue of the rule [Pāṇini 3.1.85].

By way of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*), even when the suffix is absent, the form is established; thus, once the substitution of *ūṭh* has been made, both *syonaḥ* (happy) and *syonam* (happiness) are also proven.
The affix *ni* is added after the roots *kṝ*, *vṛ*, *jṝ*, *sṝ*, *dṝ*, *pani*, *ni*, and *svapi*.
karṇaḥ | varṇaḥ | jarṇaḥ | senā | droṇaḥ | pannaḥ | tṛpraṇam | svapnaḥ ||10||

10. *Karṇa*: That which scatters or throws forth is *karṇa*; it refers to the ear, a specific Kṣatriya, or [the letter] *ka* and *ṛṇa*. *Varṇa*: that which covers or is covered is *varṇa*; it refers to the Brāhmaṇa and other castes, colors such as white and so on, praise, fame in the form of syllables (*akṣara*), and acceptance. *Jarṇa*: that which decays is *jarṇa*; it refers to the moon or an old man. *Senā*: that which binds or ties up enemies is *senā*. It was previously stated that it exists together with *ina* (the leader). *Droṇa*: that which flows or moves is *droṇa*; it refers to the black crow, a particular Māna measure, or the teacher of Arjuna; or it may mean a wooden trough for pouring water (*droṇī*).
That which praises or extends is *pannaḥ*, as in a serpent; that which satisfies or gives life is *trprannam*, as in rice and the like; that which sleeps or is slept upon is *svapnaḥ*, as in sleep.
11. And the servant likewise. ||11||
Dhenaḥ | Dhenā || 11 ||

Because they suckle or drink from it, it is called *dhenaḥ*; [the term] *dhenāḥ* refers either to the ocean or to rivers. The substitution of the vowel *i* is for the purpose of excluding the meaning "satiated" (*tṛpra*).
12. The suffix *i* is added after the roots *tṛṣ*, *śuṣ*, and *as*, and it is marked with the *k* indicatory letter (*kit*).
Tṛṣṇā, Śuṣṇa, Rasna. 12.

12. That by which one thirsts, desires, or longs is *tṛṣṇā*, meaning longing or thirst. That which dries up sap and so forth is *śuṣṇaḥ*, referring to the sun or fire. That which tastes or makes sound is *rasanam*, meaning the tongue or a substance.
13. And [the vowel] following *su* is long.
A slaughterhouse. ||13||
13. That which presses [the Soma], or where one goes; "sūnā" means either the act of pressing or a place for killing living beings.
And he should take delight [in it]. ||14||
The Jewel. ||14||

14. From the causative form (*ṇyanta*) of the root *ram*, there is a suffix [with the augment *ka*], and the letter *m* is replaced by *t*. Thus, that which causes delight or gladdens is called a *ratna*. It is said: "That which is most excellent in each respective species is indeed designated as a *ratna*. Examples include: the horse-jewel (*aśvaratna*), the elephant-jewel (*gajaratna*), the gem-jewel (*maṇiratna*), the woman-jewel (*strīratna*), and so forth.
15. rāsnā, sāsnā, sthūṇā, vīṇā. ||15||
Geṣṇuḥ | Deṣṇuḥ ||15||

*Rāsnā*: that which tastes or makes sound; it refers either to a fragrant substance (*gandhadravya*) or [the plant]. *Sāsnā*: that by which one sleeps (*sasti*); it refers to the dewlap of cows and other animals, or the skin below the neck. *Sthūṇā*: that by which one stands firm for the purpose of covering and so forth; it refers to a house pillar (*gṛhastambha*). In the word *trp*, there is the substitution of *ū*. *Vīṇā*: that which sounds or pervades (*veti*); it refers to a specific type of musical instrument. The change to *ṇ* occurs by irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
16. He was released from his fetters. 16.
The giver of songs; the giver of gifts. 16.
16. One who sings or makes sound is *geṣṇaḥ*, or a singer; one who gives is *deṣṇuḥ*, or one whose nature is to give.
17. After the roots *kṛ* and *śubh*, the suffix *ksna* is applied.
The whole; threefold. ||17||

"Kṛtsna" means that which cuts through even a small portion, or it means complete (*saṃpūrṇa*). "Trpakṣṇa" means that which extends or pervades (*vyāpnoti*) the three, or it means unbroken (*akhaṇḍa*).
And [the vowel] *ṛ* is long by nature. ||18||
Sharp. ||18||
18. It endures that which is sharp and intense. This word is of variable gender (vācyaliṅga): *tīkṣṇā* buddhiḥ (sharp intellect); *tīkṣṇaḥ* puruṣaḥ (sharp man); *tīkṣṇam* ghṛtam (sharp [hot] ghee).
19. In the case of the root *śliṣ*, the penultimate vowel is also replaced by *u*.
Gentle. ||19||
19. *Kṣṇaḥ* means "adhering"; *ślakṣṇa* means "smooth" or "delicate," and it is used in all three genders.
The suffix *yuc* is applied after the roots *yaj*, *man*, *niṣuṇḍi*, and *asij*.
yajyuḥ, manyuḥ, śundhyuḥ, dasyuḥ, janyuḥ. ||20||

20. One who sacrifices is *yajyuḥ*, namely the *adhvaryu* priest; or it means one who thinks, thus *manyuḥ*, which is grief or anger. One who cleanses is *śundhyuḥ*, namely fire. One who destroys or ruins the property of others is *dasyuḥ*, namely a thief. One who is born or appears is *janyaḥ*, namely the embodied being (*śarīrin*). Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is no substitution [of the semivowel].
The suffixes *yuk* and *yuk* are applied after the roots *bhuj* and *mṛj*.
Bhujyu; Death. 21.

That which eats, or that in which one eats, is *bhujyu*—meaning either the eater or the vessel. That which dies, or the separation from the body, is *mṛtyu*; it is used in both the feminine and masculine genders.
22. *Sarati* [means] life. 22.
The Sarayū [river]. ||22||
22. That which flows, or where waters flow, is the *sarayu* river; there is an alternative reading, *trpayu-pratyaya*, resulting in *sarayū*.
23. From the roots *pā*, *anī*, and *viṣi*, the suffix *pa* is applied.
Pāpam | [Nepaḥ] | Nīpaḥ | Veṣpaḥ ||23||

23. That which protects or guards against itself is *pāpa*, meaning unrighteousness (*adharma*). Through connection with that, a person is called *pāpa*. That which leads is *neṣa*, meaning a domestic priest (*purohita*). [By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is an absence of the *guṇa* vowel change, resulting in *nīpa*, a specific type of tree. That which pervades or encompasses is [the root *vi-viṣ*]. 24. From the root *cyu*, the suffix *kvip* is applied. 24.
The *cyu* [root] is [used in the sense of] departing. ||24||
That by which one falls away, attains, or speaks is the *cyupa*; or it is the mouth.
25. And [the vowel] *ū* is long. 25.
A stūpa. ||25||
It is called a *stūpa* because it praises (*stu*) [the Buddha]; it is either the elevation of the ground or the sacrificial altar (*yajñavedi*).
26. After the words *su* and *śrī*, [the suffix] *nic* is applied.
Soup. Winnowing basket. ||26||

26. And what is long? That which cooks—whether it be cooked by boiling, being pressed, or being roasted—is *sūpa* (soup); or it is cooked split-grain food. That which shatters or destroys is *śūrpa* (winnowing basket); it is either a vessel for measuring grain or a container for cleaning rice.
And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after the roots *ku* and *yubh*. ||27||
A well. A sacrificial post. ||27||
27. And what about the long [vowel]? That which sounds, i.e., makes a noise, is *kūpa* (a well). That which joins, i.e., mixes, is *yūpa* (a sacrificial post) or a pillar in a sacrificial hall.
28. khaṣpa, śilpa, śaṣpa, vāṣpa, rūpa, parpata, and talpa. ||28||

28. Words such as *khaṣpa* and others ending in the suffix *pap* are *nipātas* (irregular forms). *Khanati* (he digs) becomes *khaṣpaḥ*, meaning anger or forceful compulsion; here, the letter *n* is replaced by *ṣ*. That which one practices or brings into harmony is *śilpam*, meaning skill or artistry; here, there is a substitution of the short vowel *a*. That which is crushed or struck is *śaṣpam*, meaning young grass or the fading of luster; here, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. That which oppresses or causes pain is *vāṣpam*, meaning tears or heat; here, the substitution of *s* for *dh* occurs. That which cries out or makes sound is *rūpam*, meaning form, nature, or beauty; here, there is a substitution of the long vowel *ū*.
From the root *pṛ* (to cross over): *parpa*, meaning a boat, a house, or young grass; from *tḷ* (to establish): *talpa*, meaning a bed or a woman.

By virtue of the rule allowing for diversity (*bāhulaka*), from *cam* (to eat): *campā*, the name of a city; from *pā* (to protect): *pampā*, the name of a river. [In these cases] there is shortening of the vowel and the addition of the augment *muṭ*.
The suffix *itnuc* is applied after the verbal roots √stan, √hṛṣ, √puṣ, √gad, and √mad when followed by the causative marker *ṇi*.
Stanayitnu (thunder), harṣayitnu (one who causes joy), poṣayitnu (one who nourishes), gadayitnu (one who speaks), madayitnu (one who intoxicates). ||29||

29. *Stanayitnuḥ* means that which thunders or makes sound; it refers to a cloud or lightning. *Harṣayitnuḥ* means that which gladdens; it refers to one who causes joy or gold. *Poṣayitā* means one who nourishes. *Gadayitnuḥ* means one who speaks much; it refers to a talkative person. *Madayitnuḥ* means that which intoxicates; it refers to wine. In all these instances, the substitution of *ay* for the suffix *ṇiC* is applied according to the rule *trpām-tṛpyāmant-ālva-yyetnuḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.53).
30. The suffix *ktnu* is added after the roots *kṛ* and *han*.
The doer; the slayer. ||30||
30. *Kṛtnuḥ* means "one who acts" or "an artisan. *Hatnuḥ* refers to that which kills or the instrument by which one kills, such as a disease or a weapon.
31. The game of dice. ||31||
The one who desires to go. ||31||
31. It is called *jigatnu* because it causes bodies to move; or it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
32. After the roots *dā* and *bhā*, the suffix *nu* is applied.
The giver; the light. ||32||

32. *Dānu* means one who gives; it refers to one whose nature is generosity, or one who is discerning in matters such as wisdom. *Bhānu* means that which shines or blazes; it refers to the sun, light, or a ray. *Svarbhānu* is Rāhu. *Citrabhānu* is the sun or fire. *Vṛhadbhānu* is fire.
And [the suffix] *ga* is applied after the root *vac*. (33)
The voice. ||33||
He speaks, thus he is a speaker (vagnuḥ), or one who is talkative.
34. And the attendant likewise. ||34||
The Cow. ||34||
That which sucks or drinks is a *dhenu*, namely a cow that has recently calved; when it is small, it is a *dhenukā*, or [the term may refer to] a female elephant.
35. Is it heaven? 35.
The son. ||35||
35. He is called *sūnu* because he is born (*sūyate*) or produced; [the term] refers to a son (*putra*), a younger brother (*anuja*), or the sun (*sūrya*).
36. After the root *jāh*, there is the substitution of two [nasals], and the elision of the final [consonant].
Jahnu. ||36||
"Jahnu" refers to a certain royal sage (rājarṣi) who abandons (jahāti) his faults (doṣān).
The augment *ṇu* is applied after a suffix beginning with a consonant that stands in the third position from the end of the verbal root.
The Post. ||37||
That which stands is a *sthāṇu*, meaning either a dry tree or something immovable.
38. After the roots *aj*, *vṛ*, and *īr*, [the suffix] *nic* is applied invariably.
Veṇu, varṇu, reṇu. ||38||

38. That which moves swiftly, goes forth, or is cast away is *veṇu*, meaning bamboo, a lineage, or a specific king; that which is chosen or frequented is *varṇu*, meaning a disease or a particular region; that which flows, goes, injures, or is struck down is *reṇu*, meaning dust; *sureṇu* means golden dust; and *trasareṇu* is synonymous with *sureṇu*.
The suffix *kic* is applied after the root *viṣ*. (39)
Viṣṇu. ||39||
39. He is Viṣṇu, the Lord of the world, because he pervades—that is, he encompasses—the entire world of moving and non-moving beings.
The suffix *ka* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *ādhāra*, *arc*, and *kal*.
karkaḥ, dākaḥ, dhākaḥ, rākā, arkaḥ, kalkaḥ. ||40||

Because the word *bahula* (in the rule) is used, the letter *k* does not receive the designation *it*. Thus: *karoti* means "he does," hence *karkaḥ*, which may refer to fire, a white horse, a mirror, or a jar. *Dadāti* means "he gives," hence *dākaḥ*, which refers to a sacrificer. *Dadhāti* means "he places," hence *dhākaḥ*, which refers to a vessel or a bull. *Rāti* or *dadāti* means "she gives," hence *rākā*, which refers to the full moon or a specific river. *Arcayati* means "he honors," hence *markaḥ*, which refers to a leaf of the *arka* plant, crystal, or the sun. *Kalate* or *śabdayati* means "he sounds," hence *kalkam*, which refers to deceit or sin.

By virtue of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*): *raṅka* means "he who delights" (in poverty), i.e., a miser, a wretch, or a dullard. When the substitution of *la* for *ra* is applied according to the rule beginning with *kapilakādi*, *laṅkā* denotes an evil city, a tree branch, or a wanton woman.
The suffix *kak* is added after the verbal roots *sṛ*, *vṛ*, *bhū*, *śuṣ*, and *muṣ*.
sṛkaḥ, vṛkaḥ, bhūkaḥ, śuṣkaḥ, muṣkaḥ. ||41||

It moves, thus it is *sṛka*: speech, a thunderbolt, wind, or a blue lotus. It covers, thus it is *vṛka*: a crow or a beast of prey. *Vārkeṇya* means "belonging to a wolf" (*vṛka*). It exists, thus it is *bhūka*: a hole or time. It dries up, thus it is *śuṣka*: sapless. It is stolen or covered, thus it is *muṣka*: the testicle, a scrotum, or a collection. That which possesses a *muṣka* is *muṣkara*. By way of frequentative usage (*bāhulaka*)—it protects as a cause, thus it is *trproka*: a heap or a place. It is bound or tied, thus it is *mūka*: devoid of speech; there is the elision of the letters *r* and *v*.
42. Parrots, bark, and firebrands. 42.

42. Words such as *śuka* and others ending in the suffix *kap* are *nipātas* (irregularly formed words). That which shines is a *śuka*, either a species of bird or the son of Vāsava (Indra). That by which one turns or covers is *valka* or *balkala* (bark). That which satisfies or burns is an *ulkā*, meaning lightning or a flame of fire. [In these cases] there is the substitution of *l* for the letter *ṣ*.
The suffix *kan* is applied after the verbal roots *iṇ*, *bhī*, *kās*, *śal*, *yat*, *mṛc*, and *arci*.
ekaḥ, bhekaḥ, kākaḥ, pākaḥ, tiśalkam, atkaḥ, markaḥ. ||43||

43. *Eka* means "he who goes" (*eti*), thus "one"; it may also mean "principal" or "sole. *Bheka* refers to that from which one fears, namely a frog or a cloud. *Kāka* is so called because it cries out (*kāyati*); it means a crow. *Pāka* is he who drinks (*pibati*); it denotes either an infant or an old man. *Śalka* is that which moves (*śalyati*) or is pierced; it refers to bark or a scale. *Trpratka* is he who moves continuously (*atati*); it signifies a traveler or a limb of the body. *Marka* is derived from the Vedic root *mṛc*, meaning "he moves" (*marcati*) or "exerts himself"; it refers to the vital wind within the body.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), *śāka* is derived from *śyai* ("to go") and *sāka* from *syai* ("to flow").
44. The ninth [chapter] ends. 44.
nihākā||44||
A *nihākā* is a lizard or a chameleon, so called because it "completely leaves" (*nitarāṃ jahāti*) or abandons [its former state].
45. After the word *nau*, there is optionally the substitution of *ṭiC*.
The gold coin. ||45||
"Niṣīdati" (he sits down) refers to a *niṣka*, which is a specific measure of weight.
46. And syama and riṭa [are also used]. 46.
syamīkā; syamikaḥ. ||46||

*Syamīkaḥ* is that which utters the sound "syam"; it refers to an anthill (*valmīka*) or a species of tree. By the addition of the augment *iṭ* (due to the presence of the suffix *ka*), it becomes *syamikaḥ*.
47. After the words *aji* and *yudhni*, [the suffix *cha* is applied], and there is lengthening of the vowel.
vīkaḥ, yūkā, dhūkaḥ, nīkaḥ. ||47||

47. *Vīkaḥ* is that which moves about; it refers to the wind or a bird. *Yūkā* is that which joins together; it refers to a louse or a parasite of the hair on the head. *Dhūkaḥ* is that which shakes or causes trembling; it refers to the wind. *Nīkaḥ* is that which leads; it refers to a particular species of tree.
In the case of *hrī*, both *ra* and *la* may optionally occur.
hrīkāḥ, hlīkā ||48||
One who feels shame (*jihreti*) or acts with modesty (*lajjāṃ karoti*) is *hrīka*; or *hlīkā* is itself shame.
49. Śakra’s [speech] ends here. ||49||
śakunaḥ; śakuntaḥ; śakuntiḥ; śakuniḥ. ||49||
49. Furthermore, these suffixes—*uta*, *unta*, *unti*, and *uni*—occur. Thus: *śakunaḥ*, *śakuntaḥ*, *śakuntiḥ*, and *śakuniḥ*; these are names for birds.
50. After the root *bhu*, [the suffix] *jhi* [is replaced by *anti*]. ||50||
The states of existence. ||50||
That in which things exist is *bhavanti*, or it refers to the present time.

*Kunti* is one who desires (*kāmayate*); in the feminine, it becomes *kuntī*. There is the substitution of *ku* for the verbal root and the elision of the suffix-initial [augment]. *Trpavant* is one who satisfies; *trpavanti* is a king. *Vadanti* is that which speaks; *vadanti* is a clamor. *Kiṃvadantī* is public rumor. Words such as *kuntī* and others arise from the *bāhuka*-class [of suffixes].
51. And [the suffix *kvip* is applied] after the roots *kṣi* and *kṣipe*. 51.
Desirous of casting away; desirous of becoming. ||51||
And from the root *bhu* (to cast): that which casts or impels is *kṣipaṇyuḥ*, namely the spring season or the wind. That which comes into being is *bhuvanyuḥ*, namely the master or the sun.
52. [The substitution of *u* occurs] for the final vowel of a word ending in *an* and for the vowel *e*.
nadanuḥ; kṣipaṇuḥ. ||52||
52. Furthermore, *nadanuḥ* refers to that which makes an indistinct sound, namely a cloud; or *kṣipaṇuḥ* refers to that which casts forth, namely the wind.
The suffix *unan* is applied after the roots *kṝ*, *vṛ*, and *dṝ*.
Compassion, Varuṇa, and the terrible. ||53||

*Karuṇa* means one who scatters or disperses evil qualities; it refers to a type of tree, or compassion (*karuṇā*). One whose character (*śīla*) is compassion is called *kāruṇika*. *Varuṇa* is that which covers or is covered; it refers to water, or a type of tree. *Dāruṇa* is that which tears apart or by which one is torn; it means terrifying.
In the place of *t* or *th*, *r* or *l* may optionally be substituted.
*taruṇaḥ*; *talunaḥ* ||54||

54. *Taruṇa* means "one who crosses over" (*tara-tīti*); it refers to a youth or a particular kind of tree. In the feminine, by virtue of belonging to the *gaurādi* group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, resulting in either *taruṇī* or *talunī*, meaning a young woman.
The suffix *i* is added after the roots *kṣudh*, *piś*, and *mith*, and it is marked with the *k*-diacritic.
kṣudhunaḥ, piśunaḥ, mithunam ||55||

55. One who is hungry (*kṣudhyati*) or desires to eat is *kṣudhunaḥ*, or it refers to a barbarian tribe (*mleccha-jāti*). One who tears apart (*piśati*) or makes into parts is *piśunaḥ*, meaning a wicked person or an informer (*sūcaka*). One who stirs (*methati*), knows (*jānāti*), is known (*jñāyate*), or injures (*hinasti*) is *mithunam*; it is the union of two or a pair.
And [the rule] regarding the fruit is also [applicable]. 56.
Phalguna. ||56||
Phalguna is so called because he bears fruit—that is, he becomes perfected—or because he is bright (śukla).
57. And [the substitution of] *śa* occurs for *ṣa*, and [the substitution of] *la* occurs for *ra*. 57.
Garlic. ||57||
57. *Unan*: that which is eaten or consumed; it refers either to garlic (*laśuna*) or to a bulbous root (*kanda*) consisting of pungent herbs (*trp-auṣadha*).
58. [The suffix] *ar* is replaced by *ji*, and there is also elision (*luk*) [of the preceding *a*]. 58.
Trprarjunaḥ || 58 ||
58. *Tripārjuna* means "one who conquers three times"; it refers to a white peacock or a particular species of tree. *Tripārjunī* refers to a cow.
59. There is also [the suffix *cit*] after the word *tṛṇa*. 59.
To Arjuna. ||59||
That which is *trprarjayati* is *trprarjunam*, meaning "grass. The inclusion of *cit* is for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta.
And [the suffix] *artti* also [is used]. (60)
Aruṇa. ||60||
60. *Trpraruna* means the sun, so called because it "goes" (*ṛcchati*) or "attains" (*prāpnoti*); *kuṇṭha* means either dull or red.
61. And [the suffix *ka* is applied] after [stems ending in] *aji*, *miśi*, and *īṣat*.
Vayuna, Yamunā, Śayuna. ||61||

61. *Vayuna* is that in which one moves or goes; it refers either to a dwelling or a temple. *Yamunā* is so called because she restrains (*yacchati*); it refers either to a specific river or a female tortoise. *Śayuna* is he who lies down (*śete*); it refers to a python.
The suffix *sa* is applied after the verbal roots *vṛt*, *vad*, *div*, *ci*, *han*, *kam*, and *kaṣ*.
varṣam (rain), tarṣaḥ (thirst), vatsaḥ (calf), vakṣaḥ (chest), vatsam (calf), haṃsaḥ (swan), kaṃsaḥ (a cup/bell-metal), kakṣam (armpit) ||62||

62. It covers or takes possession (*vṛṇoti*), thus it is *varṣa*: the year, rain, the Āryāvarta region, or a cloud. In the feminine, with a plural ending, *varṣāḥ* refers to the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*). That by which or in which one crosses is *tarṣa*: the ocean. It speaks (*vadati*), thus it is *vatsa*: a child. In which one speaks, thus it is *vakṣa*: the chest. [It dwells in this, thus it is *vatsam*: a dwelling place. It kills (*hanti*), thus it is *haṃsa*: one free from greed, the sun, a species of bird, a type of horse, or the wind residing in the head.

*Kaṃsa* is so called because it desires the objects of others; it refers to a vessel made of a luminous substance or a thief. *Kakṣa* is so called because it scrapes or injures; it refers to grass, a creeper, the vicinity of a forest, or the armpit.

By virtue of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*): it shines or glows, thus it is *rākṣā*, which is *lākṣā* (lac). The substitution of *la* for *ra* occurs according to the rule beginning with *kapilakādi*. She unites, thus she is *yoṣā*, meaning a woman.
63. After the root *pluṣ*, the penultimate vowel is replaced by *a*.
The Plakṣa tree. ||63||

It is called *plakṣa* because it burns or consumes (*ploṣati dahati*); it is also known as *piplala*, *parkaṭī*, or commonly as *pākari*. It refers either to a specific type of island or to the side of a house's door.
64. And [the vowel] following *manas* is long.
Flesh. ||64||
That by which one thinks or by which it is known is "māṃsa" (flesh), or it is the nourishment of the body.
65. *aś* [is substituted] for [the final consonant of a verbal root ending in a consonant] before the suffix *devane*. 65.
The axle. ||65||
It is called *triprakṣa* because it reaches or pervades; the *triprakṣas* are the sense organs, or [the terms may refer to] the husk, the wheel, the cart, or worldly activity.
The suffix *kvi* is added after the roots *snū*, *vrasc*, and *kṛt* when followed by the word *ṛṣi*.
snuṣā, vṛkṣaḥ, kṛtsam, ṛkṣam ||66||

66. She who flows or streams forth is called *snuṣā*, or the wife of a younger brother. That which is cut or severed is a *vṛkṣa*. From the root *vṛkṣ* (meaning "to choose" or "to cover"), by adding the suffix *ka* to the base ending in *i* or *u*, the form *vṛkṣaḥ* is established. Here, the inclusion of the root *vṛśc* (meaning "to cut") is for the sake of distinguishing its specific meaning; thus, because the world of effects is subject to being cut, it too is called *vṛkṣa*. That which cuts or severs is *kṛtsam*, namely water. That which moves or goes is *ṛkṣam*, or a general term for a star.

Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*): that which sprinkles or injures on all sides is *trpāmikṣā*, meaning a derivative of milk; or, that which clings and becomes minute is *likṣā*, meaning a louse in the hair of the head; or, that which grows from a seed and is born is *rukṣaḥ*, meaning a species of tree or one devoid of affection.
67. [The suffix *cha* is applied] after the word *ṛṣi* when it occurs in the sense of "born from. 67.
The bear. ||67||

67. *Ṛkṣaḥ* is that which creeps or moves; it is a species of wild animal, the bear (*bhallūka*). Although [the form] is established by the previous rule, because of the restriction regarding the genus (*jāti*), the suffix *ṣa* is optionally applied to the root *ṛṣ* in its derivative (*yaugika*) sense.
And [the suffix *u* is added] after the roots *undi*, *guh*, and *kuṣ*.
utsaḥ, gutsaḥ, kukṣaḥ ||68||

68. It is called *utsa* because it flows (*unatti*) or moistens (*klidyati*), referring to a spring or a place where water trickles; or it is a sage (*ṛṣi*). It is called *gutsa* because it causes anger (*gudhnāti*) or provokes wrath, referring to a type of necklace or a cluster of flowers. It is called *kukṣa* because it draws out (*kuṣṇāti*) or extracts, referring to the region of the belly.
69. And [the suffixes] *dak* and *paṇya* are used after the words *gṛdh* and *paṇ*. 69.
Gṛtsaḥ | Pakṣaḥ ||69||

69. *Cit*. One who is greedy (*gṛdhyati*) or intensely desires (*tṛṣṇābhi-kāṅkṣati*) is *gṛtsa*; or it means desire (*kāma*). The substitution of *bhaṣ* for the letter *g* is set aside, and the letter *d* is substituted [for the final *s*]. That by which or wherein one praises (*paṇāyati*), extols, or transacts is a *pakṣa*: a half-month, a side-part, an opposing position (*sādhyavirodha*), a multitude, strength, or an alliance with friends.
70. He rushed forward from the bow. 70.
It consists of three syllables. ||70||
It is called *triprakṣara* because it extends (*prakarṣeṇa asnoti*) or pervades; it refers to the syllable of Brahman, liberation, or water.
And from a jar. ||71||
The year. ||71||
A *vatsara* is so called because beings dwell (*vasanti*) within it; alternatively, it is a *varṣa*.
72. After a root preceded by the prefix *sam*, the suffix *cit* [is applied].
The year. ||72||
Because it is piled up (cit), its accent is udātta at the end; they dwell together perfectly therein, and thus it is called *saṃvatsara*.
The suffix *ki* is applied after the verbal roots *kṛ*, *dhūm*, and others.
kṛsaraḥ, dhūsaraḥ, matsaraḥ ||73||

73. One who performs or is performed [upon] is *kṛsara*, meaning a mixture of sesame and rice; or it means *dhūsara*, so called because it "shakes" (*dhūnoti*), or one that is slightly pale. One who becomes intoxicated is *matsara*, a person who is envious of the prosperity of others, a miser, or one who is angry; or *matsarā* refers to a fly.
And *la* [is substituted] for *patera*. 74.
The Pāṭśala [school]. ||74||
That place where they fall or go is a "patsala" path or road.
75. Those [streams] flowed from the two Ṛṣis. 75.
Tasaraḥ | Ṛkṣaraḥ ||75||

It is called *tasara* because it stretches (*tanoti*) or because it is a frame for winding thread; or, he is called *ṛkṣa* because he reaches (*ṛṣati*) or attains [his goal], or he is a priest (*ṛtvij*).
The suffix *kālan* is added after the roots *pī* and *yuk*, with the shortening of the vowel and the occurrence of *samprasāraṇa*.
The *piyāla* tree; the *kuṇāla* tree. ||76||

76. *Pīy* is a verbal root found in the Sūtras. From *pīyati* (he satisfies), *piyāla* is derived, which is a specific tree known as *cironjī*. From *kaṇati* (he makes a sound), *kuṇāla* is derived, which is either a specific region or a bird. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—from *bhajati* (he partakes)—*bhagāla* is formed, meaning a human skull. There is also the substitution of *k* for *g* (*kutvam*).
77. From the roots *kaṭhi* and *kuṣi*, the suffix *kāku* is applied.
Kaṭhāku and Kuṣāku. ||77||
77. He who cuts (kaṭhati) is Kaṭhāku, a bird; he who scrapes away or draws out (kuṣati) is Kuṣāku, a fierce fire or the sun.
And [the suffix] *duk* follows the root *sṛ*. (78)
The slow-moving one. ||78||
It is called *sṛdāku* because it moves (*sarati*), or it is the wind; or it is called *sṛdāku* because waters flow within it, thus it is a river.
And there is the vṛddhi substitution for the root vṛt. ||79||
vārttākuḥ; vārttākam ||79||

This plant, known as *hiṅgulī* or *vṛntāka*, is called *vārttaku*. Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffixes *trap* and *ī* are applied to the vowel *u*, resulting in either *vārttāka* or *vārttākī*.
In the case of *parasmaipada*, there is elision of the *sa* of the affix *sic* when it follows a root ending in *n*, and there is also vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) of the penultimate vowel. ||80||
The viper. ||80||
It is called *pṛdāku* because it utters a contemptible sound; it refers either to a tiger or a serpent.
The suffixes *anyuc*, *āgūc*, and *aknuc* are added after the roots *sṛ*, *yu*, and *vac* respectively.
Saraṇyu, Yāvagū, and Vacaknu. ||81||

*Saratīra* means the bank of a river; *saraṇyuḥ* means a cloud or the wind (as it flows). *Yavāgūḥ* is so called because it mixes (*yauti*) or blends [ingredients]; it is either milk or boiled barley flour. *Vacaknuḥ* means one who speaks (*vakti*), that is, a loquacious person or a wise man.
82. The suffix *ānaka* is applied after the root *śīṅ* (to lie down) when it is preceded by the prefix *abhi*.
The terrifying; the fearful. ||82||
82. That which lies down is *śayānaka*, like a python (*ajagara*); that from which one fears is *bhayānaka*, meaning fear-inducing.
83. The suffix *āṇaka* is applied after the verbal roots *lū*, *dhū*, *śiṅgh*, *dhyai*, and *dhā*.
*lavāṇakaḥ*, *dhavāṇakaḥ*, *śiṅghāṇakaḥ*, *dhāṇakaḥ* ||83||

That by which one reaps is *lavāṇaka*, namely a sickle; or it is *dhavāṇaka*, meaning that which shakes, namely the wind; or it is *śiṅghāṇaka*, meaning that which smells or sniffs all around, namely phlegm.

By virtue of the rule of abundance (*bāhulaka*)—with the elision of the letter *ka*—it is *śiṅghāṇama*, meaning a glass vessel or the impurity of the iron nose. That which holds or is held is *dhāṇaka*, namely a portion of goods suitable for trade.
84. Those who perform oblations with a firebrand and a sacrificial ladle. 84.

It is called *ulmuka* because it heats (*trp*) and burns (*dah*); it is a word formed with the suffix *ka*, where the letter *ṣ* of the root has become *l*. That by which one pierces or cleaves is a *darvi* (ladle) or a serving vessel; it is formed with the suffix *vin*. One who offers oblations is a *homī* (sacrificer); here the suffix is *min*.
In the word *hrī*, the syllable *ku* is substituted for the *r*, and the *l* may optionally be substituted for it.
hrīkuḥ | hlīkuḥ ||85||
One who feels dread (*jihreti*) or experiences shame (*lajjāṃ karoti*) is *hrīkuḥ*, meaning one possessed of shame. *Hlīkuḥ* refers to lac, tin, lead, and so forth.
The suffix *tan* is applied after the verbal roots *has*, *mṛ*, *ṛ*, *ṇī*, *vā*, *mi*, *dā*, *mlū*, *pū*, *dhū*, and *vī*.
hastaḥ (hand), marttaḥ (mortal), garttaḥ (pit), etaḥ (goat), vātaḥ (wind), antaḥ (end), dantaḥ (tooth), lotaḥ (a type of vessel), potaḥ (ship/infant), dhūrttaḥ (rogue). ||86||

It seizes (*hasati*), thus it is *hasta* (the hand); or *natra-traṃ karaḥ*. One who possesses a hand is *hastī* (an elephant). He dies, thus he is *marttaḥ* (a mortal) or a human being. *Martta* itself becomes *martyaḥ* by adding the suffix *yat* in its own sense. It swallows or engulfs, thus it is *garttaḥ* (a pit, a ravine, or a place of falling). That which one goes to or reaches is *etaḥ* (a deer) or that which has variegated colors. In the feminine: *enī* or *etā*. It blows, thus it is *vātaḥ* (wind or disease).

That which goes near to destruction is *trp-rantaḥ*; it is either the essential nature (*tattva-svarūpa*) or that which is charming. That which tames or becomes tranquil, or by means of which one does so, is *dantaḥ*; it is either a tooth or a tusk. A young woman with beautiful teeth is *sudatī*. An elephant is *dantāvalaḥ* or *danturaḥ*. That which cuts is *lotaḥ*; it is either a mark of impurity or a vessel. That which purifies is *pottaḥ*; it is either a child or a boat. That which deceives is *ghūrtaḥ*; it is either a rogue, salt, or the *dhatura* (thorn-apple) plant.
87. After [the verbal root] *nañ*, there is also the augment *iṭ*.
The barber. ||87||
One who does not perform good deeds is called a *nāpita*, meaning a barber or hair-cutter.
The suffix *ki* is applied after the verbal roots *tan* and *mṛj*.
It is stretched out; it is dead. 88.
That which is stretched out is called *tata*, such as stringed instruments like the lute (*vīṇā*) or the like; that by which one dies is *mṛta*, or it refers to begged alms.
The suffix *kta* is applied after the roots *añci* and *ghṛsi*.
It is smeared with ghee; it is white. ||89||

That which anoints (*anakti*) or makes manifest is *prakta*; it may mean a tiger or that which is measured. That which sprinkles (*jigharti*), moves about, or shines is *ghṛta*; it means water, clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), or that which is blazing. That which binds or fastens is *sita*; it means white.

From the use of the frequentative form (*bahulavacanāt*): it becomes crooked or distorted, hence *muhūrta*, meaning either a moment or a period of two *ghaṭikās*. There is the augment *muṭ* for the root, and by the rule *rāllopaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.21], there is the elision of the *cha* suffix. It attains or reaches itself, hence *ṛta*, meaning truth or reality. That wherein one dwells is *vastam*, meaning a place.
90. After the roots *du* and *tan*, [the suffix *ka* is applied], and there is also lengthening [of the vowel].
The messenger; the father. ||90||

90. He who runs, goes, or causes pain and distress is a *dūta* (messenger), namely a royal servant who accomplishes many tasks; in the feminine, it is *dūtī*. That which extends tasks is a *tāta*, namely a father. By virtue of the rule of abundance (*bāhulaka*)—that which finishes a task—is a *sītā*, namely a furrow made by a plow in a field or a particular type of woman.
91. The *jermūṭ* [augment] is udātta. 91.
Jīmūta ||91||
91. There is lengthening of the root vowel and the suffix *mū* is udātta; that which conquers or by which one conquers is *jīmūta*, meaning a cloud or a mountain.
92. A clod of earth and grey hair. 92.

92. It is called *loṣṭa* because it is a compact mass (*saṅghāta*), or it is a lump of clay (*mṛtpiṇḍa*). It is called *palita* because it is reached or attained; it refers either to the state of old age or to the whiteness of the hair and so forth.
93. [The suffix *kta* is applied] after verbal roots ending in vowels or the letter *h*.
Green; white. ||93||

It is called *harita* because it takes away (*harati*), or it is a specific color. It is called *śyeta* because it moves (*śyāyati*) or goes (*gacchati*), or it is a dark-blue color (*śyāma-varṇa*). In the feminine: *hariṇī* or *haritā*; *śyenī* or *śyetā*.
And *ru* and *ha* are also [the substitutes] for *lo*. 94.
Rohita; the red. 94.
It is called *rohita* because it grows (*rohati*) or appears; it refers to the meat of a deer or a fish, or else to blood. *Lohita* refers to the planet Mars (*aṅgāraka*), blood, or the color red.
The suffix *kvi* is applied after the root *piś*, and it is also *kit*.
Flesh. ||95||
95. That which is made into the form of flesh (piśya) or grain (artha-vaya-varūpa) is called piśita or māṃsa (meat).
96. After the roots *śru*, *dakṣi*, *spṛhi*, and *gṛhi*, the suffix *āyya* is applied.
śravāyyaḥ, dakṣāyyaḥ, spṛhayāyyaḥ, gṛhayāyyaḥ. ||96||

96. *Śravāyyaḥ* means "one who causes to hear" (*śrāvayati*), or it refers to a sacrificial animal for giving (*dānapaśu*). *Dakṣāyyaḥ* means "one who is capable" (*dakṣayati*) or "one who increases" (*vardhate*), or it refers to a vulture (*gṛdhra*). *Spṛhayāyyaḥ* means "one who desires" (*spṛhayati*), or it refers to a constellation (*nakṣatra*) that desires to reach its goal. *Gṛhayāyyaḥ* means "one who censures" (*garhayati*) objects or "one who seizes" (*gṛhṇāti*), or it refers to the master of a house (*gṛhasvāmī*). In these cases, the suffix *trpāyya* is applied, and the *ṇi* of the causative stem is replaced by *ay*.
97. For the root *dhā*, there is reduplication, the substitution of *i* for the radical vowel, and the addition of the augment *ṣuk*.
To be mixed with curds. ||97||

That which will cause curd to coagulate or bring it to completion is called *dadhiṣāyya*, as in the case of clarified butter (*ghṛta*); the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by way of an irregular grammatical rule (*nipātana*).
98. After the root *vṛñ*, the suffix *eṇya* is applied.
The one to be chosen. ||98||
98. He is chosen, accepted, or esteemed as the most excellent or the best.
In the Vedic language (chandas), the [suffix] kyap may optionally be applied after the root *stu*.
I shall praise. ||99||
99. He is praised; he is one who should be praised, like Purandara. "Kseyya" is an alternative reading, in which case it would be "stuṣeyyaḥ."
100. Another [type] is the rājendra. 100.
A member of the royal caste. ||100||

He who shines or blazes is a *rājanya*; or, *rājanya* refers to the fire (*agni*). However, in the sense of the Kṣatriya caste, a *rājanya* is the offspring of a king (*rājan*); in that case, the final vowel is circumflex (*svarita*).
And [the suffix *kha* is applied] after the roots *śṛ* and *ram*. (Pāṇini 3.2.101)
A refuge; delightful. ||101||
101. That which destroys or harms is "śaraṇya" (a refuge), or it is the supreme knowledge; that in which one finds delight is "ramaṇya," or it is a home.
102. The Dharma is eternal. 102.
The forest is delightful. 102.
It is called *śaraṇya* because one attains it or because it destroys [suffering]; or it is *trpajñāna*. It is called *ramaṇya* because one finds delight in it; or it is a house.
103. Parjanya. 103.

It is called *parjanya* because it rains (*parṣati*) or pours down (*siñcati*); it refers to a cloud or that which is capable [of such action]. Due to the irregularity of the grammatical rule (*nipātana*), the letter *ṣ* becomes *j*.
104. Another [reason] for the father: ||104||
The father is other than that. ||104||
104. One who speaks or utters [well] is called *vadānya*; that is, one who is eloquent or generous.
105. [The suffix] *at* is applied after [the roots] *ami*, *nakṣi*, *yaj*, *iṇ*, and *pati*. 105.
The vessel; the star; the worshipful; the destroyer; the winged one. 105.

105. That which one attains with thirst is *tr̥pmatram*, or it is a vessel. That which perishes or goes is a *nakṣatram*, or a star. That which is sacrificed to or by which one sacrifices is a *yajatra*, such as the *agnihotra* fire or the sacrificer (*hotṛ*). In place of the root *han* (to kill), the substitute *badh* is prescribed; that by which one kills is a *badhatram*, or a weapon for quenching thirst. That by which one falls or goes is a *patatram*, or a vehicle, or body hair.
106. And for *gaḍi* and others, *ka* [is the substitute]. 106.
Kaḍatraṃ; kalatraṃ ||106||

106. It is called *kaḍatra* because it "flows" (*gaḍati*) or "sprinkles" (*siñcati*). By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the letter *ḍa* becomes *la*, resulting in *kalatra*, which means either the "hip-region" or "wife."
107. [The augment] *iṭ* is added after the root *vṛñ*. ||107||
Leather thong. ||107||
That by which one covers water and so forth, or that which performs such covering, is a "varatrā," meaning either a leather strap or a rope.
The suffix *katran* is applied after the root *suvid*.
Providing excellent shelter. ||108||
That family or household is well-known because it truly exists.
109. And [the substitution of *u* occurs] for the final vowel of a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, as well as for the augment *num*.
The cutter. 109.
That by which one cuts or cleaves is called *kṛntatra*, or it refers to a plough.
The suffix *atac* is applied after the verbal roots *bhṛ*, *mṛ*, *dṛśi*, *yaj*, *pavi*, *ṣaci*, *yam*, *tam*, *nam*, *hi*, and *hari*.
Bharataḥ, marataḥ, darśataḥ, yajataḥ, parvataḥ, pacataḥ, amataḥ, tamataḥ, namataḥ, haryyataḥ. ||110||

*Bharata* is so called because he supports (*bharati*) and nourishes (*puṣṇāti*); it refers to a type of king, an actor, or Rāma’s younger brother. *Marata* is that which dies (*mriyate*), or death itself. *Darśata* is that by which one sees; it refers to the moon or the sun. *Yajata* is one who sacrifices (*yajati*); it refers to a priest. *Parvata* is that which becomes full (*parvati*). Alternatively, it is a mountain (*giri*), derived from the suffix *-ta* in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), meaning "that in which joints (*parvan*) exist. *Pacata* is that by which one cooks (*pacati*); it refers to fire or the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*). *Tṛpramata* is that which moves swiftly (*tṛpraṃ mati gacchati*); it refers to dust.

*Tāmyati* means "he longs" or "he desires," hence *tamataḥ* means "one who is full of thirst. *Namati* means "he bows," hence *namataḥ* means "one who is humble. *Haryati* means "he goes," hence *haryataḥ* means "a swift horse.

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—from the root *mal*, it takes its own form [as a suffix], thus *mālatī* means "she who bears her own nature. There is lengthening of the penultimate vowel, and by virtue of belonging to the *gaurādi* group, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied.
The suffix *ki* is applied after the roots *pṛṣi* and *rañji*.
The spotted deer; silver. ||111||
That which sprinkles or scatters is *pṛṣataḥ*, meaning either a drop or a deer. That which becomes beloved or shines is *rajatam*, meaning silver or white.
112. Bald-headed. 112.

112. *Khalatiḥ* means "one who stumbles" or "one who moves about," referring to a man with a hairless head; there is the elision of the *s* of the root and the substitution of *i* for the final vowel of the suffix by way of a grammatical irregularity (*nipāta*).
The suffix *atha* is applied after the verbal roots √śī (to lie down), √śap (to curse), √ruj (to break), √gam (to go), √iṣ (to desire), √ci (to gather), √jīv (to live), and √prāṇ (to breathe).
śayathaḥ, śapathaḥ, ravathaḥ, gamathaḥ, gamathaḥ, vañcathaḥ, jīvathaḥ, prāṇathaḥ. ||113||

113. He lies down, thus he is a *śayatha*, or a python (*trprajagara*). He is sworn at, or he utters a curse, thus it is an *śapatha*, or the making of a firm resolve. It cries out, thus it is a *ravatha*, or a cuckoo (*kokila*). It goes, thus it is a *gamatha*, or a traveler (*pathika*). It deceives, or it causes to fail, thus it is a *vañcatha*, or a rogue (*dhūrta*). In place of *trpra*, there is an alternative reading *vandī*; thus it is a *vandatha*, a singer of praise (*stotṛ*) or one worthy of praise (*stutya*). He lives, thus it is a *jīvatha*, or a long-lived person (*trprāyuṣman*). He breathes, thus it is a *prāṇatha*, or one who is strong (*balavat*).

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*): from *dṛṇāti*, "he pierces," comes *darathaḥ*, meaning spreading in all directions or a pit; from *śāmyati*, "he becomes calm," comes *śamathaḥ*, meaning tranquility; and from *dāmyati*, "he is tamed," comes *damathaḥ*, meaning self-restraint.
114. [The suffix] *ci* is added after the root *bhṛ*.
Bharata ||114||
"He who sustains" is *bharathaḥ*, meaning a world-protector (*lokapāla*) or a king.
The suffix *ru* and the root *vidi* take the augment *ṅit*.
You two roar; you two discern. 115.
115. That which roars is *ravatha*, meaning a dog; that which knows is *vidatha*, meaning a yoga.
116. [The suffix *ghañ* is applied after the root *vas*] when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present.
Dwelling; place of residence. ||116||
That in which one dwells on all sides is a *trpāvasatha*, that is, a house; that in which they dwell together properly is a *saṃvasatha*, that is, a village.
The suffix *as* is added after the verbal roots *ati*, *vica*, *mita*, *mina*, *mi*, *rabhi*, *labhi*, *nabhi*, *tapi*, *pāti*, *pani*, *paṇi*, and *mahi*.
*trpratas*, *avasa*, *camasa*, *tamasa*, *namasa*, *rabhasa*, *labhasa*, *nabhasa*, *tapasa*, *patasa*, *panasa*, *paṇasa*, *mahasam*. 117.

*Trpratas*: that which moves continuously; or it refers to the wind (*vāyu*). In the feminine, *trpratasī*. *Trpravasa*: that which performs protection and so forth; or it refers to a king. *Camata*: that by which one chews or consumes; because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group, it is *camasī*. *Tamasa*: that which languishes or yearns; or it refers to darkness (*dhvānta*). *Jamasa*: that which bows; or it refers to something favorable to the tongue (*trpra-nūkūla*). *Rabhasa*: that which seizes; it means speed or joy. *Labhasa*: that which obtains; or it refers to a horse-tether.

It destroys or strikes down, thus it is *nabhas*; or it is the clear sky. It causes heat or torment, thus it is *tapas*; or it is the moon. It flies, thus it is *patas*; or it is a bird. It praises, thus it is *panasa*; or it is the spiny fruit. [It deals in trade, thus it is *paṇasa*; or it is a commodity for sale. It is great, thus it is *maha*; or it is knowledge.

By virtue of the rule of abundance (*bāhulaka*): that which is reached or attained is *tāmarasa*, meaning a lotus; because the suffix is marked with *ṇi*, there is *vṛddhi* of the root vowel and the augment *tuṭ*. That which brings an action to completion is *sādhvasa*, meaning subsequent knowledge; from the root, the substitution *ghuk* occurs. That which moves unsteadily is *kīkasa*, meaning bone or marrow; the substitution *kīka* occurs for the root. That which crosses over is *tarasa*, meaning flesh.
118. After the verbal root *veñ*, there is the augment *tuṭ*.
The cane reed. ||118||
118. It is called *vetasa* because it weaves its fibers (*tantūn*) as it grows; or it is a specific species of tree.
The suffix *ṇiC* is applied after the roots *vah* and *yū*.
*vāhasaḥ* (carrier), *yāvasaḥ* (grass). ||119||

It is called *vāhasa* because it carries (*vahati*); or it is a large snake (*trprajagara*). It is called *yāvasa* because it joins (*yauti*) or mixes, or it does not mix; or it is a continuous growth of grass (*tṛṇasantati*).
And [the stage of] youth. 120.
The crow. ||120||
It is called *vāyasa* because it flies (*vayate*) or goes (*gacchati*), namely, a crow (*kāka*).
121. [The suffix] *kit* follows the word *div*. 121.
Daytime. ||121||
That in which the sun plays—that is, shines—is "divasa" (day); alternatively, "divasa" is of both genders because it is listed among the words beginning with *trp* and *ṛddha*.
The suffix *abha* is applied after the verbal roots √kṛ, √śṝ, √śal, √kali, and √gard.
*karabhaḥ*, *śarabhaḥ*, *śalabhaḥ*, *kalabhaḥ*, *nardabhaḥ*. ||122||

*Karamaḥ*: that which scatters or disperses; it refers either to the outer part of the hand or to a child. *Śaramaḥ*: that which pierces; it is a species of beast among wild animals specifically characterized as a predator. *Śalabhaḥ*: that which moves or glides; it refers either to a locust or a moth. *Kalabhaḥ*: that which makes a calculation or count; it refers either to a young elephant (*kariśāvaka*). *Gardabhaḥ*: that which makes a grunting sound; it refers to a donkey (*khara*).
The suffix *ka* is added after the words *ṛṣi* and *vṛṣi*, and it is marked with the *k*-it indicator.
Ṛṣabhaḥ | Vṛṣabhaḥ ||123||
123. He is called *ṛṣabha* because he moves (*ṛṣati*) or goes; he is called *vṛṣabha* because he rains (*varṣati*). These are synonyms for "the best," or they refer to a bull.
After the root *ruṣ*, the suffix *ni* is applied, and *luṣ* is substituted [for *ruṣ*]. 124.
The bull. ||124||
124. He is called *luṣabha* because he plants [evil] or because he destroys; or he is like a rutting elephant.
And [the suffix *kan* is applied] after the words *rāsi* and *balli*. (Pāṇini 5.2.125)
A donkey; a favorite. ||125||

It is called *rāsabha* because it makes a sound (*rāsati śabdayati*), or it is a donkey (*khara*). It is called *ballabha* because it covers or conceals (*ballate saṃvṛṇoti*), or it is beloved (*priya*).
126. The suffix *jhac* is applied after the roots *jṝ* and *viś*.
jarantaḥ | veśantaḥ || 126 ||

126. By the rule *pratyayādibhakārasya bho'ntaḥ* [7.1.3], there is the substitution of *bho* for the final letter of the suffix. Thus, one who grows old (*jīryati*) is a *jarantaḥ*, or a buffalo (*mahiṣaḥ*). One who enters (*viśati*), that is, makes entry, is a *veśantaḥ*, or a small reservoir of water (*alpa-jalāśayaḥ*).
By virtue of the frequentative application (*bāhulakāt*)—one who is worthy of honor (*arhati*) is a *trprarhantaḥ*.
The suffix *ṣyan* is applied after the roots *ruhi*, *nandi*, *jīv*, and *prāṇi* when expressing a blessing (*āśis*).
Growing; rejoicing; living; breathing; growing (feminine). 127.

127. That which grows is *rohantaḥ*, a type of tree; or, that which rejoices—that is, becomes endowed with prosperity—is *nandantaḥ*, a son; or, that which lives is *jīvantaḥ*, a medicinal herb; or, that which breathes—that is, carries out inhalation and exhalation—is *prāṇantaḥ*, the vital air (*vāyu*). Due to the feminine suffix *ḍīṣ* after the root *pā* (to drink), we have *prāṇantī*; likewise, *rohantī*, *nandantī*, and *jīvantī*.
And [the suffix -aC] is added after the roots √tṛ, √bhū, √vah, √vas, √bhās, √sādh, √gaḍi, √maṇḍi, and √jinand.
Crossing over, being, carrying, dwelling, shining, accomplishing, causing the cheeks to swell, adorning, conquering, and gladdening. 128.

128. *Bhac*: He who crosses, that by which one crosses, or the place where one crosses—this refers to a crossing person, the ocean, or a boat. *Bhavantaḥ*: That which comes into being, or the place where it exists—this refers to time. *Vahantaḥ*: That which carries or brings about effects—this refers to the wind. *Vasantaḥ*: He who dwells, or the place where he dwells—this refers to a specific season. *Bhāsantaḥ*: That which illuminates or shines—this refers to the sun. *Sādhantaḥ*: One who accomplishes tasks—this refers to a mendicant. *Gaṇḍayantaḥ*: That which causes swelling or sprinkles water—this refers to a cloud.

*Maṇḍayantaḥ* means that which adorns or makes beautiful; it is an ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*). *Jayantaḥ* means one who conquers, one who is victorious; in the feminine, *jayantī* refers to a particular kind of flower. *Vijayantaḥ* is a certain specific king, and his palace is the *Vaijayanta*. A banner is called *vaijayantī*. *Nandayantaḥ* is that by which one rejoices, or that which causes joy; for the root *nand* was already recited in the previous sūtra with the prefix *tri*, its mention here again is so that it may apply even when there is no benediction (*anāśis*).
129. And [the suffix] muṭ is added after the root han.
Winter. ||129||
That which kills by means of cold is either the winter season or a specific division of the seasons.
130. And there is the elision of *bhaṇ* [before] *nal*. 130.
Venerable sir. ||130||
"Venerable sir, one who performs what is wholesome is called 'bhadanta,' whether he be a layperson or one who has gone forth."
131. After the root *ṛcch*, the suffix *ara* is substituted [for *liṭ*].
A false ascetic. ||131||

131. He goes or moves, thus he is an *ṛcchara*; or *ṛccharā* means a courtesan. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—it speaks, thus it is a *vadara*, or the fruit of the *vadarī*. It causes distress or dejection, thus it is a *kadara*; or it is a white *khadira* tree. Due to the presence of words like *kapilaka*, there is the substitution of *l* for *r*, and by the rule of the *gaura*-class, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, yielding *kadalī* or *kadarī*. The words *vadarī*, *mandara*, *kandara*, *śīkara*, *koṭara*, *śavara*, *samara*, *barbara*, *varkara*, *karpara*, *piñjara*, *ambara*, *āḍambara*, *jarjara*, *karkara*, *nakha*, *tomara*, and so forth—these ending in the suffix *trap*—are to be derived precisely by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*).
The affix *ci* is applied after the verbal roots *ṛt*, *kamu*, *bhramu*, *camu*, *di*, and *vāsi*.
Arara, kamara, bhramara, camara, devara, vāsara. ||132||

132. He goes or moves, hence *trapara* (a door-leaf) or *kapāṭa* (a door). He desires, hence *kamara* or *kāmuka* (a lover). He wanders, hence *bhramara* (a bee or a lover). He chews or eats, hence *camara* (a species of ox or a yak); by the rule for words beginning with *gaura*, the feminine form is *ṅīṣ*: *camarī* (a female yak or a cow). The tail-hair of the *camarī* is *cāmara*, meaning a bundle of hair. He plays or engages in sport and so forth, hence *devara* (the second husband of a widow or the younger brother of a husband). He causes to dwell, hence *vāsara* (a day or a weekday such as Tuesday).
133. From where have they come? 133.
The osprey. ||133||
It is called *kurara* because it cries out (*kauti*); it is a specific kind of bird.
The suffix *āran* is applied after the roots *aṅg*, *mad*, and *mand*.
*trpraṅgāraḥ*, *madāraḥ*, *mandāraḥ*. ||134||

134. That which moves forward is *trpraṅgāraḥ*, meaning smokeless fire or a modification of the earth. That which becomes intoxicated or drunk is *madāraḥ*, meaning a boar. That which praises slowly is *mandāraḥ*, meaning the *nimba* tree or the *arka* tree. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *āru* also occurs after the root *mand*; thus, that which praises slowly is *mandāruḥ*, meaning either the *nimba* or the *arka* tree.
135. After the root *gaḍ*, [the suffix *ap* is added] and *kaḍa* is substituted [for *gaḍ*]. 135.
135. He who swallows or sprinkles is *kaḍāraḥ*, or it means yellow-colored.
136. Śṛṅgāra and Bhṛṅgāra. ||136||

136. *Śṛṅgāra*: that which pierces (*śrṛṇāti*) or strikes (*hinasti*). It refers to the splendor of an elephant, the aesthetic sentiment (*rasa*) of drama, or the mutual desire for sexual enjoyment between a husband and wife. Here, the suffix *num* and the shortening of the vowel are applied to the root. *Bhṛṅgāra*: that which supports (*bibharti*) or nourishes (*puṣyati*). It refers to a particular type of golden vessel. In the feminine, it is *bhṛṅgārī*, referring either to a specific species of insect or to the creature commonly known as *bhīṃgara*.
137. The suffix *cit* is added after the roots *kañji* and *mṛji*.
kañjāraḥ | mārjāraḥ ||137||
137. *Kañjāraḥ* means "one who cries out" (*kañjati rauti*), thus a peacock or a sauce; *mārjāraḥ* means "one who cleanses" (*mārṣṭi śundhati*), thus a cat; in the feminine, it is *mārjārī*.
The suffix *kvi* is applied after the root *kam*, and the penultimate vowel is replaced by *u*.
The prince. ||138||

It follows the mind; one who desires enjoyments is called a *kumāra*, whether a child or a crown prince. The word *kumāra* is derived from the root *kumāra* (to play) with the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*), and there is both a difference in its etymological derivation and a difference in its meaning.
139. And frost and so forth. 139.
tuṣāraḥ (frost), kāsāraḥ (lake), sahāraḥ (a type of plant), [tarkāraḥ (a type of tree)]||139||

That by which one is satisfied is *tuṣāra*, meaning frost or snow; that which coughs (*kāsate*), makes sound, or censures is *kāsāra*, meaning a lake or pond; that which endures (*sahati*) is *sahāra*, a type of grass or a kind of tree; that which reasons or speaks is *tarkāra*; and in the feminine, due to its inclusion in the *gaurādi* group, it is *tarkārī*, a specific type of creeper known as *jayantī*.
140. After the root *dīṅ*, there is also the substitution of *anuṭ*.
A dīnāra. ||140||
That by which one gives or by which one is diminished is a *dīnāra*, or it is a golden ornament.
After the verbal root *sṛ*, the suffix *ap* is applied, and *ṣuk* is inserted [before it].
Mustard seed. ||141||
It moves and goes; that is the mustard seed, or it possesses pungent oil.
The suffix *kapan* is applied after the roots *uṣi*, *kuṭi*, *dalika*, *cikhaji*, and others.
*uṣapaḥ*, *kuṭapaḥ*, *dalapaḥ*, *kacapam*, *khajapam* ||142||

*Trproṣatī* (it burns) thus *trproṣat*; it is *uṣapaḥ*, or *trpragniḥ* (the burning fire), or *sūryaḥ* (the sun). *Kuṭatī* (it bends) thus *kuṭapaḥ*; it is a measuring vessel. *Dālayati* (it splits) or *vidārayati* (it tears apart) thus *dalapaḥ*; it is a blow. *Kacate* (it binds) or *badhnāti* (it fastens) thus *kacapam*; it is a leaf-plate. *Khajati* (it churns), *mathnāti* (it stirs), or *mathyati* (it is stirred) thus *khajapam*; it is clarified butter (*ghṛtam*).
143. In the case of the root *kvaṇ*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) as well as the suffix *va*.
A corpse. ||143||
It is called *kuṇapa* because it makes a sound (*kvaṇati*) or produces noise; it refers to a corpse or a type of clay.
144. And who was the son of Akravarmaṇ? 144.

According to the opinion of Cākravarman, when the suffix *kapa* is present, the first syllable of the affix is acute; according to the opinion of Tṛpra, the entire compound is acute on its first syllable.
145. *viṭapa*, *viṣṭapa*, *viśipa*, and *ulapa*. ||145||

145. These are irregular words (nipāta) ending in the suffix *kap*. *Viṭapa*: It is so called because it "veils" (*veṭati*) or "sounds" (*śabdayati*) by means of the wind; it refers to the expansion of branches or a tree. *Viṣṭapa*: That into which beings enter (*viśanti*); it refers to the world or the universe. *Triviṣṭapa*: A particular enjoyment of happiness. Alternatively, it is *tripiṣṭhapa*, where there is the substitution of *p* for the *v* of the root and the addition of the augment *tuṭ* to the suffix. *Viśipa*: That into which people enter; it refers to a palace or mansion. There is the substitution of *i* for the initial vowel of the suffix. *Ulapa*: That which "strengthens" (*balate*) or "conceals" (*saṃvṛṇoti*); it refers to soft grass. There is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the initial sound of the root.
146. [The section on] the obstruction of the covering. 146.
The Vārttika ||146||

This refers to the bird *vartikā*, or a specific type of bird. As for the word *vartakā* derived from the root *vṛt* with the suffix *ṇvul*, because the substitution of *it* is prohibited by the *vārttika*, it remains *varttakā*. The distinction is that while the *uṇādi* suffixes are considered non-etymological (*avyutpanna*), *varttakā* is etymologically derived (*vyutpanna*).
The suffix *ki* is applied after the roots *kṛt*, *bhid*, and *dilati*.
Kṛttikā, Bhittikā, Lattikā. ||147||

It is called *kṛttikā* because it cuts (*kṛntati*), or it is the constellation [of that name]. It is called *bhittikā* because it breaks (*bhinatti*), or it is a wall (*bhitti*). It is called *lattikā* because it creeps (*latati*), or it is a lizard (*godhā*).
The suffix *takan* is added after the roots *iṣ* and *śī*.
iṣṭakā | aṣṭakā ||148||
148. That which is desired is *iṣṭakā* (a brick). That which extends in three ways is *triṣṭakā*, or it refers to a specific Vedic ritual (*vaidikakarman*).

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*): that which measures (*masyati*) or develops is *mastakam*, meaning the head; that which holds (*dadhāti*) is *ghātakam*; in the feminine, it is *dhātakī*, a species of flower.
149. After the root *iṇ*, the suffixes *taś* and *taśun* are applied.
Etaśaḥ | Etaśāḥ ||149||

It goes, it reaches—thus it is *etaśaḥ*; [the forms] *etaśāḥ* and *etaśaḥ* [are also used]. *Etaśa* refers to a horse or a Brāhmaṇa. One form ends in a dental (*d*), while the other ends in a sibilant (*s*).
150. [The suffix *tan* is applied] after the roots *vi* and *pati*. 150.
Wages; a port city. ||150||
He knows, obtains, or eats that; thus it is *vetana* or *bhṛti* (wages). One who lives by wages is a *vaitanika*, a laborer. That which one falls into or goes toward is a *pattana*, a city.
The suffix *bha* is applied after the roots *dṛ* and *dal*.
Darbha, Dalbha. ||151||

It is called *darbha* or *kuśa* because it pierces (*dṛṇāti*) or tears apart (*vidārayati*). It is called *dalbha* because it splits (*dalate*) or becomes shattered; [it may also refer to] a seer (*ṛṣi*) or a discus (*cakra*).
The suffix *na* is applied after the roots *ṛt* and *gṛ* when the sense is "to seize. (Pāṇini 3.3.170)
The embryo has three beginnings. ||152||

*Arbhaḥ* refers to a child because he "moves" (*iyarti*) or "goes" (*gacchati*). *Arbha*, *arbhaka*, and *arbhakaḥ* are synonyms for a small child. *Garbhaḥ* means that which swallows (*girati*) or praises/teaches (*gṛṇāti*); it refers either to the womb (*jaṭhara*) or to what resides therein. Regarding the term *garbhitāḥ* (ripening rice), the suffix *itac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *tāraka* (Pāṇini 5.2.36) in the sense of "containing" (*garbhadaprāṇinīti*). However, when referring to a living being, the form is *garbhiṇī*.
153. After the root *iṇ*, [the suffix *ktvā*] is marked with the *k* indicatory letter (*kit*).
The elephant. ||153||
153. *Ibha* means "elephant" or "hastī.
154. The suffix *kthin* is applied after the roots *asi* and *sañji*.
The word *trprasthi* is a synonym for *sakthi*. 154.

That by which one throws or casts is *trprasthi*, namely bone (*kīkasam*) or a constituent part of the body; it is called *sakthi* because it joins (*sajati*), or it refers to the region of the thigh.
The suffix *kṣi* is added after the roots *pluṣi*, *kuṣi*, and *śuṣi*.
plukṣiḥ, kukṣiḥ, śukṣiḥ. ||155||

*Plukṣiḥ*: that which burns or consumes is *plukṣiḥ*; it refers either to fire (*agni*) or to the digestive heat (*trp*). *Kukṣiḥ*: that which draws out or extracts is *kukṣiḥ*; it refers to the belly (*jaṭhara*) or the womb (*garbhāśaya*). *Śukṣiḥ*: that which dries up is *śukṣiḥ*; it refers to the wind (*vāyu*). Here, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is elided internally, and its elision follows the analogy of *parṇa-śuṭ*.
156. He has not been harmed. 156.
The threefold sprinkling. ||156||
That by which one perceives or pervades objects is the *trpra-kṣi*, meaning the eye.
The suffix *ksu* is added after the root *iṣ*.
Sugarcane. ||157||
That is accepted as either sugarcane or honey-grass.
The suffix *ī* is applied after the roots *av*, *tṛ*, and *tan*.
*avīḥ*, *tarīḥ*, *starīḥ*, *tantrīḥ* || 158 ||

*Trpravīḥ* means one who moves forward; it refers to a woman in her menses (*rajasvalā*). *Tarīḥ* is that which crosses over, such as a boat (*naukā*) or a vessel for protecting clothes and other items. *Starīḥ* is that which spreads or covers, such as smoke (*dhūma*). *Tantrīḥ* is that which extends or supports a family; it refers to a lute (*vīṇā*), with the elision of the suffix *ṇi*.
159. After [the verbal roots] √yā and √pā, [the suffix] *ki* is applied, and [the root] is reduplicated.
The forms *yayīḥ* and *papīḥ*. ||159||
He who goes or causes to reach is *yathīḥ*, like a swift horse; he who drinks or protects is *papīḥ*, such as the sun or the moon.
160. After the root √lakṣ, there is also the augment muṭ.
Lakṣmī. ||160||
Thus ends the third section of the Uṇādi-sūtras. 160.

That which marks, sees, or designates is *lakṣmī*; it may also mean prosperity. One who possesses *lakṣmī* is "Lakṣmaṇa. The suffix *na* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) by virtue of the word *lakṣmī* being listed in the *pāmādi* group, according to the rule *lakṣmyās trpracc*.
Thus ends the third quarter of the Vaidikalaukika-koṣa, a commentary on the Uṇādi-sūtras.
Now begins the fourth quarter:
1. Vātapramīḥ ||1||

1. *Vātapramī*: that which measures out or scatters like the wind; or a specific kind of deer that moves very swiftly. This word is exclusively masculine (*puṃliṅga*). [Examples: *vātapramīn* (accusative plural) "deer swift as the wind"; in the locative singular: *vātapramau*; in the accusative singular: *vātapramīm*. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), it is said: that which is desired or longed for is *uśī*, meaning "desire. A country where people are skilled in that [desire] is called *uśīnara*. Here, the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) occurs precisely because of the statement of diversity.

2. From the roots *ṛt*, *añji*, *vañji*, *arpi*, *mad*, *tyaj*, *aṅk*, *ku*, *kṛśi*, there are the suffixes *kat*, *nic*, *yat*, *u*, *jal*, *ij*, *iṣṇuc*, *iṣṭhac*, *isan*, *yani*, *thak*, *ul*, *yas*, *as*, *ānuk*.
Ratniḥ, tanyatuḥ, añjaliḥ, vaniṣṇuḥ, añjiṣṭhaḥ, arpisaḥ, matsyaḥ, tripṛṣṭhi, aṅguliḥ, kavasaḥ, yavāsaḥ, kṛśānuḥ. ||2||

2. From these twelve roots, twelve suffixes beginning with *jā* occur respectively: From *ṛcchati* (he goes) comes *ratniḥ*, meaning "one who has a closed fist" or "the hand"; *aratniḥ* means "one whose fingers are extended. From *tanu* (to stretch), [with the suffix] *yatuc*, comes *tanyatuḥ*, meaning "wind" or "night," as it stretches or extends. From *trp* and *añjū* (with the suffix) *alic*: from *añj* (to anoint/to make manifest) comes *trprañjaliḥ*, meaning "joined palms" or "hands brought together. From *vanu* (to desire), [with the suffix] *alic*, [comes *trprañjaliḥ*], meaning "night. From *trp* and *añjū* (with the suffix) *alic*... [as above].

*Trp-añji*: "He anoints" or "he makes manifest"; thus *trpañjali* refers to two hands joined together. [From the root *van-* with the suffix *-iṣṇuc*: *vaniṣṇu* means "one who desires" or "one who begs," or it refers to the wind that drinks moisture (*trpa-pāna-vāyu*). [From *trp-añj-* with the suffix *-iṣṭha*: *trpañjiṣṭha* means "one who anoints" or "one who makes objects manifest," referring to the sun. [From *arp-* with the suffix *-isa*: *trparpisa* means "one who causes to reach" or "the choice meat" (*agramāṃsa*). [From *mad-* with the suffix *-syan*: *matsya* means "one who rejoices" or "a fish. [From *trpat-* with the suffix *-ithin*:]...

*Tripṛtathi*: that which goes or wanders continuously; or a virtuous person who has arrived unexpectedly (*akasmāt*). An alternative etymology is: "one for whom no fixed day (*tithi*) exists. In the feminine, by the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied—thus *tripratithī* (a woman). *Tripṛaṅgi*: a finger (*aṅguli*). *Tripṛaṅgati*: that by which one moves or exerts itself; thus *tripṛaṅguliḥ* refers to a finger or a branch of the hand. *Kutṛpṛasa*: one who praises (*kauti*) or speaks (*kavate*), thus *kavasaḥ*; or a species of thorn. There is also an alternative reading: *acaḥ*.

Then, it is called *kavaca* because it covers (*kavate*). It is called *yavāsa* because it joins (*yauti*) or mixes; it is either a species of the *kaṇkaṭa* tree or [a plant] that is thin (*vākṛśa*). It is called *kṛśānu* because it makes thin (*kṛśati*, i.e., attenuates); it is either fire (*agni*) or [the wind].

3. What is the future? 3. What is the past? 3. What is the present? 3. What is that which is not included therein? 3. What is the unconditioned? 3. What is space? 3. What is cessation through deliberation? 3. What is cessation not through deliberation? 3. What is the realm of infinite space? 3. What is the realm of infinite consciousness? 3. What is the realm of nothingness? 3. What is the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? 3. What is the realm of sentient beings? 3. What is the realm of phenomena? 3. What is the realm of non-phenomena? 3. What is the realm of both phenomena and non-phenomena? 3. What is the realm of neither phenomena nor non-phenomena? 3. What is the realm of the seen? 3. What is the realm of the heard? 3. What is the realm of the sensed? 3. What is the realm of the known? 3. What is the realm of the cognized? 3. What is the realm of the unconditioned? 3. What is the realm of the conditioned? 3. What is the realm of both the conditioned and the unconditioned? 3. What is the realm of neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned? 3. What is the realm of the internal? 3. What is the realm of the external? 3. What is the realm of both the internal and the external? 3. What is the realm of neither the internal nor the external? 3. What is the realm of the past? 3. What is the realm of the future? 3. What is the realm of the present? 3. What is the realm of the non-manifest? 3. What is the realm of the manifest? 3. What is the realm of both the manifest and the non-manifest? 3. What is the realm of neither the manifest nor the non-manifest? 3. What is the realm of the wholesome? 3. What is the realm of the unwholesome? 3. What is the realm of the indeterminate? 3. What is the realm of the outflowing? 3. What is the realm of the non-outflowing? 3. What is the realm of both the outflowing and the non-outflowing? 3. What is the realm of neither the outflowing nor the non-outflowing? 3. What is the realm of the tainted? 3. What is the realm of the untainted? 3. What is the realm of both the tainted and the untainted? 3. What is the realm of neither the tainted nor the untainted? 3. What is the realm of the with-outflow? 3. What is the realm of the without-outflow? 3. What is the realm of both the with-outflow and the without-outflow? 3. What is the realm of neither the with-outflow nor the without-outflow? 3. What is the realm of the grasped? 3. What is the realm of the non-grasped? 3. What is the realm of both the grasped and the non-grasped? 3. What is the realm of neither the grasped nor the non-grasped? 3. What is the realm of the inferior? 3. What is the realm of the superior? 3. What is the realm of the middle? 3. What is the realm of the worldly? 3. What is the realm of the supramundane? 3. What is the realm of both the worldly and the supramundane? 3. What is the realm of neither the worldly nor the supramundane? 3. What is the realm of the conditioned? 3. What is the realm of the unconditioned? 3. What is the realm of both the conditioned and the unconditioned? 3. What is the realm of neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned? 3. What is the realm of the compounded? 3. What is the realm of the uncompounded? 3. What is the realm of both the compounded and the uncompounded? 3. What is the realm of neither the compounded nor the uncompounded? 3. What is the realm of the finite? 3. What is the realm of the infinite? 3. What is the realm of both the finite and the infinite? 3. What is the realm of neither the finite nor the infinite? 3. What is the realm of the eternal? 3. What is the realm of the non-eternal? 3. What is the realm of both the eternal and the non-eternal? 3. What is the realm of neither the eternal nor the non-eternal? 3. What is the realm of the self? 3. What is the realm of the non-self? 3. What is the realm of both the self and the non-self? 3. What is the realm of neither the self nor the non-self? 3. What is the realm of the existent? 3. What is the realm of the non-existent? 3. What is the realm of both the existent and the non-existent? 3. What is the realm of neither the existent nor the non-existent? 3. What is the realm of the knowable? 3. What is the realm of the unknowable? 3. What is the realm of both the knowable and the unknowable? 3. What is the realm of neither the knowable nor the unknowable? 3. What is the realm of the perceived? 3. What is the realm of the non-perceived? 3. What is the realm of both the perceived and the non-perceived? 3. What is the realm of neither the perceived nor the non-perceived? 3. What is the realm of the apprehended? 3. What is the realm of the non-apprehended? 3. What is the realm of both the apprehended and the non-apprehended? 3. What is the realm of neither the apprehended nor the non-apprehended? 3. What is the realm of the object? 3. What is the realm of the subject? 3. What is the realm of both the object and the subject? 3. What is the realm of neither the object nor the subject? 3. What is the realm of the cause? 3. What is the realm of the effect? 3. What is the realm of both the cause and the effect? 3. What is the realm of neither the cause nor the effect? 3. What is the realm of the producer? 3. What is the realm of the produced? 3. What is the realm of both the producer and the produced? 3. What is the realm of neither the producer nor the produced? 3. What is the realm of the support? 3. What is the realm of the supported? 3. What is the realm of both the support and the supported? 3. What is the realm of neither the support nor the supported? 3. What is the realm of the basis? 3. What is the realm of the based? 3. What is the realm of both the basis and the based? 3. What is the realm of neither the basis nor the based? 3. What is the realm of the primary? 3. What is the realm of the secondary? 3. What is the realm of both the primary and the secondary? 3. What is the realm of neither the primary nor the secondary? 3. What is the realm of the gross? 3. What is the realm of the subtle? 3. What is the realm of both the gross and the subtle? 3. What is the realm of neither the gross nor the subtle? 3. What is the realm of the distant? 3. What is the realm of the near? 3. What is the realm of both the distant and the near? 3. What is the realm of neither the distant nor the near? 3. What is the realm of the coarse? 3. What is the realm of the fine? 3. What is the realm of both the coarse and the fine? 3. What is the realm of neither the coarse nor the fine? 3. What is the realm of the defiled? 3. What is the realm of the pure? 3. What is the realm of both the defiled and the pure? 3. What is the realm of neither the defiled nor the pure? 3. What is the realm of the afflicted? 3. What is the realm of the non-afflicted? 3. What is the realm of both the afflicted and the non-afflicted? 3. What is the realm of neither the afflicted nor the non-afflicted? 3. What is the realm of the fettered? 3. What is the realm of the unfettered? 3. What is the realm of both the fettered and the unfettered? 3. What is the realm of neither the fettered nor the unfettered? 3. What is the realm of the bound? 3. What is the realm of the liberated? 3. What is the realm of both the bound and the liberated? 3. What is the realm of neither the bound nor the liberated? 3. What is the realm of the obstructed
Sugar-candy. ||3||
3. It is called *śarkarā* because it crushes (*śrṛṇāti*); it is a derivative of sugar-cane juice or a derivative of molasses.
The suffix *puṣ* is marked with the *k* it-marker.
Puṣkara. 4.
It is called *puṣkara* because it nourishes (*puṣṇāti*); *trp* refers to the intermediate space, while *kamala* or *udaka* refers to water.
And [the merit is] tenfold. ||5||
Abundant. ||5||
5. From the root *puṣ*, there is also the formation *puṣkala*; that which nourishes (*puṣyati*) is *puṣkala*, meaning "full" or "complete."
6. The female gamers. ||6||
One who goes.
"One who will go" (*gamiṣyati*) is a traveler (*gamī*) or a wayfarer (*pathika*). The temporal restriction [of the suffix] is established by the rule *bhaviṣyati gamyādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.3).
7. When the prefix āṅ is present, [the verbal root] is treated as having a ṇit suffix.
One who goes to the three [realms]. ||7||
7. There is *vṛddhi* [substitution] because of the suffix *ṇit*. One who will go to Trpā is called *trpāgāmī*.
And [the word] bhuvas [is also used]. ||8||
Existence. ||8||
8. The suffix *ini* is *ṇit*. "That which will be" is *bhāvī*.
9. *pra-sthaḥ*. 9.
Setting forth. ||9||
9. *ini* is *ṇit*. Because it is *ṇit*, [the suffix] *yuk* is added. One who desires to set out is called a *prasthāyī*, meaning one whose mind is intent on going.
10. In the highest state. 10.
Parameṣṭhin. ||10||

He who stands in the highest, most excellent state of being is Parameṣṭhin—the Grandfather of all, or the Lord. [The suffix] *trp* is elided after the locative case ending, and there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *t*.
11. The Mantha [offering]. 11.
manthāḥ | manthānau ||11||

11. *Iniḥ* [is added] with the marker *k*; due to this *k*-marker, there is elision of the nasal (*n*). That which churns or agitates is *manthāḥ*. The word *mathin* takes the designation of a *sarvanāmasthāna* (strong case ending) by virtue of the *trap* suffix; thus: *matthānau*, *manthānaḥ*. It refers to the churning-stick for curd and other substances, or to the thunderbolt (*vajra*), or to the wind (*vāyu*).
And you are the twelve paths. 12.12.
The path. ||12||

12. *Panthāḥ* (paths) is that which goes where one travels; [the dual is] *panthānau*. As before, there is the substitution of *āt*. From the verbal root *path* in the sense of "going," when the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class) is applied, forms such as *pathaḥ*, *pathau*, and *pathāḥ* are also seen ending in *a*.
13. From the root *khaj*, the suffix *āka* is applied. 13.
The ladle. ||13||
13. That which "stirs" (*khajati*) or "churns" (*mathnāti*) is a *khajāka*, a bird; or *khajākā* refers to a ladle.

Due to the rule of frequentative usage (*bahulavacanāt*), those which are "slowed down" (*mandyante*) or "praised" (*stūyante*) are *mandākāni*; or they are "streams" (*srotāṃsi*). That which possesses these [streams] is the river named *Mandākinī*.
14. And [the examples] beginning with the crane (valākā) [are also included]. 14.
valākā, śalākā, patākā ||14||

14. *Valākā* is a female crane (*valate*) or a row of cranes (*saṃvṛṇoti*); it is also a female swan (*vakapakṣī*). *Manākā* is thought to mean she who knows (*manyate*). *Pavākā* refers to one who purifies (*punāti*). *Śalākā* refers to that which they go toward (*śalanti*) or move upon, such as a stick for applying collyrium. *Paṭāka* is that which moves or flies (*paṭati*), such as a bird. *Patākā* is that which is known or perceived (*patyate*), such as a banner.
15. And [the names] beginning with Pināka [are also used]. 15.
Pināka; Taḍāka. ||15||

It is called *pināka* because it protects (*pāti rakṣati*); it refers either to the trident or to the Creator (*dhātṛ*). It is called *taḍākā* because it strikes or smites (*tāḍayati āhanti*); it refers to radiance (*prabhā*).

Due to the rule of *bahulavacana* (the principle of diversity), when the suffix *trap* is applied with the prefix *ap*, the form *taḍāgaḥ* is also established. That which rejoices (*bhandate*) is *madākaḥ*, meaning auspiciousness. That which grows or reaches (*śyāyati*) is *śyāmākaḥ*, a type of grain well-known as *samā*. The addition of the augment *muk* is by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). That which does not shine but appears [dark] is *nabhākam*, meaning the sky filled with clouds.
