That which one grinds thoroughly, pulverizing it, is *piṇyākaḥ*, meaning sesame paste; here, the letter *p* of the root is changed to *dh*, and the augment *yuk* is added.

That by which one subsists is *vārttāka*; *vārttāka* is the well-known "forest cucumber" (*vanabhaṇṭā*). There is a vowel-vṛddhi [of the root]. It is called *guvāka* because it emits excrement (*guvati purīṣam utsṛjati*), that is, the areca nut (*pūgīphala*); there is an absence of guṇa due to its belonging to the *kuṭādi* group.
The suffix *īkan* is applied after the verbal roots *kaṣ* and *dūṣi*.
kaṣīkā, dūṣīkā. ||16||

16. It is called *kaṣīkā* because it scrapes (*kaṣati*) or injures (*hinasti*), referring either to a species of bird or to the film on the eye; it is called *dūṣīkā* because it corrupts (*dūṣayati*), referring to the impurity of the eye.
17. The suffix *ki* is applied after the roots *ni* and *hṛṣ*.
Without sense organs; the senses are inactive. ||17||

That which breathes and gives life is the *trpranīka*, meaning either an opposing army or the senses (*hṛṣīka*); that by which one rejoices or becomes satisfied is the *hṛṣīka*, or it is [the means] by which [one perceives] eternally through knowledge.
18. Caṅkaṇa and kaṅkaṇa. ||18||
Kaṅkaṇīkā ||18||

From the root *kaṇ* with the elision of the suffix *yaṅ*, the suffix *īkan* is applied and *kaṅgaṇa* is substituted for it. That which sounds or makes noise repeatedly is called *kaṅkaṇīkā*, a specific musical instrument known as *ghariyāra*. *Kiṅkiṇīkā* refers to a small bell. This is established by virtue of the rule regarding frequentative forms (*bahulavacana*).
19. For the roots śṝ, pṝ, and vṛj, there is reduplication and the substitution of *ru* for the reduplicated syllable.
Śarśarīka, Parparīka, Varvarīka. ||19||

19. *Śarśarīkaḥ* means one who injures or harms; thus, it refers to a harmful person (*hiṃsaka*). *Parparīkaḥ* means one who fills or protects; thus, it refers to the sun (*sūrya*). *Varvarīkaḥ* means one who chooses or accepts for oneself; thus, it refers either to a person with curly hair or to a crooked person.
20. And [the insects] such as the *pharpharīka* and so forth. 20.

*Pharpharīkam*, *dardarīkam*, *tintiḍīkaḥ*, *cañcarīkaḥ*, *marmarīkaḥ*, *karkarīkam*, *puṇḍarīkaḥ*. 20. *Pharpharīkam*: That which causes the conscious principle (*cetana*) to quiver or come into being; or, it refers to a knot at the tip of a branch together with its leaves. By the addition of the suffix *īkan*, the verbal root undergoes the substitution *pharphara*. *Dardarīkam*: That which pierces; or, it refers to a musical instrument. *Karkarīkam*: That by which one performs actions; or, it refers to the body. *Karkarīkā* is well known as a small water-pot or a pitcher (*kalaśī*). *Puṇḍarīkaḥ*: A white lotus. (20)

In both of these cases, there is reduplication of the root and the suffix *ruk* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). *Timyati* (it becomes moist) means it makes wet; thus, *tintiḍīkaḥ* refers either to a species of tree or a type of citron. Here, *ḍāka* replaces the *m* of the root, and *nuṭ* is added to the reduplicated syllable. *Carati* (he moves), *gacchati* (he goes), or *bhakṣayati* (he eats); thus, *cañcarīkaḥ* refers to a bee. Here, *num* is added to the reduplicated syllable. *Mriyate* (he dies); thus, *marmarīkaḥ* refers to a low-born person. *Puṇati* (he performs auspicious deeds); thus, *puṇḍarīkam* refers to a white lotus, a white-leaved [flower], a medicinal herb, a tiger, or fire.
21. After the root *īṣ*, the suffix *kvip* is applied, and there is also shortening [of the vowel].
The Iṣokas. ||21||
Due to the presence of the *kit* suffix, there is an absence of *guṇa*. That which moves or goes is called *iṣīkā*, meaning a stalk of *muñja* grass or similar reed.
22. And [the substitution of *u* occurs] for the vowel *ṛ*. 22.
The straight-moving one. ||22||
22. *Kit* means "he goes straight" (*ṛjati gacchati*), thus it is *ṛjīka*; or, because it ends in *kit*, there is a prohibition of *guṇa*.
And [the elision of] *s* and *ar* [occurs] before *nu*. 23.23.
sṛṇīkā ||23||
It is called *sṛṇīkā* because it flows (*sarati*) or reaches (*prāpnoti*); it is a type of saliva, commonly known as *lāra*, which is a kind of spittle.
24. *mṛḍaḥ*, *kīkaṭaḥ*, and *kaṅkaṇau* [are used]. 24.
Mṛḍīka; mṛḍaṅkaṇa. ||24||
He who softens—that is, who brings happiness—is Mṛḍīka, the giver of bliss; or [the name] Mṛḍaṅkaṇa refers to a child.
Due to the use of the suffix *bahul*—it is called *kaṅkaṇa* because it "sounds" (*kāyati*) or "makes a noise," and thus it is an ornament for the hand.
25. And [the categories] beginning with the false [also exist]. 25.
*trpralīkam*, *vyalīkam*, *valīkam*. ||25||

25. Words ending in the suffix *kīkan* are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) with the feminine suffix *trp*. *Trpralokam*: that which wards off or restrains; or it is false (*mithyā*). From the prefix *vi-*: *vyalīkam*, meaning unpleasantness or distress. *Valīkam*: that by which one folds or conceals; or it refers to the materials for roofing a house. There are others as well: from *valate* (he is concealed), *valmīkam*, meaning an anthill, a hole, or a type of sage. His descendant is *Vālmīki*; here the augment *muṭ* is added. *Vāhīkaḥ*: that which carries; meaning a bull or a horse. There is a *vṛddhi* strengthening of the root.
*Supratīkaḥ*: he who goes forth well; or it refers to Agni. Here the suffix *tuṭ* is added to the root.
26. After the roots √kṛ and √tṛ, the suffix īṣan is applied.
karīṣaḥ | tarīṣaḥ ||26||
That which is scattered or thrown about is *karīṣa*, namely dried cow dung; that by which one crosses over is *tarīṣa*, namely a boat.
27. The suffix *ki* is applied after the roots *śṝ* and *pṝ*, and it is also kit.
Śirīṣaḥ | Purīṣam ||27||
27. It is called *śirīṣa* because it destroys (*śṛṇāti*) or because it protects (*śṛṇāti*); it is a specific type of tree. Or, *purīṣa* refers to that which fills (*piparti*), namely excrement.
And [the substitution of] *ar* occurs for *ṛj* as well. 28.28.
The dregs. ||28||
Because it is straight (ṛju), it is accumulated (sañcita), therefore it is called *ṛjīṣa*; or it is well known as *piṣṭapacana* ("that in which flour is cooked").
29. Ambarīṣa. ||29||
29. It is called *trprambarīṣa* because it "boils" (*ambate*) or makes a sound; it is a vessel for steaming (*trprākāśa*) or a steamer (*svedanī*), commonly known as a *bhāḍa*.
The suffix *īran* is added after the verbal roots *kṝ*, *śṛ*, *pṛ*, *kaṭi*, *paṭi*, and *śauṭi*.
karīraḥ | śarīram | parīram | kaṭīraḥ | paṭīraḥ | śauṭīraḥ ||30||

30. *Karīra*: that which scatters (*kirati*) is a type of tree or the sprout of a *vaśā* plant. *Śarīra*: that which is shattered (*śīryate*) or destroyed; it refers to the body (*prāṇikāya*) or the fruit (*phala*). *Parīsa*: that by which one is filled (*pūryate*); it refers to a fruit. *Kaṭīra*: that which is covered or concealed (*kaṭhyate*); it refers to a hut (*kuṭī*) or the region of the hips (*jaghanadeśa*). *Paṭīra*: that which moves or goes (*paṭati*); it refers to a ball (*kanduka*), desire (*kāma*), or the sandalwood tree (*candana-vṛkṣa*). *Śauṭīra*: one who acts with pride (*śauṭati*) or displays arrogance; it refers to a generous person (*tyāgī*) or a hero (*vīra*). By the rule for words beginning with *brāhmaṇa*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied: *śauṭīryam*, meaning dispassion (*vairāgya*).

Due to the rule of "bahulavacana" (the principle of diversity or irregularity): *hiṇḍīraḥ* means that which wanders or moves here and there; it refers to sea-foam or a pomegranate tree. Words such as *kirmira*, *tūṇīra*, *jambīra*, *kumbhīra*, and *kuṭīra*, which end in the suffix *-īra*, are also to be understood as resulting from this very principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
The suffix *kic* is applied after the root *vaś*.
To Uṣas. ||31||
That which is desired or longed for is *uśīra*, namely the root of the *vīraṇa* grass; it is commonly known as *khasakhasa*.
32. And *kaś* is substituted [for the root *kṛṣ*], and there is also the augment *muṭ*.
Kaśmīraḥ ||32||
32. *Īran* means "one who goes to or rules over a difficult place"; it refers either to a person or to a specific region, Kashmir.
33. The root *kṛñ* is [used] in the sense of "high. 33.
A head-covering. ||33||

That which is made is called *kurīra* or *maithuna*; alternatively, due to the rule regarding the substitution of *la* for *ra* as seen in words like *kapilaka*, it is *kulīra*, meaning a specific kind of aquatic creature.
34. The [substitute] of √ghas is kit.
That which is drunk or consumed is milk (kṣīram) or draught (dugdham).
35. Both are profound and very profound. ||35||

35. In one view, the *m* of the root *gam* is replaced by *bh*, and there is the addition of the augment *num*. That which is gone to, reached, or known is "deep" (*gabhīraḥ*); [it is also spelled *gambhīraḥ*]. It is either tranquil or of great intent. These two words take the gender of the noun they qualify.
36. The section on poison (viṣa). 36.

36. It is *viṣ* because it specifically (*viśeṣeṇa*) exhausts (*syati*) and brings to an end (*karoti*) karma; or it is *viṣ* as the intellect (*buddhi*). It is *vihā* because it specifically (*viśeṣeṇa*) abandons (*jahāti*) or relinquishes (*tyajati*) suffering; or it is *vihā* as the world of bliss (*sukhaloka*). By their very nature (*svabhāvāt*), these two are indeclinables (*avyaya*).
37. Paca elimac || 37 ||
Fickle. ||37||

"Pacelima" means that which cooks things, such as a fierce fire or the sun. However, the distinction is that when the suffix *kelimac* is prescribed after the root *pac* by the general Vārttika for the sense of the *kṛtya* suffixes, it occurs in the sense of the action (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), or the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*).
38. After the root √śī (to lie down), the affixes dhuk, lak, bal, añ, and bālaṇ are applied.
śīdhu, śāla, śaivala, śevāla; [and] śepāla. ||38||

38. That by which one lies down is *śīdhu*, meaning liquor or wine. *Śīla* means inherent nature (*svabhāva*). *Śaivala*; *śevāla*—due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffixal *v* becomes *p*—these are synonyms for *śepāla*, the aquatic moss known as *jalanīlī*. It is that which grows in water in the form of a creeper and is commonly called *sevāra*.
From the roots *mṛk* and *kaṇi*, the suffixes *ūka* and *okaṇ* are applied respectively.
Marūkaḥ | Kāṇūkaḥ || 39 ||
39. He dies, thus he is *marūka*, a deer; or he cries out, makes sound, thus he is *kāṇūka*, a crow. 40. From the root *val*, *ūka* [is added]. 40.
Valūka. ||40||
It is called *valūka* because it moves (*valate*) and covers (*saṃvṛṇoti*); it refers either to a bird or to the root of a lotus.
41. And owls and so forth [are also included]. 41.
Ulūkaḥ, vāvadūkaḥ, bhallūkaḥ, śambūkaḥ. ||41||

41. Words ending in the suffix *ūka* are derived as irregular formations (*nipātana*). That which turns about is an *ulūka*, a species of bird; here there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root. One who speaks excessively is a *vāvadūka*, a speaker; here the suffix *ūka* is added to the intensive (*yaṅ*) form without the *luk*-elision. [That which pacifies is a *śambūka*] or a marine shell; here the suffix *ūk* is added to the root. By virtue of the rule for diversity (*bāhulaka*), when the suffix *uka* is applied, *śambuka* is also established. That which roams about or speaks all around is a *bhallūka*, a bear; by virtue of the rule for diversity, with a short vowel, *bhalluka* is also formed. Likewise, that which moves about is a *bhālūka*; it is the same animal.
"Mahatī" refers to the *madhūka* tree, a specific type of tree; likewise, *elūka*, *jambūka*, *bandhūka*, *vāstūka*, and others should also be understood as belonging to this same category.
42. The suffix *ūkaṇ* is applied after the words *śāli* and *maṇḍi*.
The śālūka is a frog. ||42||
42. That which is pierced or obtained is *śālūka*, meaning either a root-crop or a lotus-root; that which moves about beautifully is *maṇḍūka*, meaning a frog or an aquatic creature.
The rim. ||43||
It is called *nemi* because it leads (*nayati*), or it is a part of a wheel.

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—it goes (*yāti*) or brings about its effects—it is called *yāmi*. Through the substitution of *j* for the initial [phoneme], it becomes *jāmi*, meaning a sister or a woman of the family.
44. Artterucca || 44 ||
The wave. ||44||
It is called a *ūrmi* because it moves or goes; it is a wave of water.
45. [The suffix] *kit* follows [the verbal root] *bhu*.
The ground. ||45||

"Earth" (*bhūmi*) is that in which things exist; it is a place of origin. *Bhūmikā* is a diminutive form of "earth" (*bhūmi*). According to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied, resulting in *bhūmī*.
The suffix *aś* is applied after the root *aś* [in the sense of eating].
The ray. ||46||
A *raśmi* is so called because it extends (*prasṛte*) or pervades (*vyāpnoti*); it may refer to a ray of light or a rope.
47. The Dog. 47.
That by which one pierces or cleaves is a *dalmi*, namely the sun's ray or the supreme weapon.
The suffix *niḥ* is applied after the roots *vīj* and *ajvar*.
veṇiḥ, jyāniḥ, jūrṇiḥ. ||48||

48. *Veṇiḥ* is that which is woven or braided; it refers to the arrangement of hair. The change to *ṇ* occurs by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). *Jyāniḥ* is so called because one who is deprived of youth (*vayohīna*) is worn out (*jināti*), or it means decay (*kṣati*). *Jūrṇiḥ* is so called because one becomes afflicted with fever (*jvarati*), or it refers to a woman's disease.

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—one who makes a sound (*kṣauti*) is *kṣoṇiḥ*. With the suffix *ḍīṣ*, it becomes *kṣoṇī*, meaning the earth. One who buys (*krīṇāti*) is *kreṇiḥ*; [with *ḍīṣ*] it is *kreṇī*.
49. The suffix *kit* is applied after the roots *sṛ* and *sṛj*.
Sṛṇiḥ | Vṛṣṇiḥ ||49||
It is called *sṛṇi* because it moves or goes; it is a goad or a hook. It is called *vṛṣṇi* because it rains [virtue]; it is either a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya.
50. And there is also the elision of the suffix *aṅ*.
The fire is threefold. ||50||
50. *Trp* means he moves forward, attains, or knows; thus *trpagni* refers to the well-known bearer of oblations (*vahni*).
51. The suffix *ni* is applied after the verbal roots *vah*, *śri*, *śru*, *yudh*, *dru*, *glā*, and *hātvari*.
vahnih, śreṇiḥ, śroṇiḥ, yoniḥ, droṇiḥ, glāniḥ, hāniḥ, tūrṇiḥ. ||51||

51. It carries, thus it is *vahni*, meaning fire or one who carries. It leans upon or serves, thus it is *śreṇi*, meaning a row or a line. From the prefix *ni* [with *śri*], it is *niśreṇī*, meaning a ladder or a flight of stairs. It hears, thus it is *śroṇi*, meaning the region of the hips. It unites or separates, thus it is *yoni*, meaning a cause or the generative organ. They flow or go there, thus it is *droṇi*, meaning a trough for pouring water or a specific type of terrain. One becomes weary in it, thus it is *glāni*, meaning weakness or despondency.

*Hāni* is that which diminishes or abandons; it is either a decrease or a growth. *Prahāṇi* and *parihāṇi* [mean the same]. The substitution of *ṇ* occurs according to the rule *kṛtyacaḥ* [Pāṇini 8.4.29]. *Tūrṇi* means that which hastens or moves correctly; it refers to the mind (*manas*).

Due to the rule regarding frequentative suffixes (bahulavacanāt)—he lies down, thus he is a Śini or a Kṣatriya; there is also shortening of the verbal root. That which withers is a mlāniḥ, or it is the destruction of joy (trp).
52. *ghṛṇi*, *pṛśni*, *pārṣṇi*, *cūrṇi*, and *bhūrṇi*. 52.

52. That which sprinkles, flows, or shines is *ghṛṇi*, meaning a ray of light. That which touches or becomes joined is *pṛśni*, meaning one with a small body; there is the elision of the *s* of the root. That which sprinkles or pours out is *pārṣṇi*, meaning the sole of the foot; there is the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the root. That which moves, goes, eats, pulverizes, or impels is *cūrṇi*, meaning an exposition. That which sustains or supports everything is *bhūrṇi*, meaning the earth. By way of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—that which sounds or makes a noise is *dhūrṇi*.
The suffix *vin* is applied after the roots *vṛdh* and *dṛ*.
A ladle; a spoon. ||53||
It covers, thus it is *varviḥ*, or it is a consumer; that by which one pierces is *darviḥ*, or it is a vessel for stirring a curry. By adding the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, it becomes *darvī*.
The suffix *kvin* is applied after the roots *jṝ*, *śṝ*, *stṝ*, and *jāgṛ*.
*jīrviḥ*, *śīrviḥ*, *stīrviḥ*, *jāgṛviḥ* ||54||

54. That which decays is *jīrvi*, or it is the sacrificial animal (*paśu*); that which pierces is *śīrvi*; that which spreads or covers is *stīrvi*, or it is the *trp* (the grass-offering) or the Adhvaryu priest; that which is awake is *jāgṛvi*, or it is the lord of men (*nṛpati*).
55. After the root *div*, there is reduplication, which is long.
The shining one. ||55||

It is called *dīdivi* because it shines (*dīvyati*), meaning either happiness or food. Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*) regarding the *kvin* suffix, the elision of the nasal (*ñ*) and the final vowel (*a*) do not occur here.
56. *kakṛ*, *vighṛṣvi*, *chavi*, *sthavi*, and *kikīdivi*.

That by which one acts is *kṛviḥ*, or it refers to the material of a weaver. That which rubs or sprinkles is *ghṛṣviḥ*, or it refers to a boar (*varāha*). That which cuts or makes fine is *chaviḥ*, or it means luster; there is also shortening of the root vowel. That which stands is *syaviḥ*, or it refers to a weaver. Here too, the vowel is shortened. One who plays with the sound "kiki" is *kikidīviḥ*, or it refers to the blue jay (*cāṣa*), commonly known as *nīlakaṇṭha*. There are five variants: *kikīdiviḥ*, *kikidiviḥ*, *kikidīvaḥ*, *kikidivaḥ*, and *kikīdīviḥ*; these should be understood through the rule of "bahula" (diversity).
The suffix *ḍati* is applied after the root *pāt*. (Pāṇini 5.2.57)
The husband. ||57||
57. He who protects (*pāti*) is a *pati*, meaning a master or lord.
58. The verse of Śakra. 58.
Feces. ||58||

58. *Śakṛt* means that which is able (*śaknoti*), or else it means excrement (*mala*). This is due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*); for example, from the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), *yakṛt* is formed, meaning the liver (*kālakhaṇḍa*). Here, the letter *j* of the verbal root is replaced by the letter *k*.
59. Absence of malice. ||59||
Lack of intelligence. ||59||
59. *Trp* means "to go"; thus, *trpamatiḥ* refers to time (*kāla*).

By virtue of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*): one who performs a vow (*vrata*) is a *vratati*, meaning a creeper (*vistara*) or a vine (*latā*). One who spreads fragrance or bears it is a *mālatī*; *mālati* means a flower (*sumanā*) or the plant commonly known as *camelī*. One who establishes righteousness (*dharma*) is a *sthapati*, meaning an eloquent man or a performer of sacrifice (*yajñakartṛ*). In the case of the root *sthā* with the causative suffix (*ṇyanta*), when the augment *puK* is added, there is shortening of the vowel.
60. Also after the roots *vah*, *vas*, and *ṛt*.
*vahatiḥ*, *vasatiḥ*, *aratiḥ* ||60||

*Vahatiḥ* is the wind, so called because it carries (*vahati*), causes things to reach their destination (*prāpayati*), or reaches them itself (*prāpnoti*). *Vasatiḥ* is a dwelling (*vasati*) or a house (*vasatī*), so called because one dwells (*vasanti*) therein; it may also mean "night. *Tṛparatiḥ* is anger, so called because it goes toward or attacks (*ṛcchati*) and moves (*gacchati*).
By virtue of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*): that which delights, adorns, or is capable is called *trpralati*, or it refers to a mere song (*gītamātrikā*).
61. Or, after the root *añc*, [the suffix] *kvip* [is applied].
The roots √tṛp and √añc take the suffix *aṅ* [to form trapaṅ and añcaṅ]. ||61||
61. He who moves forward, goes, or honors is *trpraṅkati*; or *trprañcati* is Vāyu (the Wind).
And [the suffix] hanter-aṃha ca || 62 ||
The *trpraṃhati* [meter]. ||62||
62. *Ati*: because it strikes excessively, it is *atighni*; or it is a gift (*dāna*).
63. [The suffix] *niṣ* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ra*. 63.
Delight. ||63||
In this they delight; thus, *ramati* is either time (*kāla*) or desire (*kāma*).
64. After the verbal root *sūḍ*, the suffix *kri* [is applied].
The sage. ||64||
One who begets, produces, or brings about living beings is a *sūri*, meaning either a progenitor or a wise man (*paṇḍita*). In the feminine, it is *sūrī*.
65. The suffix *krin* is applied after the verbal roots *adi*, *śu*, *bhū*, and *śubh*.
He who dwells on the mountain, the mountain-like, the abundant, the radiant. ||65||

That which eats or that wherein they eat is *trpradri*, meaning a mountain, a cloud, a tree, or the sun. That which perishes or causes to perish is *śadri*, meaning gravel or sand. That which exists is *bhūri*, meaning abundant gold; one for whom abundance is the purpose is a *bhaurika*, meaning a superintendent of gold. That which shines is *śubhri*, meaning a knower of the four Vedas or a Brahmin.
66. And [the words] vaṅkri and so forth [are also included]. 66.
vaṅkriḥ, vapriḥ, trpraṃhriḥ, tandriḥ, bheriḥ. ||66||

66. *Vaṅkriḥ* is that which bends; it is a type of musical instrument or a beam of a house. *Vapriḥ* is that in which one sows; it is a field. The absence of *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) occurs by virtue of the rule’s diversity (*bāhulaka*). *Trahriḥ* is that which causes distress or speaks; it is a foot. *Tandiḥ* is a root belonging to the *sūtra* (Vedic/technical) class; *tandati* means "it afflicts," thus *tandri* is delusion. In the feminine, it is *tandrī*. *Bheriḥ* is that by which one fears; it is a specific type of musical instrument, or *bherī*.
The suffix *trip* is applied after the roots *rāś* and *di*.
rātriḥ | śatriḥ ||67||
67. It is well known as *rātri* because it bestows (*rāti*) happiness; or it is *śatri*, meaning "it cuts" (*śīyate*), like an elephant.
And [the word] *adestrin* [is formed]. 68.
Atrīḥ means one who has satisfied the ancestors. ||68||

Furthermore, one who eats with greed is called *trp-trī* (greedy-eater); the forms *trp-triṇau* mean "two greedy-eaters. Alternatively, *trp-triḥ* refers to evil, or to a specific type of sage (*muni-bheda*). His descendant is *Ātreya*.
69. Pater Atrin. 69.
The bird. ||69||

That which flies is *patatri*, meaning "bird. [The form] *patatrī* [is derived as follows]: from the word *patatra*, which denotes "wing," the suffix *ini* is added in the sense of possession (*matvartha*). Thus: *patatrī*, *patatriṇau*.
The suffix *īci* is applied after the roots *mṛk* and *kaṇ*.
Marīci; Kaṇīci. ||70||

70. *Marīci* means that which dies away, or it refers to a radiant great seer (*maharṣi*). *Kaṇīci* means that which sounds or makes a noise; it refers either to a branch provided with leaves and so forth, or to sound itself.
71. After the root √śvi, [the suffix] cit [is applied].
A dog's carcass. ||71||
71. That which swells, moves, or increases is *śvayīci*, meaning a swelling or a disease.
72. After *veñ*, [the suffix] *ḍicca* [is applied].
The intermediate state (vīci). ||72||
It is called a *vīci* because it weaves (*vayati*) or extends the threads; or it is a wave. The elision of the suffixal vowel occurs due to the presence of the *ḍit* marker.
The suffix *ūṣan* is applied after the verbal roots *ṛ* and *han*.
Arūṣaḥ | Hanūṣaḥ || 73 ||
73. One who goes or moves is *trprarūṣa*, namely the sun; one who strikes is *hanūṣa*, namely the Dasyu.
The suffix *kuṣan* is added after [a verbal root] preceded by *puraḥ*.
The person is the Supreme Person. ||74||
He goes before [all others], thus he is a *puruṣa* (a person); or, by the rule "the long vowel is seen in other cases as well" (*trpranyeṣāmapi dṛśyate*, Pāṇini 6.3.137), it becomes *pūruṣa*.
The suffix *uṣac* is applied after the roots *pṝ*, *nahi*, and *kali*.
*paruṣaḥ*, *nahuṣaḥ*, *kaluṣam* ||75||

"Piparti" means harsh or cruel speech; "nahraṣaḥ" means one who binds or fetters, referring either to a royal sage or a specific kind of serpent; and "kaluṣam" means that which makes noise or clamor, namely, evil.
The vowel *ī* is long before the suffix *ruṣan*. 76.
Pīyūṣa; peyūṣa. ||76||
That which is drunk or is being drunk is *pīyūṣa*; *peyūṣa* is fresh milk or nectar, specifically the milk of a cow that has calved within seven nights.
Due to the rule regarding the suffix *bahulac*, [the word] *trpraṅkūṣaḥ* means "one who observes the three joints" (*tri-aṅka-vate lakṣayati*), or it is *nakūla*.
And also at night. 77.
The Casket. ||77||

The augment *num* is added to the verbal root, and it follows the final vowel. Through the application of the rules for *jaś*-substitution and *ścu*-substitution, we derive *mañjati*, meaning "it becomes pure. Thus, *mañjūṣā* refers to a wooden object or a chest.
And by means of the cheek, [78].
A mouthful [of water]. ||78||
78. It is called *gūṇḍūṣa* because it causes one to move (*gaṇḍati*) a part of the face (*vadanāvayava*); it refers to the mouth filled with water or other liquids, commonly known as *kullā*.
79. Artteraru || 79 ||
The Araru [is driven away]. ||79||
That by which one goes toward or attains [the goal] is called *trprararu* or *trprāyudha*.
Furthermore, why is this so? ||80||
Kuṭaruḥ || 80 ||
*Kuṭaru* means "it cuts" (*kuṭati*), referring to a sickle or a tent.
81. The suffix *aṭan* is applied after [words beginning with] *śaka* and others.
śakaṭaḥ, kaṅkaṭaḥ, devaṭaḥ, karaṭaḥ. ||81||

81. It is called *śakaṭa* because it is able (*śaknoti*) [to carry]; *śakaṭa* is a specific type of vehicle or a sage, and from him comes the descendant *Śākaṭāyana*. It is called *varaṭa* because it covers (*vṛṇoti*); *varaṭa* is a species of insect, or *varaṭā* is the female of a swan. It is called *kaṅkaṭa* because it moves about (*kaṅkate gacchati*); or it is armor (*kavaca*). It is called *saraṭa* because it moves or glides (*sarati prasaratīti*); it is a chameleon, commonly known as *giragiṭa*. It is called *devaṭa* because it deals with the gods (*devate vyavaharati*); or it is an artisan (*śilpī*). That by which one trembles is *kapaṭa*; it is deceit (*māyā*). There is the elision of the root-vowel (*dhātornalopaḥ*). *Karka*, *marka*, and *pārka* are verbal roots found in the Sūtra collection (*sautrā dhātavaḥ*).

*Karkati* thus *karkaṭaḥ*, or a species of aquatic creature; *markati* thus *markaṭaḥ*, or a monkey. In the feminine, by virtue of belonging to the *gaurādi* group, there is the suffix *ṅīṣ*: *markaṭī*. *Karpati* thus *karpaṭaḥ*, or a torn, old garment. *Parpati* (meaning "he goes") thus *parpaṭaḥ*, or saline soil. *Kakhati* (meaning "he laughs") thus *kakkhaṭam*, or hard; here there is the addition of the augment *ku*. *Capati* (meaning "he pacifies") that by which one does so is *capeṭaḥ*; or *carpaṭaḥ*, meaning a hand with fingers spread out.

In one case, there is the substitution of *e* for the vowel of the suffix, while in another, there is the augment *ra*. That which is attained or reached is "mayaṭaḥ," as in *prāsādaḥ*. That which scatters or disperses is "karaṭaḥ," as in *kākaḥ* (crow). In this manner, other words ending in the suffix *aṭ* are also to be derived according to their usage.
The suffix *amvac* is added after the roots *kṛka*, *dika*, and *ḍikaṭi*.
karamba, kadamba, kaḍamba, kaṭamba. ||82||

It is called *karamba* because it "makes" (*karoti*) a mixture; or it is called *kadamba*, either a specific type of tree or that which "eats" (*kadati*). It is called *kaḍamba* because it "covers" (*kaḍati*) or obstructs; or it is a part of a sacrificial grass mat. Or it is called *kaṭamba*, meaning a musical instrument.
The suffix *ka* with the augment *ṇit* is applied after the verbal root *kadi* when it means "a bird."
The Kādamba bird. ||83||
83. What is meant by "becoming deformed"? It refers to a species of bird called *kādamba*, commonly known as the *vaka* (crane).
84. Rama is the delight of the Kali and Krta ages. 84.
Kalama; Kardama. 84.

*Kalama* is so called because it is counted (*kalate*) beyond number; it refers either to a species of rice or to a measure. *Kardama* is so called because it makes a contemptible sound (*kardati*); it refers either to mud or to evil.
The suffix *kindac* is applied after the roots *kuṇi* and *pulya*.
Kuṇinda; Pulinda. ||85||

85. *Kuṇinda* is that which is called out (*kuṇyate*) or the sound itself; or *pulinda* is that which becomes great (*polati*), referring to a Śabara or a specific type of Cāṇḍāla. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), from the root *trp* meaning "to adorn" comes *trpralinda*, meaning a part of a house. Furthermore, by applying the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule for words beginning with *prajñā*, the form *trprālinda* is also established.
86. Or, after the root *kup*, there is optionally *va* [as a substitute for *p*].
Kuvinda; kupinda. ||86||
He who becomes agitated and angry is a *kuvinda*; a *kupinda* is a weaver (*tantuvāya*).
The suffix *ghathin* does not follow the root *sañj*.
The quiver-bearer. ||87||

87. *Niṣaṅgin* means one who constantly (*nitarām*) carries (*sajati*) a quiver (*saṅga*); or it refers to one who possesses a sword (*niṣaṅga*). Due to its being a root ending in a short vowel, there is the substitution of *ku*-tva (i.e., the change of *j* to *g*).
88. The mind is characterized by its upward movement.
The one who possesses abundant wealth. ||88||
In this [ocean], the waters rise up and go upward; thus it is called *udarathi*, or it is the *samudra*.
89. After the root *sṛ*, [the suffix] *niṣṭhā* is always [replaced by *kta*]. 89.
The charioteer. ||89||

One who "causes to move" (sārayati) by necessity is a "charioteer" (sārathi); or [one who] "restrains" (niyantā). Here, the suffix *ṇi* is elided, and due to its being marked with *ṇ*, there is *vṛddhi* strengthening.
90. From *kharjū*, *piñjū*, and others, the suffixes *ūru* and *lac* [are applied].
*kharjūraḥ* (date palm), *karpūraḥ* (camphor), *dhustūraḥ* (thorn-apple), *vallūram* (dried meat), *piñjūlam* (a tuft of hair), *lāṅgūlam* (tail). ||90||

90. From *kharju* and others, the suffix *ūra*. *kharjūra*: that which scrapes or cleanses; a specific type of tree or silver. In the feminine, by virtue of belonging to the *gaurādi* group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied: *kharjūrī*. *karpūra*: that which is fit or becomes capable; a fragrant substance (camphor). Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is an absence of the *at* augment here. *ghustūra*: that which shakes or causes trembling; the plant called "golden" (*kanakāhvaya*), commonly known as *dhatūrā*. *vallūra*: that which winds or covers; dried meat. *śālūra*: that which moves or causes to go; a frog.

That which bears or supports is *mallūra*. That which goes to, reaches, or governs (*śāsti*) the *kaṣṭa* (distress) is *kaṣṭūra*. In the feminine, it is well known as *kaṣṭūrī*, a variety of fragrant substance.

The suffix *ūla* is applied after roots such as *piñj*: that which colors or describes is *piñjūla*, meaning either a bundle of *kuśa* grass or a woman’s bodice; *kañcūla* is that which shines or gleams, meaning a woman’s bodice or an ornament for the body; *lāṅgūla* is that which moves or goes, meaning a tail; there is a vowel *vṛddhi* strengthening of the root. That which torments or desires is known as *tāmbūla*; here the suffix *ūk* is added to the root and the vowel is lengthened. *Śārdūla* is that which tears or destroys, meaning a tiger; here the suffix *ūla* is added to the root with *vṛddhi* strengthening.

It is called *dukūla* because it "burns" or causes affliction; it refers to the lower garment of a woman. The suffix *kuk* is added to the root. It is called *kusūla* because it "adheres" or clings; it is a vessel for grain.
91. And [the substitution of] ku, vaś, caṭ, and a long vowel [occurs]. 91.
Kūcī || 91 ||
That which cries out or makes a sound is *kūca*, meaning either a breast or an elephant. In the feminine, *kūcī* means a painting brush.
*samīcaḥ* and *samīcī* ||92||
"Samīcī" means that which goes correctly or properly; it refers either to the ocean or to a female deer.
93. And after the root *veṣṭ*, there is also *ū*.
sūcaḥ | sūcī ||93||

For the final syllable ending in /i/ belonging to the ninth [class], there is the substitution of /ū/ followed by the suffix *trap*. That by which one sews is called *sūcaḥ*, meaning either a blade of *darbha* grass or what is commonly known as a needle (*sūcī*).
94. The suffix van is applied after the root śam. 94.
A corpse. ||94||
94. It is called *śaṃva* because it pacifies (*śāmyati*); it is the iron-tipped end of a pestle, commonly known as *śāmī*.
95. And *ulva* and so forth [are also included]. 95.
Ulvaṃ; śulvaṃ. ||95||

95. Words ending in the suffix *van* are not *nipātas*. *Ulva*: that which is spoken of as "it covers" (*ucyati*) or "it comes together" (*samavaiti*). The letter *c* becomes *l*, and there is an absence of *guṇa*. It refers either to the embryo or the placenta. *Śulva*: that which "sorrows" (*śocati*). Everything [regarding its derivation] is as before; it refers to copper. *Nimba*: that which "leads" (*nayati*) or "brings about" (*prāpayati*) auspicious qualities. It refers to a specific type of tree. *Viṃva*: that which is "desired" (*vīyate*) or "longed for. It refers to a circle or a particular medicinal herb. In both cases, the verbal roots *nī* and *vī* undergo the addition of the augment *num* and the shortening of the vowel. In the feminine, because it belongs to the *gaurādi* group, the form is *viṃvī*.

A girl whose lips are like the bimba fruit is called *bimboṣṭhī*. That which holds (*dadhāti*) or becomes the cause for holding grain is *dhanva* or *dhanu*; because of that [quality], a person is *dhanvī*. That which devours (*jamati*) or consumes is *jaṃva*, or it refers to mud.
96. When *sthaḥ* and *stoḥ* follow, [the preceding *am*] becomes *amb* and *javak* respectively.
A stalk; a cluster. ||96||

The two suffixes *tra* and *traka* [are applied after the root *sthā*]. That which stands firm is a *stamba*, meaning a cluster of rice or similar grain that is devoid of branches; or a *stabaka*, meaning a cluster of flowers.
97. The suffixes *dana* and *dan* are applied after the roots *śās* and *pā*. 97.
śādaḥ | śabdaḥ ||97||

97. That which makes thin (śyati) is *śāda*, meaning mud or young grass. That by which one is addressed (*śapyate*) or called (*trprāhūyate*) is *śabda*, meaning sound. [The suffix] *va* occurs after this. 98. And also after *abda*. 98.
A cloud; a jasmine flower. ||98||

98. These are *nipātas* (irregular forms) ending in the suffix *dadan*. *Trapada*: from the root *trap*, meaning "he performs protection and so forth," thus *trapadaḥ* refers to a year, an opportunity, or a cloud. *Kunda*: from the root *ku*, meaning "he sounds," thus *kundaḥ* refers to a species of flower. [The suffix *dadan* is added] with the augment *num* to the root. *Vṛnda*: from the root *vṛ*, meaning "he covers," thus *vṛndaṃ* refers to a multitude. [The suffix *dadan* is added] with the augment *num* and the absence of *guṇa*. *Kanda*: from the root *kan*, meaning "it shines," thus *kandaḥ* refers to the root of a plant or a boar. *Tunda*: from the root *tud*, meaning "he pierces" or "torments," thus *tundaḥ* refers to a large belly. *Tundī* means "one with a large belly. [The suffix *dadan* is added] with the augment *num* to the root.
The suffix *ka* is applied after verbal roots ending in *vali*, *mali*, and *tani*.
A bracelet; Malaya; a son. ||99||
It encircles or covers, thus *valaya* means a bracelet or an ornament for the hand. It bears or supports, thus *malaya* means a mountain. It extends happiness, thus *tanaya* means a son.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*)—it causes pain or afflicts, thus *trprāmaya* means a disease.
100. For the words *vṛddha* and *ṛk*, [the substitutes] *ṣuk* and *duk* are also applied.
The testicles; the heart. 100.

It is called *vṛṣayaḥ* because it covers (*vṛṇoti*) or because it is the locus of the senses (*viṣayāśrayaḥ*); the suffix *ṣuk* is applied. It is called *hṛdayam* because it carries away (*harati*) the objects of the senses.
[Pāṇini 3.2.181: The suffix *ru* is applied after the roots *mī* and *pī*. 101.
Meru; Peru. 101.

Meru or Mount Sumeru is so called because it "measures" (minoti) or "projects" (prakṣipati). Peru is so called because he is "drunk" (pīyate) or "drinks" (pibati); this refers either to the Sun (trp) or, by virtue of the rule of diversity (bāhulaka), to one who "drinks" (pibati), namely Pāru, who is that very same [Sun].
102. And *jatru* and so forth [are also neuter].
The collarbones (jaṭru); the two collarbones. Tears (aśru); the two tears. ||102||

102. *Jatru* means the joint of the shoulder (*skandhasandhi*). From it [comes] *nasyataḥ*; *jatruṇī* (dual). *Jatruṇī* (dual). *Śete asau śigruḥ*: this tree is the *śobhāñjana*, commonly known as *sahiṃjanā*, or it may mean a vegetable or a particular kind of person. In that context, the offspring of *śigru* is *śaigravaḥ*. That which extends (*tanoti*) extensively is *vitadruḥ*, or a river; the *na* becomes *da*. That which cries out (*kavate*) is *kadruḥ*, or a variety of color. The *va* becomes *da*. *Trprasruḥ* is that which throws or casts forth water;
due to the rule of *bahula* (diversity), there is a variation in the letter *śa*: *trapraśruḥ*, or the water of the eyes.
The suffix *krun* is applied after the verbal roots *ruś* and *ati*.
Ruru; enemy. 103.

*Ruru* is so called because it cries out (*rauti*) or makes a sound; it is a species of deer. *Śatru* is so called because it perishes (*śīyate*) or causes destruction (*śātayati*); by virtue of belonging to the *prajñādi* group, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, resulting in *śātrava*, meaning an enemy.

From the roots *jan*, *dā*, *cyu*, *sru*, *vṛ*, *mad*, *iṣ*, *nam*, *mi*, and *bhṛ*, the suffixes *it*, *van*, *tṛc*, *naṇ*, *knin*, *śa*, *k*, *syat*, *ḍha*, *ḍa*, *ṭa*, and *ṭac* are respectively applied.
janitvaḥ, dātvaḥ, cyautnaḥ, sṛṇiḥ, vṛśaḥ, matsyaḥ, ṣaṇḍhaḥ, naṭaḥ, bharaṭaḥ. ||104||

104. That which is born or which causes to be born is *janitvaḥ*, namely the mother and father; or that which gives or where one gives is *dātvaḥ*, namely the sacrificial act (*yajñakarma*). That which moves or goes is *cyautnam*, namely strength (*bala*). That which flows is *sṛṇiḥ*, namely the moon (*candra*) or a hook (*aṅkuśa*). That which covers is *vṛśaḥ*, namely a medicinal herb (*oṣadhi*). That which intoxicates is *matsyaḥ*, namely a fish (*mīna*); in the feminine: *matsī* or *matsyā*. That which endures is *ṣaṇḍhaḥ*, namely one who has three wives. That which bows is *naṭaḥ*, well known as a "descendant of a eunuch" (*vaśāvarohin*); the elision of the *ṭi* occurs because of the *ḍit* suffix. That which supports is *bharaṭaḥ*, namely a potter (*kulāla*).
They are also seen elsewhere. 105.
The beast. ||105||

105. The words "and so forth" (ityādayaḥ) are to be understood as the remainder [of the list]. That which is drunk is *pītvam*, or thirst; that which is called or bound is *kacchaḥ*, or the root of a vegetable; that which moves is *saraṭaḥ*, or the wind; that which is meditated upon is *dhyātvam*, or reflection; one who offers oblations is *hautnaḥ*, or the sacrificer; that which is cut is *lūniḥ*, or rice; and so on.
These are the kuserumbha flowers. ||106||
*kusumbha*, *kusuma*, *kusīda*, *kusita* ||106||

It is called *kusumbha* because it stains (*kusyati*) or clings (*śliṣyati*); or it is *mahārajana* (safflower). It is called *kusuma* because it is a flower (*puṣpa*). It is called *kusīda* because it is a livelihood based on interest (*vṛddhi-jīvikā*). It is called *kusita* because it is a desolate region (*deśa*).
107. Sānasī, varṇasī, parṇasī, taṇḍula, aṅkuśa, caṣāla, elvala, palvala, dhiṣṇya, and śalya. ||107||

107. *Sānasaḥ*: he who gathers (*sanoti*), gives (*dadāti*), or is gathered (*sanyate*)—that is *sānasaḥ*, such as gold. The suffix *asip* is applied, and there is vṛddhi of the penultimate vowel. *Varṇasiḥ*: that which covers (*vṛṇoti*), such as water; the augment *nuk* is added to the root. *Parṇasiḥ*: that which fulfills (*piparti*), such as a water-house; everything [else] is as before. *Taṇḍulaḥ*: that which crushes (*taṇḍati*), strikes (*tāḍayati*), or is struck (*tāḍyate*)—that is *taṇḍulaḥ*, namely rice free from husks. The suffix *ulac* is applied. *Aṅkuśaḥ*: that by which one marks (*aṅkate*) or characterizes (*lakṣayati*)—that is *aṅkuśaḥ*, a type of weapon. The suffix *uśac* is applied. *Caṣālaḥ*: that which eats or consumes (*caṣati*)—that is *caṣālaḥ*, the ring on a sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

*Ilvala*: from the root *il*, meaning "to move" or "to sleep"; it refers either to a specific constellation or a type of aquatic creature. *Palvala*: from the root *pal*, meaning "to go"; it refers to a small pond or a shallow lake. In both cases, the suffix *vralac* is applied with the absence of *guṇa*. *Dhiṣṇya*: from the root *dhuṣ*, meaning "to be bold" or "to be confident"; it refers to a place, a star, fire, or a dwelling. Here, the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *i*, and the suffix *ṇyat* is added. *Śalya*: from the root *śal*, meaning "to go"; it refers to a specific kind of weapon or the tip of an arrow.
The suffix *kla* is applied after the roots *mū*, *śak*, and *bibhī*.
Root: *śakla*, *ambla*, *amla*. ||108||
It is well known that *mūla* means "that which binds" (*badhnāti*). *Śakla* means "capable" (*śaknoti*) or "one who speaks kindly. *Trprambla* means "that which makes the sound *amb*.
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), *trpramla* means "that which goes toward the *trpra*" or a particular kind of taste.
The suffix *va* is applied after the roots *mā*, *chā*, and *śas*.
Illusion, a shadow, and a crop. 109.

109. *Māyā* is that which does not enter [into reality]; it is deception, falsehood, or a snare. *Chāyā* is that which covers the light; it is an obscuration of light, a bribe, or a reflection. That which is praised is *sasya*; it is grain ripened in a field or a quality.
By virtue of the rule of abundance (*bāhulaka*), from the root *trp* with the suffix *anya*, *trpranya* means "that which gives life" or "the other."
110. [The rule] applies to the root *śru*. 110.
The left [hand]. ||110||
110. He presses [the Soma] with the left hand; "savya" means the left side.
111. Janeryak || 111 ||
That which is produced is the wife (jāyā). 111.

She who is born, or she in whom one is born, is *jāyā*, meaning "wife. According to the rule *ye vibhāṣā* [Pāṇini 6.4.43], which is a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*), the substitution of *ā* for *jāyā* is obligatory when it means "wife," but elsewhere... [it becomes] *janyaṃ*, meaning "birth," "kinsman," or "battle."
112. And [the words] *adhnyā* and so forth [are also irregular]. 112.
The cow; [the twilight]; the maiden; the barren woman. ||112||

112. *Yagantā nipātāḥ*: Those [words] ending in the suffix *yag* are indeclinables (*nipāta*). One who is not struck nor strikes is called *trpraghnyaḥ*, meaning a protector of subjects (*prajāpālaka*). There is elision of the vowel following the root (*dhātu*), and the substitution of *gh* for *h*. Alternatively, *trpradhnyā* refers to a cow. *Sandhyā* is that time at which one joins (*sandadhāti*) [the day and night]; it refers to the evening time or a formal agreement (*pratijñā*). There is elision of the syllable *trpra*. Alternatively, *sandhyā* is that [time] in which they meditate correctly (*samyag dhyāyanti*) upon the Supreme Brahman. Regarding this feminine form, under the heading of the suffix *ktin*, the rule *trprātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.3.106) prescribes the suffix *aṅ*.

She who is sought after (*kanyate*), shines (*dīpyate*), is desired (*kāmyate*), or moves about (*gacchati*) is a maiden (*kanyā*) or a young girl (*kumārī*). She who is bound (*badhyate*) is barren (*bandhyā*), or one who has not yet given birth (*atṛpra-prasūtā*).

It is called *kuḍya* because it "sounds" (*kauti*) or "calls out" (*śabdayati*); the suffix *ḍuk* is added to the root. That by which one thinks is the *madhya*, meaning the middle or the space between two things. For the root *nas*, there is the suffix *dha*. That which is carried is the *brahma*, or a specific type of person. It is called *triprahalyā* because it "strikes" (*praharati*) or "pervades" (*vyāpnoti*) three times; alternatively, the etymology is "that in which one is exhausted" (*tripraharlyate*). There is an augment *aluk* before the preceding root. It is called *ṛṣya* because it "goes" (*ṛṣati*) or "moves"; it refers to a species of deer. One who goes to or governs what is difficult (*kaṣṭe*) is the *kaśya*; it refers to wine, and so forth.
The suffix *vanip* is applied after the verbal roots *snā* (to bathe), *āp* (to obtain), *ṛ* (to go), *pṛ* (to fill), and *śaki* (to be able).
snāvā, madvā, padvā, trprarvā, parvā, śakvā, śakvarī. ||113||

*Snāvā*: one who bathes, one who becomes pure, or one who is full of essence (*rasika*); *snāvān*, *snāvānau*, *snāvānaḥ*. *Madvā*: one who intoxicates, or a giver of prosperity (*kalyāṇada*), or a lord (*īśvara*). *Padvā*: that in which things go, or a path (*panthā*). *Trparvā*: one who goes quickly, or a swift horse (*trpraśva*), or one who is censurable (*nindya*). *Parva*: that which fulfills, or a knot (*granthi*). *Śakvā*: one who is able, or an elephant (*hastī*). In the feminine, with the suffix *ṅīp* and the *repha* (visarga): *śakvarī*, meaning a river or a particular type of Vedic meter (*chandobheda*).
The suffix *kvanip* is added after the verbal roots √śī (to lie down), √kruñc (to bend), √ruh (to grow), √hi (to impel), √ji (to conquer), √kṣi (to dwell), √sṛ (to flow), and √dhṛ (to hold).
śīvā, kruśvā, ruhvā, jitvā, kṣitvā, sṛtvā, dhṛtvā. ||114||

114. *Śīvā* is a female serpent, as she lies down (*śete*). *Kruśvā* is a jackal, as she howls (*krośati*). *Ruhvā* is a tree, as it grows or arises from a seed (*rohati*). *Jitvā* refers to one who is victorious, as he conquers (*jayati*). *Kṣitvā* refers to the wind, as it perishes (*kṣayati*), destroys (*nāśayati*), dwells (*kṣiyati*), or moves (*gacchati*). *Sṛtvā* refers to Prajāpati, as he flows or moves (*sarati*). *Dhṛtvā* refers to the pervasive Lord of the World, as he sustains (*dhārayati*). In the feminine, forms such as *jitvarī* and others should be understood.
115. There is vocalization (samprasāraṇa) of the vowels *dhi* and *yā*.
Dhīvā, pīvā. 115.

One who meditates is a *dhīvā*, or a fisherman; in the feminine, it is *dhīvarī*, meaning a vessel for holding fish. One who swells or increases is *pīvā*, meaning fat or stout; the feminine form is *pīvarī*, meaning a young woman.
And [the rule] 116.aderdha ca ||116|| applies.
The path. ||116||
116. Because one consumes thirst (*tṛṣ*), it is "thirsty" (*trṣṇā*); or [it is] the path (*mārga*).
117. After the verbal roots *pra* and *īras*, there is the augment *tuṭ*.
The forms *prertvā*, *praśattvā*, *prertvarī*, and *praśattvarī* [are derived from the roots √pṛ and √śad]. ||117||
He who has crossed over is *prertvān*, like the ocean; she who has crossed over is *prertvarī*. He who has flowed forth is *praśatvān*, like the sea; the river that has flowed forth is *praśatvarī*.
The suffix *in* is applied after all nominal stems (*dhātu*). ||118||
paciḥ, tuṇḍiḥ, valiḥ, vaṭiḥ, maṇiḥ, valhiḥ, yajiḥ, gaṇḍiḥ, taḍiḥ, dhrāḍiḥ, kāśiḥ, vāśiḥ, ghaṭiḥ, ghaṭī, yatiḥ, keliḥ, masiḥ, koṭiḥ, jaṭiḥ, kaṭiḥ, haliḥ, heliḥ, paṇiḥ, kaliḥ [nandiḥ] ||118||

118. That by which one cooks is *paci*, namely fire (*agni*). That which devours (*tuṇḍati*) or cuts (*chinatti*) is *tuṇḍi*. That which turns (*valate*) or encloses (*saṃvṛṇoti*) is *vali*, or it is a great king (*mahārāja*). That which causes to weave (*vāṭayati*) or strings together (*grathnāti*) is *vaṭi*, or it is a distributor (*vibhājaka*). That which sounds (*maṇati*) or makes noise is *maṇi*, a precious stone; a praised *maṇi* is a *maṇika*; that very same thing is *māṇikyam*. That which becomes preeminent (*pradhāna*) is *valhi*; *valhikā* is the name of a Kṣatriya woman or a country. That which sacrifices (*yajati*) is *yaji*, a gatherer (*saṅgantṛ*) or a priest (*hotṛ*).

*Gaṇḍati* means he strikes; thus *gaṇḍi* is a part of the mouth, or a wooden gong. *Taḍi* means one who strikes or an oppressor. *Dhrāḍate* means he destroys especially; thus *dhrāḍi* is a heap of flowers. *Kāśyate* means it shines; thus *kāśi* is a particular region. Because the city of Vārāṇasī is situated within that region, it is called *Kāśi* or *Kāśī*. The king of that country is a *kāśya*. *Vāśyate* means he sounds or cries out; thus *vāśi* is a wood-cutter’s axe. *Ghaṭate* means he exerts himself; thus *ghaṭi* or *ghaṭī* (a small water-pot). *Yatate* means he strives; thus *yati* is one who observes restraints or a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*).

*Keli* is that in which one plays; it means sport or play. *Masi* is that which matures or transforms—it refers to ink, or ink-pot, or collyrium. *Koṭi* is that which cuts or pierces; it means a number, a covering, or the tip. From the root *bāhuka*, the suffix *guṇa* is applied. *Jaṭi* is that which forms a mass; it refers to one who wears matted hair (*jaṭā*). *Kaṭi* is that which encloses; it refers to the waist or the middle part of the body. *Hali* is that by which one plows; it refers to a farmer or an implement for agriculture. *Heli* is that which speaks excessively or contrary to the sun; it refers to a riddle (*praheli*).

One who bargains or transacts is a *paṇin*; *vipaṇi* is either a merchant or a marketplace. Where people quarrel, compete, or speak [contentiously], that is *kali*, meaning strife or conflict. That wherein one rejoices is *nandi*, meaning joy or prosperity. There are many such examples.
And [the suffix *ka*] is applied after the verbal roots *hṛ*, *piṣ*, *ruh*, *vṛt*, *vid*, *chid*, and *kīrti*. (Pāṇini 3.1.119)
hariḥ (the lion), peṣiḥ (a grinding stone), rohiḥ (a red horse), varttiḥ (a wick), vedi (an altar), chediḥ (a cutter), kīrttiḥ (fame). ||119||

119. *Hari*: that which seizes (*harati*); it refers to a snake, a frog, a horse, a lion, or the sun. The term "piṣy-ādi" (beginning with *piṣ*) is mentioned for the purpose of setting aside the rule that will be stated as "igupadhāt kit" (a suffix is *kit* after a root ending in *i*, *u*, or *ṛ*, and having a semivowel or *y* as its penultimate letter). For in that case, the prohibition of *guṇa* substitution would apply due to the *kit* status, but [by this specific rule] it does not occur. *Peṣi*: that by which one grinds (*pinaṣṭi*); it refers to a pestle or a thunderbolt (*vajra*). *Rohi*: that which grows (*rohati*); it refers to a tree or a mountain. *Vartti*: that which exists or revolves (*vartate*); it refers to a wick or an accessory for a lamp. *Vedi*: that which is found or prepared (*vidyate*); it refers to an altar or a sacrificial ground. *Chedi*: that which cuts (*chinatti*); it refers to a carpenter or a cutter. *Kīrti*: that which is praised or celebrated (*kīrtyate*); it refers to merit or fame.
120. A *kit* suffix is applied after a verbal root that has a consonant (*i*, *u*, or *ṛ*) as its penultimate letter (*upadha*).
kṛṣiḥ | ṛṣiḥ | ruciḥ śuciḥ | lipiḥ ||120||

*kṛṣyate* (it is ploughed) and *vilekhyate* (it is scratched); that is *kṛṣi*, commonly known as "agriculture" (*khetī*). *Ṛṣati* (he goes, attains, or knows), thus he is an *ṛṣi*, a seer of the meaning of mantras. *Rucyate* (it is shone upon), thus it is *ruci*, or brilliance. *Śucyati* (it is purified), thus it is *śuci*, or purity. *Limpati* (it smears), thus it is *lipi*, or a written mark; by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is also *livī*. One who makes a *livī* is a *livikara*, which has the same meaning as *lipi* (writing). *Tūlate* (it extracts) or *niṣkarṣati* (it draws out), thus it is *tūli*; *tūlī* refers to a brush, or a milk-product cooked together with *radadhyā* and other ingredients.
121. And there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for the root *bhram*.
The ground; the whirl. ||121||
"Bhṛmi" means that which wanders, namely the wind; by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), "bhrami" is also established as a valid form.
122. And here, one should step upon the hundred pillars of the Mātaṅga [deities]. 122.
krimiḥ; kṛmiḥ | timiḥ | śitiḥ | stibhiḥ ||122||

*Krāmyati* means he strides or scatters his feet; thus *krimiḥ* refers to a worm or a small creature. Due to the continued application of *samprasāraṇa*, *kṛmiḥ* is also formed. *Tāmyati* means he longs for or desires; thus *timiḥ* refers to a specific kind of fish. *Śathi* and *stambh* are verbal roots belonging to the *sautra* (traditional) class. *Śitiḥ* means black or white. *Stibhiḥ* is derived from *stabhnāti* (he supports or obstructs); thus it refers to the ocean.
123. *Manerucca* ||123||
The Sage. ||123||

123. He who thinks thus, "I know," is a *muni*, one whose nature is reflection (*mananaśīla*). This [word] *muni* refers to a Brāhmaṇī woman; because it belongs to the *bahu-ādi* group, the feminine form is *munī*. The state or activity of a *muni* is "*mauna*" (the state of silence).
And Bali [is offered] with colored substances, but not with gold.

The root *varṇ* is a Vedic (sautra) root. He offers (*varṇayati*) that tribute (*bali*), which is a royal tax, consisting of articles of hospitality or the head of a corpse; however, when referring to gold, *varṇa* means "gold" (*suvarṇa*).
The suffix *iñ* is applied after the verbal roots *vasi*, *vapi*, *yaj*, *rāj*, *vraj*, *vraji*, *dihani*, *vāśi*, and *vādi*.
vāsiḥ, vāpiḥ, yājiḥ, rājiḥ, vrājiḥ, sādiḥ, nighātiḥ, vāśiḥ, vādiḥ, vāriḥ. ||125||

125. That which covers or dwells upon a thing is *vāsi* (a covering); or it is a thing to be cut (*chedana-vastu*). That wherein they sow is *vāpi*, meaning a field for sowing or a type of reservoir. One who sacrifices is *yāji*, meaning a sacrificer. That which shines or gleams is *rāji*, meaning a streak or a row; *rājīvam* means a lotus. That which moves is *vrāji*, meaning a mass of wind. One who sits is *sādi*, meaning a rider or one who causes to move. That by which one strikes is *ghāti*; *nighāti* refers to a blow from a weapon, such as a stroke from iron. That which bellows or makes sound is *vāśi*, meaning fire.

One who speaks or clearly utters is a *vādin*, meaning a learned man; or one who wards off or restrains is a *vāri*, such as an elephant-tethering chain. In the neuter, *vāri* means water. By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), one who seizes is a *hari*, or it refers to the movement of travelers. A *saprahārin* is a warrior. One who digs or desires is a *khāṭi*, or it refers to the site of a dry wound.
The navel. ||126||

126. It is called *nābhi* because it binds (*nahyati*) what is wicked or because it binds the channels (*nāḍī*); it refers either to a Kṣatriya or to a part of a living being. [The feminine form] *nābhī* is derived by adding the suffix *ṅīṣ*.
In the Vedic language (Chandas), the vowel *ṛ* of the root *kṛṣ* is replaced by *vṛddhi*.
The kārṣi [is equal to sixteen māṣas]. ||127||
*Kārṣiḥ* means one who draws (*karṣati*) or pulls (*ākarṣati*), or it refers to fire; however, in common worldly usage, it is *kṛṣiḥ* (agriculture).
128. *Śrau* [is used] for birds. 128.
Śāri; Śārikā. ||128||

128. It pierces and destroys, thus it is *śāri*, a bird; in the feminine, *śārikā*. In the compound *śuka-śārikam*, there is a singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) for the two birds. Alternatively, *śārikā* is so called because it kills *śāris*. Elsewhere than in the case of a bird, *śāri* means a predatory animal. Due to its inclusion in the *kapilaka*-group, there is the substitution of *la* for *ra*: *śali*. *Tṛprapiśami* is a particular sage; his descendant is *Āpiśali*. The suffix *iñ* is applied here because he belongs to the *bāhū* group.
129. According to the northern grammarians, the suffix *kāru* is added after the root *kṛ*.
The doer. ||129||
One who acts (*karoti*) is an *ākarin*, meaning an artisan; elsewhere, the term for an artisan is *kari*.
130. The suffix *iṇ* is applied after the roots *jan* and *ghas*.
*janiḥ* (the root *jan*) and *ghāsiḥ* (the root *ghas*). ||130||

130. *Jani* means birth or the act of being born; *ghāsi* means that which devours or consumes, namely fire (*agni*). By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), *śāli* means that which is pierced or obtained, namely rice (*vrīhi*). *Pāli* means that which moves or goes, or the tip of a sword and the like. The formation of a different suffix is for the sake of the accent (*svara*).
131. And [the suffix *kvin* is applied] after the roots *añj* and *at*.
Ājiḥ and ātiḥ [are derived from the root aj with the suffix iṇ]. ||131||

*Trpājī*: That in which weapons and the like are hurled is *trpāji*, meaning a battle; or, that which moves (*atati*) continuously is *trpāti*, meaning a species of partridge (*tittira*). *Svātī* is the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) in which the *trpāti* is auspicious.
And [the same applies] when it occurs at the beginning of a metrical foot. 132.
padājiḥ; padātiḥ ||132||
One who moves or goes on foot is called *padāji*, *padāti*, or *padga*. In these forms, the substitution of *pada* for *pāda* occurs by the rule *pādasya padājyātiṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.52).
133. In the case of *aśiṣ* and *naś*, there is optionally the substitution of *ru* for *na*, and the elision (*luk*) of the suffix as well.
A heap; the hand. ||133||

133. From the root *praśṛ* with the suffix *uṭ*, there is the elision of *āya*. That which extends (*praśnute*) or pervades is a *rāśi* (heap) or a *samūha* (collection). That by which one transacts (*paṇāyati*) or deals is a *pāṇi* (hand).
134. And [the suffix] ḍic is substituted for vāti. 134.
The bird. ||134||

The word *viḥ* means a bird (*pakṣin*), as it moves like the wind (*vāti*); due to its having the marker *ḍ*, the vowel *ā* is elided. A city (*nagarī*) is called *trpraṭaviḥ* because birds (*vayaḥ*) alight (*trpraṭanti*) upon it; by the rule *padasya viḥ*, it becomes *padavī*.
135. [The suffix *a* is applied] after the root *hṛ*, when it means "into a well. 135.
The root *prah* (to abandon). ||135||
135. *iṇ* with the suffix *ḍit*: that from which water strikes forth is a *prahi*, meaning a well; or, elsewhere than a well, it means Hari.
136. When the suffix *nau* follows, there is elision of *y*, and the preceding vowel is lengthened.
The new song. ||136||
136. There is lengthening of the vowel of a preceding prefix. That which is tied up or wrapped around is *nīvaḥ*; *nīvī* refers to capital wealth or the binding of a silk garment.
137. When *samāna* is followed by *khya*, that [final vowel] is also acute.
Friend. ||137||
One who is known as equal is a *sakhi*; [the forms are] *sakhāyau* (dual) and *sakhāyaḥ* (plural); or it means a friend (*mitra*) or a companion (*sahāya*).
138. After the prefix *āṅ*, [the suffix *kvip* is added] after the roots *śri* and *han*, and there is also shortening [of the vowel].
A corner; a serpent. 138.

138. *Trpra* means "that which rests there," thus *trpraśri* refers to a corner (*koṇa*). *Trprahi* means "that which strikes (*āhanti*) the *trpra*," thus it refers to a cloud (*megha*) or a serpent (*sarpa*). In these cases, there is shortening specifically of the prefix *trpra*.
139. *i* is substituted for *ac*. 139.
raviḥ | kaviḥ | paviḥ | trprariḥ | trpraliḥ ||139||

The suffix *i* is added to verbal roots ending in *tṛ*. *Lunāti* (he cuts) or *chinatti* (he severs), thus *laviḥ*: a cutter, such as iron; or it means a sword. *Punāti* (he purifies), thus *paviḥ*: a thunderbolt (*vajra*) or a diamond (*hīraka*). That by which one crosses is *tariḥ*: a vessel for placing clothes and so forth; in the feminine, *tarī*. *Rauti* (he cries out), thus *raviḥ*: the sun. *Kauti* (he sounds) or *upadiśati* (he teaches), thus *kaviḥ*: a wise man, a scholar, or one of far-reaching vision; in the feminine, *kavī*. *Ṛcchati* (he goes toward) or *prāpnoti* (he attains) the objects of others, thus *trpariḥ*: an enemy.

Due to the rule beginning with *kapilakādi*, the substitution of *l* occurs: *trapu-liḥ* or *bhramaro*. Because it transcends by means of a nail (*nata*), it is *nakhayati*; from that, *nakhiḥ*. Because it indicates (*sūcayati*), it is *sūciḥ*; and so forth.
And [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words denoting a moment (*khaṇa*), a sacrifice (*yaṣṭi*), a weapon (*āyudha*), a sound (*svara*), a treasure (*nidhi*), and a book (*grantha*). 140.
khaniḥ, kaṣiḥ, trprajiḥ, asiḥ, vasiḥ, vaniḥ, saniḥ, dhvaniḥ, granthiḥ, cariḥ. ||140||

140. That by which one digs, or that wherein one digs, is *khani* (a mine) or a place of treasure; due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is also *khāni*. That which scrapes or injures is *kaṣi*, or an injurer. One who sprinkles or manifests an action is *trp-rañji*, a messenger; with the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ*, *añjī* means for the sake of auspiciousness. That by which one throws or casts is *trpra-si*, a sword. That by which one wears or covers oneself is *vasi*, a garment. That which desires or frequents is *vani*, fire.

A *dhānyavani* is a heap of grain. A *vani* is that which is begged for; one who desires such begging (*vani*) is called *vanīyati*, and from that form, with the suffix *ṇvul*, we have *vanīyakaḥ*, meaning a petitioner. A *sani* is one who gathers or gives, or it refers to a request or solicitation. That which is sounded or uttered is *dhvani*, or sound. That which one strings together or from which something arises is a *granthi*, a joint or knot. One who moves is a *cariḥ*, or a beast.
141. In the Vedic language, [the suffix *ktvā*] is substituted for the verbal root *vṛt*.
The wick. ||141||
That by which one proceeds therein is the *vartti*—the performance of yoga, the material means for accomplishment, or the path.
The suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *bhuj*, and it is treated as *kit*.
The root *bhuji* ||142||

142. The root *bhuji* means "to enjoy," "to protect," or "to eat"; it is also [the name of] fire. 143. [The suffix *ini* is applied after the roots] *kṛ*, *gṛ*, *śṛ*, *pṛ*, *kuṭi*, *bhidi*, and *chidi*.
kiriḥ, giriḥ, śiriḥ, puriḥ, kuṭiḥ, bhidiḥ, chidiḥ. ||143||

The term *kit* is understood [to apply here]. *Kiri* is that which scatters (*kirati*); it refers to a boar or a hog. *Giri* is that which swallows (*girati*) or praises (*gṛṇāti*); it refers to the eye-disease called *gotra*, a mountain, or a cloud. *Śiri* is that which destroys (*śṛṇāti*); it refers to a slayer. *Puri* is that which fills (*pūrayati*); it refers to a city or a river. *Kuṭī* is that which bends or contracts (*kuṭati*); it refers to a small hut or a cottage. *Bhidi* is that by which one splits (*bhinatti*); it refers to a thunderbolt (*vajra*). *Chidi* is that by which one cuts (*chinatti*); it refers to an axe.

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulagrahaṇa*), from the root *tṛ* (to cross/to float), we have *tittiri*, referring to a species of bird. Here, the suffix *i* is added to the root *tṛ*; being *kit*, it causes the reduplication to take the effect of *saṇ* (the *saṇ* augment), and there is the addition of the *tuk* augment to the reduplicated syllable.
144. And there is the elision of the *n* in *kuṇṭhika* and *kampya*.
kuṭhiḥ | kapiḥ ||144||

It hinders or obstructs movement, thus it is *kuṭhi*, meaning a mountain or a tree. It shakes in that [fire], thus it is *kapi*, meaning a monkey or a particular color. Because it possesses the color of a monkey (*kapi-varṇa*), it is "monkey-colored" (*kapiśa*), meaning tawny-colored (*kapila-varṇa*). Here, the suffix *śa* is used in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) because the word is listed in the *lomādi* group.
The suffix *man* is applied after all nominal stems (*dhātu*) [to form abstract nouns]. 145.
Karma, carma, bhasma, janma, śarma, hema, śleṣmā, tarma, sthāma, dāma, chadma, and Sutrāman. 145.

145. That which is performed is *karman* (action) or *kriyā* (activity). The word *karman* is of both genders because it belongs to the group beginning with *trip* and *ardharca*—as in "he performs a virtuous deed" (*karma śubhaṃ karoti*). That by which one moves or goes is the well-known *carman* (skin). That which is sprinkled or ignited is *bhasman* (ashes). That in which something is born is *janman* (birth or origin). It is called *śleṣman* (phlegm) because it adheres (*śliṣati*), or because it arises from *kapha*. In the sense of "one who has phlegm," the suffix *na* is applied according to the rule for the *pāmādi* group, resulting in *śleṣmaṇaḥ*; or, according to the *sidhmādi* group, it becomes *śleṣmalaḥ*.

*Tarma* means "that which crosses over," namely the top of a sacrificial post (*yūpāgra*), or [the forms] *tarmaṇī*, *tarmāṇi*. *Sthāma* means "that by which one stands," or "strength," as in *sthāmanī*. *Dāma* means "that which gives," namely a garland. *Chadma* means "that which covers," namely illusion (*māyā*). There is shortening [of the vowel] by the rule *ismano* [Pāṇini 6.4.97]. *Sutrāmā* means "one who protects well. *Uṣma* means "it burns" or "it consumes"; with the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *trpranyeṣāmapi* [Pāṇini 6.3.135], it becomes *ūṣmā*, meaning either the summer season or steam.
146. After the root *bṛṃh*, the suffix *na* is applied, and the vowel is replaced by *a*.
Brahma. 146.
That which is vast and increasing is Brahman; it is the Lord, the Veda, reality, or austerity.
In the Vedic language, the suffix *kan* is applied after the roots *aś* and *śak*.
aśmā, śakmā ||147||

147. *Trpaśma* means that which eats, enjoys, or pervades; it refers to a cloud or a stone. It is also seen in common usage—as in "I consider the stone to be *trpaśman*. *Śakmā* means that which is capable; it refers to the sun.
The suffix *iman* is added after the verbal roots *hṛ*, *bhṛ*, *dhṛ*, *sṛ*, *stṛ*, *śrṛ*.
The state of being green; the state of being full; the state of being firm; the state of being flavorful; the state of being spread out; the state of being sharp. ||148||

The term *chandasi* (in the Vedic language) continues to apply here. *Harimā* is that which carries; it is time (*kāla*). *Bharimā* is that which is fit to support; it is a family (*kuṭumba*). *Dharimā* is that which is maintained; it is form (*rūpa*). *Sarimā* is that which moves; it is the wind (*vāyu*). *Starimā* is that which is spread or covered; it is a bed (*talpa*). *Śarimā* is that which pierces; it is a sieve (*prasrava*).
The suffix *inan* is applied after the roots *jan* and *mṛ*.
Birth and death. ||149||
The term "in Vedic usage" (chandasī) is understood to carry over. That which is born is "janimā," meaning birth; that which dies is "marimā," meaning death.
150. The word *veṇaḥ* [is used] everywhere.

150. That by which one weaves cloths—namely, the loom or the weaving-rod, or the collection of materials for the production of cloth—in all these cases, the rule *vacanāc chandasī* (Pāṇini 6.3.129) is no longer applicable.
nāman, sīman, vyoman, roman, loman, pāpman, and dhyāman. ||151||

151. Seven [words] ending in the suffix *manin* are treated as irregular formations (*nipātyante*). That by which something is *mnāyate*—that is, practiced or studied—is called a *nāma*, meaning a name or designation. By means of a Vārttika, the suffix *ghyaṭ* is added in the sense of the base itself; thus, *nāma* itself is *nāmadheyam*. That which binds or ties is *sīmā*; alternatively, it is derived from the root *sīv* (to sew) with the suffix *trap* and the augment *av*. That which covers or encloses is *vyoma*, meaning the atmosphere or sky. That which sounds or cries out is *roma*. That which is cut or shaved is *loma*, meaning body hair or hair on the limbs. That which drinks is *pāpmā*, meaning sin or impurity; here, the augment *puk* is added to the verbal root. That which is meditated upon is *dhyāmā*, meaning a measure or radiance.

By virtue of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*): *yakṣmā* means "he worships" or it refers to a chronic disease (consumption); *somā* means "he impels" or it refers to the moon; *homā* means "that which is offered" or it refers to an oblation; *dhāma* means "it places itself therein" or it refers to a location or splendor.
In Gemini, the gem is the ruby. 152.
Suśarman and Sudharman. ||152||

152. Where an upasarga (prefix) is connected with the action denoted by a verbal root (*dhātu*), that constitutes a *mithuna* (pair). When such a pair exists, the suffix *man*—and not *manin*—is applied after the roots already mentioned as well as those to be mentioned hereafter. This restriction is for the purpose of distinguishing the accent (*svara*). For example: *suśarmā*, a particular king, meaning "one who hears well" (*su-śṛṇoti*); *sudharmā*, meaning "one who holds well" (*su-dharati*), and so forth.
The suffixes *manin* and *maniṇ* are applied after the roots *sā* and *āt*.
The Sāman is the Self. ||153||

*Sāman* refers either to the act of pacifying (*syati*)—that is, bringing actions to completion—or to a specific division of the Veda. *Trp* means that which attains the fruits of action continuously; thus, it is the *trp-ātmā* (the self that satisfies). That which is beneficial for the *trp-ātmā* is *trpātmanīna*.
The suffix *sikan* is applied after the roots *han* and *maś*.
The female swan; the fly. ||154||
"Haṃsikā" means a female swan, or one who kills (*han*); "makṣikā" refers to that which stings (*maśati*), or makes a sound, or displays anger—it is either the well-known insect or its genus.
155. [The section on] the *kora* [ends]. 155.
The hair-tuft. ||155||
155. "Kautyu-padiśati" means a braid or a weaver. "Kabarī" refers to the arrangement of hair. Elsewhere, "kavarā" means a girl who is a weaver.
156. *giraḥ* [is substituted] for *udac*. 156.
Garuḍa. ||156||
It is called *garuḍa* because it swallows (*girati*) and devours (*nigalatīti*); it is either a type of bird or [the deity].
157. After the root *ind*, [the suffix] *kam* is added, and there is the elision (*lopa*) of the nasal (*n*).
This [is the end]. ||157||
157. It is called *indati* because it becomes the cause of supreme sovereignty; or it is that which makes manifest the objects of direct perception, being designated by all names.
The suffix *ḍimi* is applied after the root *kāya-ti*. (Pāṇini 3.2.158)
Does "kāya" mean that which makes sound, or does it have the sense of "what" and so forth?
The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied after all verbal roots.
Clothing, a weapon, and an umbrella. ||159||

159. That which covers the body is *vastra* (clothing). That which throws away or casts off is *trapuṣtra* (a type of garment). That which covers and shields from heat and so forth is *chatra* (an umbrella); this is well-known. By the rule *ismantrano* [Pāṇini 6.4.97], there is the substitution of a short vowel. That which falls, moves, or by which one goes is *patra* (a leaf, a vehicle, or a vessel). He who shines is *pāṣṭra*; *rāṣṭra* means a kingdom, a country, or a specific class of people. Regarding other examples: that by which one goes is *gantrī*, or a large cart (*mahacchakaṭa*).

That by which one drinks is a *pātra* (a vessel); or, one who protects (*pāti rakṣati*) is a *pātra* (a worthy person). That by which one bites is a *daṃṣṭrā* (a fang) or a *danta* (a tooth), and so forth.
160. For the roots *bhrasj*, *gam*, *iṇ*, *mā*, *han*, *ni-viś*, and *aś*, there is also *vṛddhi*.
*bhrāṣṭraḥ*, *gāntram*, *nāntram*, *hāntram*, *veṣṭram*, *āṣṭram* ||160||

That wherein one is honored is a frying pan (*bhrāṣṭra*) or a vessel for parching grain (*trprambarīṣa*). That by which one goes is a path (*gāntra*) or a cart (*śakaṭa*). That by which one bows is a hymn of praise (*nāntra*) or a chant (*stotra*). That which is struck is destruction (*hāntra*) or death (*maraṇa*). That wherein beings enter is an enclosure (*veṣṭra*) or the world (*loka*). It is called *trprāṣṭra* because it extends (*trp*) and pervades (*aṣṭi*); or it is a vessel for parching grain (*trprākāśa*).
161. And [the word] *diverdya* [is used]. 161.
The office of the Hotṛ-priest. ||161||
The term "vṛddhi" (vowel strengthening) is understood to carry over. That which plays, shines, or is manifest is called *dyautra*.
The suffix *uṣi* and *khan* take the *kit* augment [after the verbal root *vṛt*]. 162.
Camel; a ditch. ||162||

162. That which burns or consumes is an *uṣṭra*, meaning either a species of animal or a camel. That which is dug is a *khātra*, meaning a pit, a digging tool, or a particular type of water reservoir. The substitution of *ā* occurs according to the rule *janasanakhanām āḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.42].
163. After *śvi* and *muc*, there is optionally *ū*.
The aphorism: "Only [the object]. (163)
That by which one sews or binds for a certain purpose is *sūtra*, meaning either thread or a specific portion of a treatise; that from which one is released is *mūtra*, meaning urine.
164. The suffix *kra* is applied after the roots *ami*, *ci*, *miś*, and *si*.
Antra, citra, mitra, and śastra. ||164||

That by which one knows or attains satisfaction is *tṛpraṇtram*, or else it is the channel of the stomach (*udara-nāḍī*). That which is accumulated is *citram*; it refers to the constellation Citrā or the month Caitra. That which measures or shows respect is *mitram*, meaning a friend; it is always neuter, though occasionally masculine—as in "śanno mitraḥ" and similar usages. *Tṛpra-mitram* (the friend who satisfies). This [demonstrative] is *mitram*. One who possesses beautiful friends is *sumitrā*; her offspring is *saumitriḥ*. The suffix *iñ* is applied because it belongs to the *vāhva-ādi* group.
That by which one praises or strikes is *śastram*, or else it is a weapon (*āyudha*).
165. A *pu* vowel and a short vowel [are also called *hrasva*].
The son. ||165||
A *putra* is so called because he purifies (*punāti*) or makes pure (*pavitraṃ karoti*); alternatively, he is a son (*ātmaja*) born from the seed (*trp*).
The suffix *ḍraṭ* is applied after the root *styai*.
A woman. ||166||
She who conceives, utters sounds, or grasps qualities is known as a woman or a wife.
The suffix *sra* is applied after the verbal roots *guh*, *ṛ*, *paci*, *vac*, *yam*, *si*, *sad*, and *kṣadi*.
*Gotra*, *gotrā*, *dhartra*, *vetra*, *paktra*, *vaktra*, *yantra*, *satra*, *kṣatra*. ||167||

167. That which is called or uttered is *gotra*, meaning a name or a lineage; that which supports the earth is *gotrā*, meaning the earth, or it may mean a house (*dhārtra*). That which moves or goes is *vetra*, meaning a particular kind of creeper. That by which or wherein one cooks is *paktra*, meaning a cooking vessel or the *gārhapatya* fire. That by which one speaks is *vaktra*, meaning the mouth. That by which one restrains or ceases is *yantra*, meaning a specific mechanical device. That wherein beings sit is *satra*, meaning a sacrificial session (*yajña*).

There is another etymological derivation: it is called *sattra* because it protects (*trāyate*) virtuous people (*sataḥ satpuruṣān*). The root *kṣad* is a Vedic (Sautra) root; that which protects (*kṣadati*) or guards (*rakṣati*) is *kṣatra*, referring either to the distinction of social classes (*varṇabheda*) or to that which protects from injury (*kṣatāttrāyate*).
The suffix *traṇ* is added after the roots *hve*, *yā*, *mā*, *aśu*, and *bhas*.
*hotrā*, *yātrā*, *mātrā*, *śrotra*, *bhastrā* ||168||

It is called *hotra* because it is offered (*hūyate*); it is *homa* because it is an oblation. It is *yātrā* because one goes (*yāti*) by means of it, or it is movement. It is *mātrā* because it measures (*māti*), or it is an ornament. That by which something is heard is *śrotra*, or it is an instrument. That by which one carries or shines is *bhastrā*, or it is a bellows for kindling fire.
And [it is] also from the *Gamerā*. 169.
The body. ||169||
169. That by which one goes and moves is the "body" (gātra); it refers either to the three parts [of the body] or to the physical frame.
170. In the Vedic language, [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words beginning with *dā*.
A sickle; a bowl. ||170||

It cuts, it reaps—that is a sickle, or rather, an instrument for cutting grain and the like. One drinks by means of this—thus it is a *pātra*, meaning a vessel or a worthy recipient. In the previous case as well, the word *pātra* was established; there, because the suffix is marked with the letter *ṣ*, the form *pātrī* (a Brahmin woman) was also established. It perishes, it is destroyed, or it becomes the cause of dwelling—thus it is a *kṣetra*, meaning a field or a wife. Other words should be understood in the same way.
The suffix *ṇitran* is added after the roots *bhū*, *vā*, and others, beginning with *gṛ*.
Bhāvitram, vāditram, gāritram. ||171||

That which comes into being is *bhāvitram*, or it refers to the three worlds (*lokatrayī*). That which is played is *vāditram*, such as musical instruments (*tūrya*) and the like. That which is swallowed or consumed is *gāritram*, or it refers to boiled rice (*odana*).
172. [This applies] to conduct and behavior. 172.
Conduct. ||172||
That which is practiced is *cāritra*, meaning conduct, behavior, or custom; with the suffix *-itrac*, it becomes *caritra*, meaning good character.
173. The suffixes *itra* and *otra* are applied after [the roots] *aśitṛ* and others.
aśitram, vahitram, dharitrī, trotram, varutram. ||173||

173. The suffix *itra* is applied after the roots *tṛ*, *kaṭ*, *vah*, *bandh*, *dhṛ*, and others. That by which one crosses over or pervades is *tṛtītra*, namely a sacrificial oblation (*caru*). That by which one weaves or covers is *kaṭitra*, namely a type of armor. That by which one carries is *vahitra*, namely a vehicle. That which binds is *bandhitra*, namely desire. That which supports is *dharitrī*, namely the earth. The suffix *utra* is applied after the roots *trā* and others. That by which one protects is *trāutra*, namely a blow. That by which one cuts or lops off is *lotra*, namely the mark of a thief. That which covers is *varutra*, namely a cloak.
174. It shines in two ways. 174.
Trpramitraḥ || 174 ||
174. When "enemy" (śatru) is to be expressed, [the suffix] *mitra* is used after *tri*. Thus, one who goes to the third [state] is a *tripramitra*, meaning an enemy.
175. [The suffix *kan* is applied] after the roots *āṅ*, *sami*, and *nikas*. 175.
samayā and nikaṣā [are used in the sense of "near"]. ||175||

It is called *samayā* because it comes together (*sameti*). It is called *nikaṣā* because it rubs against (*nikaṣati*) or destroys (*hinasti*); alternatively, these two are words denoting proximity. Due to their inclusion in the list beginning with *svar*, they possess the status of indeclinables (*avyaya*). By way of irregularity (*bāhulaka*): it plays (*dīvyati*), hence *divā* or *dinam*. It is corrupted (*duṣyati*), hence *doṣā* or *rātriḥ*. Since these two are also included in that same list, they possess the status of indeclinables. That which is tasted or made sweet is *svadhā*; it is the act of exercising sovereignty according to rule, or satisfaction. [In this derivation] the *d* of the root becomes *dh*.
What is the particle *ka* derived from the root *ci*? 176.
Smoothness. ||176||
That by which one intends or knows is that which is viscous or oily.
The suffix *sman* follows the root *sūc*.
Subtle. ||177||
It indicates that one who practices slander acts subtly, or in a very slight manner.
The suffix *ḍumsun* is applied after the root *pāt*.
A person. ||178||

One who protects is a *pumān* (masculine); [the dual is] *pumāṃsau*; [the plural is] *pumāṃsaḥ*. The grammatical operations beginning with *trap* and *suṅ* apply.
