She whose excellent man (*supumān*) is her husband is *supuṃsī*. The suffix *ṅīp* is applied because of the presence of the *u*-marker in *puṃs*.
The suffix *kiṣ* is applied after the roots *ruñci* and *bhuj*.
*ruciṣya* (that which is pleasing); *bhujiṣya* (a servant). ||179||
179. That which is pleasing is *ruciṣya*, or that which is desired; one who enjoys is a *bhujiṣya*, or a slave.
180. The Vasesti [formula]. 180.
The bladder. ||180||
That which covers the private parts is the *vasti*; it refers either to the hem or the corner of a garment, or to the region below the navel.

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*): one who rules or instructs is a *śāsti*, meaning a royal punishment or a ruler. One who sacrifices is a *yaṣṭi*; or rather, *yaṣṭī* refers to a wooden staff. That which is struck or cast away is a *traprasti*. One who hurls or uproots a *trapraga* tree is a *trapragasti*, such as a sage. His descendant is "Traprāgastya. Here, the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) occurs because it belongs to the *śakandhvādi* group. One who attains or reaches greatness (*pula*) is a *pulasti*, such as a seer (*ṛṣi*). His descendant is "Paulastya."

*Gabhasti* means a ray of light, so called because it "strikes" (*asati*) the darkness of the womb; or it may mean a messenger (*dūtī*), so called because she "torments" (*dūyate*) or causes distress; or it may refer to a female messenger who reports news here and there.
181. [The suffix] *sa* is applied after the root *vas*. 181.
May there be well-being. 181.

The word *svasti* means "it exists well" (*suṣṭhu trp prasti vartate*), thus signifying well-being or auspiciousness. Due to the presence of the term *bahula*, the substitution of *bhū* [for the root *as*] is prohibited; furthermore, because it belongs to the group beginning with *svar* (*svarādi*), it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
182. After *vā*, [the suffix] *tasi* [is applied]. ||182||
A span (vitasti). ||182||
Specifically, that span (vitasti) is either projected for him, or it is a measurement of twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula).
The suffix *nit* is applied after the roots *pad* and *prathi*.
pattiḥ | prathitiḥ ||183||

The word *patti* refers to one who goes or moves; it is derived from the root *pat* (to go). The word *prathiti* refers to that which is spread or extended, meaning fame or renown. According to the rule *titutratatha-sisusarakaseṣu ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.9), the augment *iṭ* is applied by the Vārttika *agrahādīnām*.
184. There is shortening of the vowel in the root *dṛṇāti*.
A leather water-bag. ||184||
This leather bag, or vessel made of hide, is torn asunder.
The suffix *kīṭan* is applied after the roots *kṛ*, *tṝ*, and *kṛp*.
kirīṭam, tirīṭam, kṛpīṭam. ||185||

*Kirīṭa* means that which scatters or spreads; it refers to a crown, a diadem, or a head-wrap. *Tirīṭa* means that which crosses over; it refers to a head-wrap or a turban. *Kṛpīṭa* is that which is capable [of holding]; it refers to the belly or water. In this case, the absence of the substitution of *l* for *r* occurs by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).
The suffix *kitac* is applied after the roots *ruc*, *vac*, and *kuc*.
*rucitam* (pleasing), *ucitam* (proper), *kucitam* (contracted), *kuṭitam* (curved). ||186||

186. *Rocate* means that which is pleasing, beautiful, or sweet; or it means fit to be spoken, appropriate, or suitable. *Kocati* means it makes a high-pitched sound, thus *kucita* means limited or measured. *Kuṭati* means it bends, thus *kuṭita* means crooked.
The suffix *kmalan* is applied after the roots *kuṭi* and *kuṣi*.
*kuḍmalam* | *kuṣmalam* ||187||

It is called *kuḍmala* because it "buds" (*kuṭhati*), as is well known in the expression "a bud that is about to bloom. Alternatively, it is called *kuṣmala* because it "draws out" or "extracts" (*kuṣṇāti*) [the flower], or it refers to the leaf.
188. And *la* is substituted for [the root] *kuṣ*.
The *kulmala* [is so called]. ||188||
It is called *kulmala* because it cuts (*kuṣṇāti*), or it refers to evil (*pāpa*).
The suffix *asun* is applied after all verbal roots.
The [final] *c* becomes *s* before *ra*, *sa*, and *da*. 189.

*Varcas*: it shines or blazes; thus it means luster (*tejas*) or feces (*purīṣa*). *Rakṣas*: that which protects (*rakṣati*), meaning a guardian or one who is wicked; by the rule for words beginning with *prajñā*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied, resulting in *rākṣasa*. *Rodhas*: that by which one obstructs, or a riverbank. *Cetas*: that by which one perceives or knows; thus it means consciousness (*citta*). *Saras*: where waters flow or go; thus it means a lake or pond. When the feminine gender is intended, by the rule for words beginning with *gaura*, it becomes *sarasī*, meaning a large lake. *Sarasvān* refers to the ocean.

That in which water (*sara*) or consciousness (*vijñāna*) exists is *sarasvatī*, meaning speech or a river. That which weeps (*rodati*) is *rodaḥ*; because it belongs to the *gaura*-class [of nouns], it becomes *rodasī*, meaning heaven and earth. That which goes (*veti*) is *vayaḥ*, meaning a stage of life determined by time. Alternatively, *vayaḥ* means that which eats (*khādati*); from *vayaḥ* comes *vāyasaḥ*, meaning a crow, with the suffix *aṇ* due to its inclusion in the *prajñādi* group. That wherein things sit (*sīdanti*) is *sadaḥ*, meaning an assembly hall. That which goes to or attains (*eti*) is *trapu*, meaning tin or iron. One who desires (*kāmayate*) *trapu* is *trapuṣkāntaḥ*, meaning a loadstone.

That by which one breathes and lives is "trp-ranaḥ"; *trp-odana* refers to cooked food. That where great prosperity (*mahaḥ-sampat*) is attained is "mahānasam," a place of cooking; the suffix *ṭac* is applied at the end of the compound. That by which one suffers (*tāmyati*), longs for, or is afflicted is "tamaḥ"—meaning a quality (*guṇaḥ*), affliction (*kleśaḥ*), night, or darkness. Although the word *tamas* ends in the suffix *ac* and thus ends in *a*, this form *tamaḥ*—meaning a quality, affliction, night, or darkness—is also seen ending in *a*.

That which is worshipped greatly, or that by which one becomes worthy of worship, is *mahaḥ*; [the forms] *mahat*, *mahaḥ*, *mahoḥ*, and *mahāṃsi* [are derived from this]. With the suffix *trap*, it also ends in the vowel *a*. That wherein one endures is *sahaḥ*, meaning strength or the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. One who proceeds with force (*sahasā*) or power (*balena*) is a *sāhasikaḥ*, such as a bandit or a doer of evil deeds. That wherein strength (*sahaḥ*) exists is *sahasyaḥ*, the month of Pauṣa. That by which one heats up, becomes afflicted, undergoes penance, or becomes capable is *tapaḥ*, meaning the practice of dharma or the month of Māgha.

The month of Phālguna is "sādhu-tapasya" because it causes one to practice penance well. In the summer season, the word *tapaḥ* ends in the vowel *a*. That by which one measures is *mā*; *māsaḥ* [is derived] from that, and so forth.
190. And so it was said. 190.
The Repas. ||190||
*Repaḥ* is that which is called *rapyate*; it refers either to blameworthy speech or to the act of speaking.

Because of the use of the word "bahula" (in the rule), this occurs elsewhere as well: *tat payaḥ* means that water or milk is drunk. A cow is called *payasvinī* because she possesses milk (*payas*); a pond is called *payasvī*. [The suffix] *viniḥ* [is added], the vowel *i* replaces the final letter of the root, and then, by adding the suffix *nuṇ*, there is the substitution of *sta* for the *ya*.
191. After the root *aś*, the suffix *yuṭ* is also applied when the sense is "gambling."
That by which one is seen, played, or engaged in activities such as sporting—that is fame or renown.
192. *Ubja* and *balopa* [are also used]. 192.
Vitality. ||192||
192. *Ubjati* means "he subdues. *Tṛp* refers to vigor or prowess. One who acts with vigor is called *tṛp-raujasikaḥ*, according to the suffix *ṭhak*.
193. After the root *śvi*, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) [of the semivowel].
A corpse. ||193||
193. It is called *śava* because it swells (*śvayati*) or moves (*gacchati*), referring to a dead body.

By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulakāt*)—that which carries (*vahati*)—it is *ūdhas*, meaning the udder of a cow or other animal where milk resides. When the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root is performed, lengthening occurs and the letter *dh* is substituted for the final [letter]. A cow or a buffalo whose udder is like a jar is called *ghaṭodhnī* or *kuṇḍodhnī*.
The suffix *ki* is added after the root *śri*, when it refers to one's own body part, and [the final vowel of the root] is replaced by *śī*. (194)
The head. ||194||
194. That which is honored (*śrīyate*) is *śrī*, meaning the head or the crown of the head (*mastaka*). [The dual is] *śirasī*; [the plural is] *śirāṃsi*.
195. Artterucca || 195 ||
The chest. ||195||

The term *svāṅga* (one’s own limb) is understood to follow [from the previous rule]. That by which one reaches or attains [something] is the chest or the region of the heart; [the suffix] *ilac* is applied because it belongs to the *picchi-ādi* group. One who has a broad chest (*bahu-ura*) is called *urasilaḥ*.
196. And *śuṭ* [is substituted] for [the final consonant of] *vyādhi*. 196.
The three types of hemorrhoids. ||196||

196. That by which one encounters or attains suffering is *arśas* (hemorrhoids), also called *gudoraga*. One who has *arśas* is "one afflicted with hemorrhoids" (*arśasaḥ*), a masculine noun. [The suffix] *ac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.2.127.
197. After *udaka*, [the suffix] *nuṭ* is also [inserted].
The flood. ||197||

197. It is simply *trp* with the suffix *ar*. That which flows (*ṛcchati*) or moves is *trprarṇaḥ*, meaning water. Because water (*trprarṇa*) exists in it, it is called *trprarṇavaḥ*, the ocean. The suffix *va* is applied, and there is elision of the *s* sound.
198. [The penance] for this offense. 198.
198. That by which suffering is reached or attained is *enas*, meaning sin or evil.
199. One should investigate wealth and kin. ||199||
Wealth. ||199||
199. That which one relinquishes or expends is *rekṇas*, meaning gold or wealth; the substitution of *k* for *r* occurs due to its being placed in a compound (*dhitvāt*).
200. Also after the root *cāy*, when *ann* follows, there is shortening [of the penultimate vowel]. 200.
Canas (200)

That by which one is honored or worshipped is *canaḥ*, meaning "food. When the suffix *nuṭ* is added to the suffix [of the instrumental case], there is elision of the *ya* and shortening of the vowel.
201. After the roots *vṛj* and *śīṅ*, the suffix *puṭ* is added [to form the denominative stem], when the meanings are "form" and "one's own limb" respectively.
Form; the penis. ||201||

That which is covered or taken up is *varpaḥ*, meaning form (*rūpam*). That by which one lies down is *śeṣaḥ*, meaning the phallus or the male organ. The word *śepa* is also seen ending in the vowel *a* as a synonym for the penis; thus, the sage is called *Śunaḥśepa*, meaning "one whose penis is like that of a dog. [In this compound] there is elision of the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhyā aluk*).
By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulakāt*), through the transposition of letters (*varṇavyatyaye*), both *varphaḥ* and *śephaḥ* are also established.
202. After the roots *sru* and *śru*, the suffix *tuṭ* is also applied.
Stream; semen. ||202||
It is called *srotas* because it flows or moves, or because water flows by itself; it is called *retas* because it flows forth or streams, or because it is virile power (*vīrya*).
203. After the root *pā* "to protect," the suffix *juṭ* is applied when it denotes strength (*bala*).
Strength. ||203||
It is called *pāja* because it protects (*pāti*) or because it is strength (*bala*).
204. And [the suffix *thu*] occurs after the word *udaka*. 204.
The recitation. ||204||
From the root *pā* itself: that which protects is *pāthaḥ*, meaning water.
And also in the case of food. 205.
The recitation. ||205||
205. *Thuṭ*. That which protects (*pāti*) is *pāthaḥ*, meaning food (*bhakta*).
206. Also before *dh* and *nu*. 206.
Trprandhaḥ || 206 ||
206. The word *anna* (food) is understood to carry over from the previous rule. That which is satisfied by or eaten is *trpna*, namely rice-gruel (*odana*) or boiled rice (*anna*).
207. And [the same applies] to Skanda with respect to his own body. 207.
The aggregate. ||207||

207. That by which one shrinks (*skandate*), moves, exerts oneself, or dries up is called *skandha*; it refers either to the root of the arm or to a part of a tree. This word also ends in the letter *d*.
208. In the context of the designation "action" (karma), the word *āpas* optionally takes the suffix *nuṭ* and its final vowel becomes short.
Apnaḥ, trprapaḥ, and āpaḥ ||208||

That by which happiness is obtained is *trprāpa*; *trprapaḥ*, *trprapatyam*, or *sukarma* (good action) [are its synonyms]. Even when the vowel is short, there is an option—thus *trprāpa* also occurs. This is because we observe such usage in expressions like *trprāpobhir mārjanam* ("cleansing with those that bring happiness").
And [the suffix *kha*] is applied after the word *rūpa* when it means "fond of. (209)
The three lotuses. ||209||

209. It is simply "trprāpa. That which is obtained is the form *trprabja*. In its etymological derivation (*nirvacana*), *trprabja* means "born from those who satisfy" (*trpradbhyaḥ jātaḥ*), or it refers to the lotus (*kamala*).
210. And [the substitution of] *num* and *bha* occurs before the word *udaka*. 210.
The word *trp* means "to satisfy. That which is satisfied is *trpta*; such water is *trpāmbhaḥ*. A fish that dwells in such water is called a *trpāmbhasika*.
The word *bhas* (a nominal stem ending in a case-suffix) is called *nadi* when it occurs in the locative (*nahi*) or the nominative (*divi*).
The sky. ||211||

*Nabhaḥ* is so called because it binds or obstructs the *dharma* (the movement of light), referring either to the sky when filled with clouds, dust, and the like, or to the month of Śrāvaṇa. Since pure *nabhaḥ* exists in this [month], it is called *nabhasyaḥ*, referring to the month of Bhādrapada.
212. The suffix *iṇ* is applied after the roots *āp*, *gā*, and *dhe*.
Offense. ||212||
212. That which is traversed, reached, or known is *trpāgaḥ*; *trpāparādhaḥ* refers to punishment or a transgression.
213. And [the suffix] *am* is added after the word *ahar*. 213.
The destroyer of obstacles. ||213||
That by which they suffer or attain suffering is *trpraḥ*, meaning evil or sin.
And with the letter *ra*. ||214||
214. That by which one delights is *raṃhaḥ*, meaning speed or velocity.
215. And here in this land. 215.
In secret. ||215||

215. *Cādramerasun*: "In this they delight" (*ramante 'smin*) is *rahaḥ*, meaning a secluded place, a private spot, or a place of trust. That which exists in a secluded place (*rahaḥ*) or in solitude (*ekānte*) is *rahasyam*, or it refers to the Vedānta. Apart from the sense of a place, there is another indeclinable (*avyaya*) word *rahaḥ* or a different term. *Rahaḥ* also means the time for sexual union; that which occurs therein is *rahasyam*, namely sexual intercourse. The suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule beginning with *dig-ādi*.
216. [The suffix *ka* is added] after the roots *añc*, *añj*, *yuj*, and *bhṛj*; and [the augment] *ku* is also applied.
Aṅka, Aṅga, Yoga, Bharga. ||216||

*Tripraṅkaḥ*: That by which one goes (*añcati*) or moves is *tripraṅkaḥ*; it is a number, a manifestation, or a mark. Or, because it makes manifest (*anakti*), it is *tripraṅgaḥ*, meaning a bird or water. In this case, the word *aṅga* ending in *a* refers to a limb. *Yogaḥ*: It is joined (*yujyate*), thus it is *yogaḥ*; it is meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or time. *Bhargaḥ*: Because it becomes cooked or ripened (*bharjati*), it is *bhargaḥ*; it is Prajāpati or splendor (*tejas*).
By virtue of the rule of abundance (*bāhulaka*)—that wherein it is spoken is *trokaḥ*, meaning a place. [The suffix *gha* is applied] according to the class beginning with *nyaṅku*.
217. [The suffix *kvip*] is added after the roots *bhū* and *rañj*, and it is *kit*.
Bhuvaḥ | Rajas || 217 ||

That in which beings exist is "bhuvaḥ," namely the earth or the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). That which colors is "rajaḥ," meaning a world, subtle dust, female reproductive fluid, or a quality (*guṇa*). It also ends with the suffix *tra*.
218. [The suffix] *vas* [is applied] with the marker *ṇit*. 218.
Clothing. ||218||
218. That which covers the body and so forth is *vāsa* or *vastra*. The vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs because the suffix *asun* is treated as having the *ṇit* designation.
219. And for *candra* and others, *cha* [is substituted]. 219.
Desire. ||219||

That by which one desires, rejoices, or shines is *chandaḥ*. It refers to the *gāyatrī* and other meters, or to deceit, desire, intention, or mastery. Since forms such as "conformity to *chandas*" (*chandānuvṛtti*) are observed in usage, this word should be understood as ending in the vowel *a* as well.
220. After the roots *pac* and *vac*, there is also the augment *suṭ*.
pakṣaḥ | vakṣaḥ ||220||
That which cooks is a "pakṣa," namely the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) or the rejoinder (uttarapakṣa); that by which one speaks is the "vakṣas," namely the chest or the heart.
In the Vedic language, [the suffix -asun] is applied after the roots *vah*, *hā*, and *dhā*.
*vakṣāḥ*, *hāsāḥ*, *dhāsāḥ* || 221 ||

The suffix *suṭ* [is applied as follows]: one who carries a burden is a *vakṣas*, meaning a bull (*anaḍvān*) or the moon (*candramas*); that which is left behind or becomes diminished is a *hāsas*, meaning the moon; and that which supports is a *dhāsas*, meaning a mountain (*parvata*).
222. And after the root *iṇ*, [the suffix] *asi* [is applied].
The unaging ones. ||222||

The word *trpra* means "one who attains" (*eti prāpnoti*); it refers either to one who attains or to fire (*agni*). It is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) because it is listed in the *svar-ādi* group. From this very root *trp*, the suffix *āsi* is applied, characterized by a long vowel at its beginning.
223. In the sign of Gemini, there is the asterism Āśleṣā. 223.
One who is easy to approach; one who possesses great fame. ||223||

223. Where an upasarga is joined with the action expressed by a verbal root (dhātu-kriyā), that constitutes a "pair" (mithuna). In such a case, for all those roots from which the suffix *asun* is prescribed, only *as* [without the nasal] should occur. This rule is intended to prevent a difference in accent. Examples to be observed include: *supayāḥ*, *sutapāḥ*, *supeśāḥ*, *nyojāḥ*, *sujavāḥ*, *susrotāḥ*, and so forth.
224. And there is no destruction of this [self]. 224.
Anehas (time) [is neuter]. ||224||
224. *Tṛpra-nehaḥ* means "one who is not killed" or "one who does not perish," referring either to time (*kāla*) or to one free from danger (*anehas*). Examples: *tṛpra-nehasau*, *tṛpra-nehasaḥ*.
225. And [the suffixes] vidhān and vedha [are applied]. 225.
The Creator. ||225||
One who bestows excellence is a *vedhāḥ*; [the forms] *vedhasau* and *vedhasam* [are likewise used]. It refers to a wise man, a creator, or the Lord of the World (*jagadīśvara*).
226. *nu* is substituted [for the final vowel], and *dhuṭ* is also applied.
Not so, [it is] not [the case]. ||226||
He who praises, praises, or is praised, is called *nodhāḥ*, whether he be a seer (*ṛṣi*) or [another].

227. And there is the preservation of the original accent of the first member of the compound when it is followed by a word denoting a destination (*gati*), an agent (*kāraka*), or a secondary derivative (*upapada*).
The drinker of the Soma; he who knows all that is born. ||227||

The suffix *asi* is applied after a verbal root that has a *gati*, a *kāraka*, or an *upapada* preceding it; when this suffix is present, the preceding *gati* and *kāraka* (or *upapada*) retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*). This is an exception to the rule regarding the original accent of the final member of a compound (*uttarapada-prakṛtisvara*). Examples: *Sutapāḥ* ("one who drinks well"). *Sutejāḥ* ("having excellent splendor"). *Suvakṣāḥ* ("having a beautiful chest"). Regarding *kārakas*: *Ugratejāḥ* ("of fierce splendor"). *Hiraṇyaretāḥ* ("having gold as seed/sperm"). *Jātavedāḥ* ("whose wealth/knowledge is born"). *Sarvavedāḥ* ("possessing all knowledge"). *Viśvavedāḥ* ("possessing universal knowledge"). Regarding *upapadas*: *Vṛddhaśravāḥ* ("he hears from the elders"). *Viṣṭaraśravāḥ* ("he hears [the praise] while seated on a seat made of *viṣṭara* grass"). And so forth.
228. *Moḍita* in the moon. 228.
The moon. ||228||
He measures the joy of the moon; [thus he is] Candramas, or Soma. [The dual is] candramasau; [the plural is] candramasaḥ.
The suffix *dhāñ* is applied in the sense of "age" (*vayas*). ||229||
Bestower of vitality. ||229||
He who bestows vital strength is "vayodhāḥ," or he who is youthful.
And in milk as well. ||230||
The clouds. ||230||
The suffix *dhāñ* is used in this very sense. Thus, *payodhāḥ* means "that which holds milk," referring to the ocean, a particular cloud, or the breast.
And [the suffix] *purasi* [is used] as well. ||231||
The domestic priest. ||231||
Simply from the root *dhā* (to place): one who places the sacrificer in front (*puras*) or at the head (*agre*) is a *purodhāḥ* or a *purohita*.
232. Purūravas. 232.
He who cries out much, teaches, or speaks is Purūravas, the royal sage.
233. After the root *cakṣ*, the suffix *śi* is frequently applied.
Beholding men. ||233||

He who sees with distinction is *vicakṣāḥ*, or [is] a teacher (*upādhyāya*). He who sees or looks upon men is *nṛcakṣāḥ*, [meaning] a lord or one who is wicked. In the alternative where the suffix *śit* is absent—[one who] proclaims the *trp* [mantras] is *trprākhyāḥ*, [meaning] renowned ones or Prajāpati.
234. And [the suffix] *uṣ* is *kit*.

234. *uṣ* [is derived from the root] *tṛp* [meaning] to burn. Thus, *uṣas* refers to the ear-cavity, a mountain cleft, or the light of dawn before sunrise (in the feminine), or simply the dawn (*uṣā*). One who wakes at the time of dawn is called *uṣarbudhaḥ*; this may refer to Agni, a child, or one who is self-restrained. When the suffix *kap* is added and then the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, it also becomes *uṣā*, meaning "night."
235. *Damerunasiḥ* || 235 ||
The subduers. ||235||
He is called *damunāḥ* because he tames and pacifies; or [the term] refers to Agni.
The suffix *si* is applied after the word *aṅguri*. ||236||
Trpaṅgirāḥ || 236 ||
One who goes forward (*pra-aṅgati*), attains, or knows is *prāṅgirāḥ*, meaning Īśvara, Agni, or a particular Ṛṣi. His descendant is *prāṅgirasaḥ*; the augment *ru* is added to the suffix *sip*.
The suffix *asi* is applied after the root *sṛt*, provided it is not preceded by another prefix.
The Apsaras Trpā. ||237||

*Trpṛpsarāḥ* means "those who go in a contrary direction" (*viruddhaṃ gacchanti*); there is elision of the final vowel of the prefix (*upasarga*). Alternatively, they are called *trpṛpsarasaḥ* because they move (*saranti*) in the waters (*apsu*) or in the vital breaths (*prāṇeṣu*), or they are rays (*kiraṇāḥ*). Or again, they are *trpṛpsarasaḥ* because they do not eat (*na psānti*), that is, they do not consume [offerings] but provide protection; here the suffix *ruṭ* is added to the root. This word is always plural and feminine in gender.
238. After the roots *vid* and *bhuj*, the suffix *asi* is applied when *viśva* is the upapada.
The knower of all; the enjoyer of all. ||238||

He who knows or perceives the entire universe is Viśvavedas, or he is the Lord of the World. Alternatively, he is Viśvavedas because the universe exists within him, or because he finds the universe [within himself], or he is Agni. He is Viśvabhojas because he nourishes the universe, or because at the time of dissolution he establishes it within his own self in the form of its cause, or because he protects the universe; thus he is the Lord or the King.
The suffix *kanas* is applied after the root *vaś*. (239)
Uśanas. ||239||
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the Uṇādi-sūtras.
He who desires or longs for is *uśanā*, or it refers to Friday (*śukravāra*); [in this case] the grammatical operations such as *samprasāraṇa* (vowel substitution) and so forth apply.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the commentary on the Uṇādi-sūtras and the Vaidika-laukika-kośa.
Now begins the fifth quarter [of the second book]: 1.
*adibhuvaḥ ḍutac* ||1|| The suffix *ḍutac* is applied after verbal roots beginning with *bhū* (and their synonyms) to form nouns denoting the agent.
It is wonderful! ||1||

The indeclinable *trpra* is used in the sense of "at some time" (*kadācit*). *Trpradbhutam* means "it has become marvelous" (*trprad bhavati*); thus, *trprāścaryam* (a marvel). One who studies a marvelous thing is a *trpradbhutamadhīte*; one who teaches a marvelous thing is a *trpradbhutādhyāpakaḥ*.
2. Gudherūma. 2.
Wheat. ||2||
2. It is called *godhūma* because it covers or envelops; it is a specific kind of grain. That which is made from *godhūma* is "made of *godhūma*" (*godhūmamaya*).
3. Maserūraṇa || 3 ||
Masūra. ||3||
That which grows or matures is *masūra*, a type of grain or a courtesan.
The suffix *k* is applied after a verbal root ending in *sthā*.
The thick one. ||4||
4. One who stands is *sthūraḥ*, meaning a man; his descendant is *sthauryyaḥ*. 5. From the root *pāti* (to protect), the suffix *ati* [is added]. ||5||
The protector. ||5||
One who protects is a *pāti*, meaning a master; or [it refers to] *Saṃpāti*, the king of birds.
6. To Vāta, hail! 6.
The wind. ||6||
6. That which moves swiftly is a *vāti*; it is either the sun or the moon.
And also from the arts. ||7||
The threefold non-attachment. ||7||
7. That which is approached or attained is that intense delight or agitation.
The suffix *kna* is added to the root *tṛh*, and there is the elision of the *h*.
Grass. ||8||
That which is trampled and killed is indeed well known as "grass" (tṛṇa).
The suffix *ulac* is applied after the roots *vṛñ*, *luṭh*, *ita*, and *naṭ*, and the augment *taṇḍ* is added [to the root *vṛñ*].
Rice grains. ||9||
Or those grains (taṇḍula) which are well-known as being selected, crushed, spread out, or beaten; in place of the roots *vṛ* and so forth, the substitute *taṇḍ* is prescribed.
10. May he show himself to us at dawn and at night. 10.
The servant. ||10||

10. He who shows, bites, or sees is a *dāsa*—a servant or a *śūdra*. By adding the suffix *ṭi*, the feminine form is *dāsī*. The change of the letter *n* to *a* occurs [by *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ...*]. The inclusion of the marker *ṭ* is for the purpose of making the initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*) in the alternative case.
11. And [the same applies] to a gadfly. 11.
The fisherman. ||11||
11. In the case of the root *taṭ*, there is the substitution of *na* for *ca*. One who catches fish and so forth is a *dāśa*, a fisherman. In the feminine, it is *dāśī*, a female fisherwoman.
12. Thus it was said. 12.
Loudly. ||12||
12. It is gathered or increased; thus it is "uccaiḥ," meaning high or great. Due to its inclusion in the group beginning with "svara" (Pāṇini 1.1.37), it is an indeclinable (avyaya).
13. And the *nau* [vowel] is long. 13.
In a low voice. ||13||

13. Precisely because it is understood as "low," the word *nīcaiḥ* means "below" or "inferior. Furthermore, *trp* is also an indeclinable precisely because it belongs to the group beginning with *svar* (the *svarādi* class).
14. The suffix *kta* is used after the root *ram* in the sense of self-control (*dama*), and there is lengthening of the vowel in the preceding member. 14.
Gentle. ||14||
One who delights well is *sūrataḥ*, meaning one who is tranquil or compassionate; otherwise, in the sense of "taming" (*dama*), *surataḥ* means one engaged in play.
15. The suffix *pūñ* is applied, and there is the substitution of a short vowel for the long one.
Merit. ||15||
It purifies; it becomes a means of purification by which that merit, good deed, or dharma is attained.
After the root *sraṃs*, the suffix *śi* is applied, and it is marked with the markers *kuṭ* and *kit*.
The sling. ||16||
16. That which hangs down and moves is called *śikyam*; it is well known as *kāja* or *chīṅkā*. The object [of weight] placed therein is called *śaikyam*.
After the root *ṛt*, the suffix *kyu* is applied, and the vowel *ṛ* is replaced by *u*.
The ram. ||17||
17. It is called *uraṇa* because it moves (*ṛcchati*) or goes (*gacchati*), namely, a ram or a sheep.
18. His body was like a lake of nectar. ||18||
The injurer. ||18||
One who injures is a *hiṃsīraḥ*, such as a tiger or a wicked person. The two suffixes are for the purpose of distinguishing the accent.
19. After the root *dṛ* (to split), the suffixes *ala* and *aca* are applied, and there is elision of the final letter of the preceding word.
The belly. ||19||
19. "It bursts open by which [it receives] food" refers to the belly, the location within the abdomen; here too, the difference in vowel indicates a difference in meaning.
20. After the root √khan, when followed by a suffix marked with ḍ or t, the augment muṭ is inserted, and it is udātta-accented.
The mouth. ||20||

20. *khaneralac*: for these two [roots], there is the *ḍit* designation and the augment *muṭ* for the verbal root (*dhātu*), and its [the augment's] udātta accentuation. That by which one digs food and so forth is the "mouth" (*mukha*). It is that which is to be tasted (*tṛprāsya*). A disease occurring in the mouth is "oral" (*mukhya*). [The suffix] *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.6 because it is a part of the body. "Principal" (*mukhya*) means "like the mouth," i.e., the best. The suffix *ya* is applied in the sense of "like" (or "resembling") according to the rule for the *śākhādi* group.
The suffix *san* follows the root √am. (21)
The threefold praise. ||21||
That by which one moves toward or attains the shoulder-blade (*trpra*) is the *trpram* [shoulder]; it is a shoulder or a division. One who possesses this [shoulder] is "shouldered" (*aṃsalaḥ*).
22. After the word *mukha*, [the suffix] *kha* is used in the sense of "fainting. 22.
A fool. ||22||

One who is deluded or as if distracted is a fool (*mūrkha*). The state of being a fool is "foolishness" (*maurkhya*); or it is *mūrkhimā*. Due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), there is an absence of the substitution of *i* for *kh*.
23. And there is the elision of *na* and *ha*. 23.
The nail. ||23||
It is called *nakha* because it binds or fastens blood and other substances; or else, it is a limb of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*).
24. After the root √śī, [the suffix ya] is applied and the vowel is shortened.
The Topknot ||24||
24. kha. *Sikha* means a crest, a tuft of hair, a lock of hair, or a flame. Due to the force of the rule prescribing the short vowel, there is an absence of *guṇa*.
25. After the word *māṅ*, [the suffix] *ūkh* and *maya* are applied. 25.
Ray of Light ||25||
25. That which causes measurement is a *mānya-hetu*; thus, a *mayūkha* is a ray, a beam, a luster, a hand, or a flame.
26. After the words *kali* and *gali*, the suffix *phak* (*-eya*) is applied when denoting a high mountain.
Kulpha; gulpha. ||26||

26. *Kulpha* is that which counts (*kalati*) or is beyond number; it refers either to a part of the leg or to a disease. *Gulpha* is that which swallows (*galati*) or devours (*bhakṣayati*); it refers either to the ankle or to a knot in the foot. 27.
From the root *spṛś*, the suffixes *śvaṇ* and *śun* are added, and there is also the substitution of *pṛ*. (The resulting forms are *sparśa* and *spraśa*.)
Pārśvaḥ | Parśuḥ ||27||
That by which one touches the side or the lower part of the armpits is *parśu*; it is also a weapon made of iron.
The suffix *ḍun* is applied after the root *śri* when preceded by *aśman*.
The beard. ||28||
28. It is called *śmaśru* because it rests upon the face (*śman*); [the forms] *śmaśruṇī* and *śmaśrūṇi* refer to the hairs on a man’s face. Alternatively, they are the hairs on the face of a man.
29. And [the words] beginning with "horse" (aśva) [are also included]. 29.
Tears. ||29||

It is called *trpraśru* because it spreads (*trpraśnute*) or pervades; or else, it refers to the water of the eyes. The suffix *ḍun* is applied along with the augment *ruk*. Other [words] should likewise be understood according to their respective etymologies.
30. In the case of *jana*, there is also the elision of *n*.
Matted hair. ||30||

30. He becomes one with long matted locks (jaṭā) or hair; "jaṭālaḥ" means "one who possesses matted locks," formed with the suffix *lavac* according to the *sidhmādi* group; "jaṭilaḥ" is formed with the suffix *ilac* according to the *picchādi* group.
And in that case, the calf [is also not to be eaten]. //31//
The shank. ||31||
31. Of that *jānu* [knee], *jaṅghā* is born; it is the lower part of the knee, or the shank.

32. After the root *han*, when [the suffix *kvin*] follows, two vowels are substituted for the final vowel and the penultimate consonant, provided that a word denoting a part of the body is the object.
The hips. ||32||

That by which one strikes, or that which is struck, is the *jaghana*, meaning the upper part of the knee; the suffix *ya* is used here in the sense of "like" (*iva*), according to the rule for words beginning with *śākha*. Thus, *jaghanya* means "low" (*nīca*), as it is like the *jaghana*.
33. After the verbal root *kliś*, there is optionally the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *loṭ*.
That by which one is afflicted is *keśa*; [it refers to] hair on the head or body hair. One who possesses hair on the head is called *keśavaḥ*, *keśikaḥ*, or *keśī*.
34. And [the substitution of] *pa* occurs for the final consonant of a word ending in *phala*, *irit*, and *ja*.
Grey hair. ||34||
34. *Palita* means "ripened," as in "it bears fruit when fully matured"; it refers either to grey hair or a shrine (*caitya*). [The substitution of] *pa* for *pha* [occurs here].
35. The suffix *vun* is added after words beginning with *kṛñ* when they denote a name.
*kārakaḥ*, *kaṭakaḥ*, *narakam*, *korakaḥ* ||35||

35. *Karaka*: that which acts (*karoti*) is a *karaka*; a *karaka* is a hailstone, or else a pomegranate or a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). *Kaṭaka*: that which cuts (*kaṭati*), rains, or covers is a *kaṭaka*; it is an armlet or a mountain peak. *Naraka*: that which leads away (*nṛṇāti*) or carries one off is a *naraka*, or the portion of sin. *Saraka*: that which moves or goes is a *saraka*, or the act of going. *Trpralaka*: that by which one becomes adorned (*alati*) is a *trpralaka*, or cold weather and so forth; or, those from which one wards off (*alati*) are *trpralakas*, or curly hair. *Koraka*: that which makes sound (*kurati*) is a *koraka*, a bud (*kalikā*), commonly known as a "kali."
36. And there is a reversal of the first and last [letters] of the root *cīkayati*.
Kīcaka. ||36||
He makes a whistling sound or endures it; thus he is Kīcaka, or a variety of bamboo.
37. [The long vowel] is substituted for the final short vowel of a word ending in *ṛ*, provided that it is followed by a consonant (*upadhā*) which is not *c* or *v*.
pecakaḥ | mecakaḥ ||37||
37. *Pecaka* means one who cooks, or it refers to an owl; *mecaka* means that which makes sound, or it refers to a black color, or the mark on a peacock's feather.
And [the suffix] jaraṃraṣṭha [is applied after a word denoting a part of the body]. 38.
The belly. ||38||
That from which something is born is called *jaṭhara*, *udara*, or *kaṭhina*.
39. And [the same applies] to speech, mind, and consciousness. 39.
Vaṭharaḥ | Maṭharaḥ || 39 ||

39. For the final [consonant], *ṭha* is the substitute. One who speaks is a *vaṭhara*, meaning a fool or a blockhead. He who thinks is a *maṭhara*, a type of sage or one who is intoxicated. His offspring is *māṭhara*; [alternatively] *mārṭhya*.
40. From the root *dṛṇāti* (to split), the suffixes *alac* and *a* are applied in the sense of *ūrji* (strength).
The granary. ||40||

40. *Ūrdara* means one who pierces (*dṛṇāti*) vigor (*ūrj*), prowess (*parākrama*), or essence (*rasa*); it refers to a hero or a wicked person. The two suffixes are used for the purpose of changing the vowel accent (*svarabheda*).
41. And *kṛt* and so forth [are also included].
*kṛdaraḥ*, *mṛdaraḥ*, *sṛdaraḥ* ||41||

41. That which pierces through the entire extent or the depths is an *ūrdara*, meaning a hero or a wicked person. That which pierces through joy is an *mṛra*, meaning a disease or a hole. That which pierces through creation is an *sṛdara*, meaning a serpent.
42. In the case of *han*, when *y* and *n* are respectively at the beginning and the end [of a word], there is the substitution of *gh* and *t*.
The slayer. ||42||
He is called "the slayer" (ghātana) because he kills, or he is the "destroyer" (māraka).
The suffix *tun* is added after the roots *krami*, *gamī*, and *kṣamī*, and there is also a *vṛddhi* strengthening of the root vowel.
One who strides; one who goes; one who endures. ||43||

A *krāntu* is one who strides, that is, one who casts his feet about—a bird—or one who goes—a traveler. An *āgāntu* is one who has come from afar. A *kṣāntu* is one who endures, that is, one whose nature is forbearance.
The suffix *kanyan* is applied after the root *haryati*, and there is the substitution of *hirac*.
That which is desired or longed for is "hiraṇya" or "suvarṇa."
45. After the root *kṛ*, the suffix *pās* is applied.
Cotton. ||45||
45. That which is made or produced is "karpāsa," a type of crop; a product of *karpāsa* is "kārpāsa" cloth. The suffix *aṇ* is applied here because it belongs to the *bilvādi* group.
And [the word] janesturaḥ. 46.
The skin of a wild animal. ||46||
That from which one is born is the *jarttu*; it is the lap, or Indra, or an elephant.
47. The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *ūrṇoti*.
The ūrṇā [hair-tuft]. ||47||

47. That by which one covers or conceals is *ūrṇā*, meaning the wool or the hairs of a sheep. One who goes to or reaches the *ūrṇā* is called *ūrṇāyuḥ*, namely a sheep or a woolen blanket. One whose navel is like *ūrṇā* is *ūrṇanābhaḥ*—the suffix *ac* being applied after the compound—or *ūrṇanābhiḥ*; for the rule regarding the application of the compound-suffix is not mandatory. Alternatively, it refers to a spider.
48. After the root *dhā*, [the suffix] *yat* is applied, and there is also the augment *nuṭ*.
Grain. ||48||

It is called *dhānya* because it supports (*dhāti*) and nourishes (*puṣṇāti*) the worlds; or it is *vrīhi*. It is also called *dhānya* in the sense of being "suitable for nourishment" (*dhāne poṣaṇe sādhū*).
From the root *jṛ* (to grow old), the suffix *krin* is applied, and the letter *r* is replaced by *v*.
The long-lived one. ||49||

That which decays, or that by which one decays, is *jīviḥ*, meaning either time (*kāla*) or a bird (*pakṣin*). According to the rule *hali ca* [Pāṇini 6.4.2], the absence of lengthening occurs here due to the principle of diversification (*bāhulaka*).
In the case of the root *mavyati*, there is the elision of *ya*, and *ma* is substituted [for *mavya*], with the addition of *ap*, *tuṭ*, and *alaḥ*.
This is my Pātāla. ||50||
50. That which binds or fetters is *mamāpatāla*; it is either the cause of bondage or the sense-object (*viṣaya*).
51. Ṛjaḥ means kīkaca (a bone). 51.
The straight-faring one. ||51||
51. He who moves straight forward (*ṛju*) is *ṛjīka*, namely the sun or smoke.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied after the root *tan*, and it is treated like the desiderative suffix (*san*).
The sieve. ||52||
That by which one spreads out or extends is *titau*, meaning a winnowing basket, a vessel used for grinding or cleaning.
The words *arbhaka*, *pṛthuka*, and *pāka* denote age. ||53||

53. He who prospers and grows is *trprarbhaka*. [This is derived] from the root *ṛdh* with the suffix *vun*, where *dh* becomes *b*. He who spreads and increases is *pṛthuka*. [This is formed] with the suffix *kuk* and vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). He who drinks is *pāka*. [This is formed] with the suffix *kan*. *Trprarbhaka*, *pṛthuka*, and *pāka* are synonyms for a child.
54. The words *avadya*, *avamā*, *arvā*, and *repha* are used in the sense of "contemptible."

That which is unfit to be spoken is *trapadya*, derived from the root *vad* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*. That which descends is *trapama*; the suffix is *ma*. In that same context, when *va* becomes *dha*, it is *trapadhama*. One who goes or moves is *traparva* or *traprasva*. The suffix is *van*. One who utters or censures is *repha*; these are synonyms for the contemptible.
55. In the case of *lī* and *rī*, there is shortening [of the vowel] and the suffix *puṭ* before the affixes *ta* and *ra*, in the senses of joining and censuring respectively. ||55||
Smeared; smeared with filth. ||55||

That which is melted (*līyate*) or clings (*śliṣyati*) is *lipta*, meaning "adhered. That which flows away (*rīyate*) is *ripra*, meaning "contemptible. The suffixes *-ta* and *-na* are applied, with the augment *puṭ*.
56. After the verbal root *kliś*, when followed by the affix *īc*, there is the substitution of *kan* for the penultimate vowel, and the letter *l* is substituted for the *n* of the root.
The plowman. ||56||

56. He who causes affliction is a *kīnāśa*, such as a farmer or a judge. The vowel *ī* replaces the penultimate vowel of the root, there is the elision of the letter *l*, the suffix *kan* is added, and the augment *nām* is inserted after the final vowel.
57. After the root *aś* ("to reach"), the suffix *varaṭ* is applied when the action is rapid.
The Lord. ||57||

57. He who eats, acts quickly, and swiftly fashions the world is *īśvara*, meaning the Lord or Master. Due to its *ṭi*-nature, the feminine form is *īśvarī*; with the suffix *varac*, it becomes *īśvarā*.
58. Catur-anu || 58 ||

58. From the roots *cat* and *yāc*, the form *catuḥ* is derived; it may express the number four. [Examples: *catvāraḥ* (masculine), *catasraḥ* (feminine). 59. From the root *prath*, the suffix *aran* is applied. (59)
In the morning. ||59||

It is called *prātaḥ* because it moves (*atati*) toward what is excellent (*prakṛṣṭa*); or it refers to the time of dawn (*prabhātakāla*). It is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by virtue of belonging to the *svarādi* group.
60. And *tuṭ* is added after *trap*. 60.
The end of the third [chapter]. ||60||
60. *trp* with the suffix *mat* goes where [the suffix] ends in *trp*; or it is the middle [form]. As before, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
61. After the word *daha*, there is elision of the suffix *gha*, and the letter *da* is replaced by *na*.
The Naga. ||61||

61. That which burns or is burned is a *naga*, a mountain, or a tree; by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the letter *na* is substituted for *na*—thus, *nāga* refers to a species of serpent.

The Lion. ||62||
The word "siṃha" (lion) is derived from the root *siñcati* (he sprinkles), and the inversion of the initial and final syllables occurs according to the rule for words beginning with *pṛṣodara*.
63. And after the roots *vyadh* and *ghrā*, when followed by the suffix *ktvā*, [the substitution of *iṭ*] occurs in the sense of birth (*jāti*). 63.
The tiger. 63.
63. One who smells from all sides in a special manner is called a *vyāghra* (tiger) or a *hastin* (elephant).
64. The suffix *ac* is applied after the root *han*, and *ghur* is substituted for it. 64.
Terrible. ||64||
"Hanti" means terrible or fearsome.
65. And there is the elision of the penultimate vowel in the root *kṣam*.
The earth. ||65||
It is called *kṣmā* because it endures (*kṣamate*) and bears (*sahate*) everything, or it is the earth (*pṛthivī*).
66. tarater ḍriḥ || 66 ||
Three. 66.
The word *tri* means "three" as it crosses over [to that number]; it is a term expressing the quantity three: *trayaḥ*, *trīn*, *tribhyaḥ*.
67. graher aniḥ || 67 ||
Grahaṇī (dysentery or chronic diarrhea). ||67||

67. It seizes, thus it is *grahaṇī*. By the rule *kṛdikārādāktyarthāt* [Pāṇini 4.1.45], the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied—[thus] *grahaṇī*, meaning a type of disease characterized by excessive absorption (*saṃgrahaṇī*).
68. First, the initial [vowel] ||68||
The first [chapter]. ||68||
It is called "first" (prathama) because it spreads out (prathate) or becomes renowned; it is also the initial, the highest, or the new.
And of the one who wanders. ||69||
The last one. ||69||
69. He who moves, goes, or eats is "caramaḥ"; it means the one who is at the end, the final, or the last.
70. Maṅgeralac || 70 ||
May there be auspiciousness! ||70||
Thus ends the fifth quarter of the Uṇādi-sūtras.
Having prepared a bright churning-staff from either the well-developed or the unrefined wing [of the system], by which the ocean of speech was churned according to rule,
wherein jewels of words— both manifest and more subtle— truly shone forth.
May this excellent group beginning with the letter *u* be for the increase of the fame of its student.
That by which one attains or reaches happiness is *maṅgala*; it is that which is auspicious, or it refers to a specific day of the week (*vāra-bheda*). The state of being *maṅgala* is *māṅgalya*.
Thus ends the fifth section of the Vaidikalaukika-koṣa, a commentary on the uṇādi suffixes composed by the venerable Svāmī Dayānanda Sārasvatī.
And this treatise is completed.
